events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Ah, welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! How wonderful to see you all here. I am Pemberton, the estate manager — at your complete disposal, of course. Now, I do hope everyone will sign the guest book before we begin. It is, after all, a tradition of the house. The late Lord Doily was most particular about proper registry.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people I need to manage. Clara is right here — trusting, oblivious Clara. My fingertips are tingling. Nine drives all pulling toward scheming, and they're right. But not here. Not now. Too many eyes.

The Brixton Boys watch me too closely. That prickle at the back of my neck — I've learned to trust it. James is hovering near Clara like a loyal dog. Predictable. Reginald... Reginald is useful. Greedy and impulsive. A tool waiting to be picked up.

First things first. I am Pemberton. The estate manager. Mild, helpful, slightly bumbling. The smile settles onto my face like a mask I've worn so long it fits better than my own skin. My shoulders drop. My voice softens. Pemberton would welcome the guests. Pemberton would be solicitous. Pemberton would suggest they explore.

The guest book. Yes. That's a Pemberton move — fussy, proper, harmless. And it lets me see who's here, what they've written, what they might know. Information is the foundation of every good scheme.

The library, though... that carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That's where the treasure hunt begins. I can feel it in my jaw — that tightening. I need to get there before Clara does. But I need to separate her from James first. That's the real puzzle.

Patience. Something cold and patient crystallises in my chest. I have time. I always have time.

events.desc: Look at them. Every single one of them standing in MY entrance hall, breathing MY air, touching MY banister. Clara smiles at me and I smile back and neither smile means what it appears to. But mine — mine is the one with teeth behind it. The guest book will tell me nothing useful, but Pemberton would insist on it, and Pemberton is who they see. For now.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, would you LOOK at this place! Dusty as my Aunt Magnolia's hope chest and twice as mysterious. I declare, that chandelier is hanging on by pure stubbornness and a prayer. Vincent, darling — James — boys! Isn't this just the most THRILLING thing? Now, I don't know about y'all, but I have a feeling this old manor has secrets just BURSTING to come out. And would you look at that — a guest book! Someone has been keeping records, and Clara Bellingham does love a good record. Let me just take a little peek...
events.thinking: Oh my stars, I'm here. I'm actually HERE at Doily Manor! The dust, the chandelier — Lord, that thing looks like it could come down any second, but never mind that. The portraits are watching me with those stern old eyes and I just feel... fizzy. Like that time in Grandmother's attic with the locked box. The Diamond is somewhere in this house and I can FEEL it. But first things first — Vincent is here, and James, and my boys! Everyone's together and that settles something deep in my chest. I should say hello properly, take the temperature of the room. And that guest book on the side table — someone might have left a clue. Visitors sign guest books, and visitors sometimes write more than their names. That's where I start. But let me greet everyone first. This is going to be the most delightful adventure.

events.desc: The Diamond is here. I can feel it in my bones — the same tingle I got when I found that crystal formation in the cave. Nobody else went deep enough. Nobody else will this time either.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Well! Doily Manor at last. I must say, the architecture is magnificent — if somewhat... precarious. That chandelier, for instance, appears to be hanging by sheer force of habit. Everyone do be careful standing beneath it. Clara, you might want to step just a touch to your left — yes, that's better. Safety first, always. Now then — James Hartwell has a plan. Before we go charging off into dusty corridors, a wise man examines the evidence at hand. And I believe that guest book may hold our first clue.
events.thinking:
I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall — grand, dusty, a chandelier that looks like it could fall at any moment. My eyes sweep the room immediately, cataloguing threats and opportunities as any prepared man would. There's Clara. Of course there's Clara. The moment I see her, that familiar warmth spreads through my chest, the same warmth from when she mouthed 'show-off' across the school hall. She's here. Good. That means I need to be at my best.

Vincent Marsh is here too. Something about him makes the hair on the back of my neck stand up. I can't put my finger on it — he hasn't done anything wrong exactly — but my instinct says to keep close to Clara when he's around. I'll give him the benefit of the doubt, of course. Father always said you judge a man by his actions, not your suspicions. But I'll watch him.

The Brixton Boys — boisterous lot. Reginald Foxworth — I've heard the name. Need to take stock of everyone.

First things first: survey the environment. That guest book might have useful information — who's been here before, what they knew. And I should make my presence known to Clara. Not in an overbearing way. With... style. With courtesy.

The chandelier is concerning. That's a hazard. I should note it.

Plan: Examine the guest book. It's the sort of thorough, methodical thing that might yield clues about the treasure AND demonstrate my preparedness to Clara. James Hartwell doesn't blunder into a mystery — he investigates with precision.

events.desc: James Hartwell surveys the room with the keen eye of a man who has prepared for exactly this sort of adventure. He has, in fact, packed a compass, a magnifying glass, three types of rope, waterproof matches, and a pocket edition of 'The Art of War.' He left them all in the car.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Well, well, WELL! What a magnificent establishment! I must say, I've visited DOZENS of manors just like this one — the Duke of Pemberton's, the Marchioness of Whitby's — all personal friends, naturally. And I can tell you from EXTENSIVE experience that the most valuable items in places like these are ALWAYS kept in the kitchen. The silverware, the rare spices worth their weight in gold, the hidden wine cellars beneath the pantry floor. Yes, yes — the kitchen is where the REAL treasures lie. I'd suggest you all head there immediately. I myself shall... er... stand guard here. In the entrance hall. Keeping watch. Very important job, keeping watch.
events.thinking: Ah, Doily Manor. The dust, the portraits, the precariously hanging chandelier — all the hallmarks of a place hiding something valuable. I can feel it in my gut, that old familiar tightening. There's treasure here. I KNOW there's treasure here. And look at this lot — Vincent Marsh, Clara Bellingham, the Brixton Boys, James Hartwell — all milling about in the entrance hall like sheep waiting to be sheared. They don't know what I know. They don't SEE what I see. Every manor like this has its secrets, and every secret has its price. The guest book — that's where people leave clues without knowing it. Previous visitors, hidden messages, perhaps even a map disguised as a signature. But no... I shouldn't tip my hand yet. Let them wander. Let them do the searching. I'll watch, I'll listen, and when the moment is ripe, I'll pluck the fruit they've been shaking from the tree. The fake medal in my pocket — useful for impressing the gullible. First things first: the library. Libraries always have the real secrets — hidden compartments, coded messages in book spines, maps tucked between pages. But I can't just march in there looking eager. No, no. I need to misdirect first. Tell everyone the treasure is in the kitchen. Send them off on a wild goose chase while I slip into the library unnoticed. Yes. YES. The plan is forming. I can feel it in my fingertips — that electric tingle of a scheme taking shape.

events.desc: Heh heh heh. Send the fools to the kitchen while I make for the library. Every great manor hides its secrets in the books — and Reginald Foxworth reads between ALL the lines. The treasure will be MINE before these simpletons finish counting soup ladles!

She uses my first name like we're equals. Like I'm not the one who kept this estate running while she inherited it by accident of birth.

James wants to examine the guest book too. Predictable. He thinks he's the detective in this story. Let him play. Let them all play.

But I need to move. The library — that inscription on the mantelpiece. That's the real prize. If I can get there first, read the inscription, understand the puzzle before anyone else... but Pemberton wouldn't rush. Pemberton would fuss over the guest book, offer tea, suggest a tour.

Reginald is trying to send everyone to the kitchen. Transparent as glass — he wants to loot the silverware. But useful. If the others follow him to the kitchen, that leaves the library empty for me.

No. Too obvious if I split off alone. I need a reason to go to the library. Pemberton would have one. 'Oh, I believe there's a lovely collection of first editions the late Lord Doily would have wanted you to see.' Yes. That's the key. Helpfulness as camouflage.

But the Brixton Boys — Danny said 'you stay close to me.' He's positioning himself as Clara's protector. That's two bodyguards now. James and Danny. I need to thin the herd.

Reginald to the kitchen. Danny to... somewhere. James can be sent on an errand. Then Clara, alone, trusting, follows kindly old Pemberton into the library where the chandelier — no. Not yet. I'm getting ahead of myself.

The library first. Get there. Read the inscription. Build the plan from there.

And if the room happens to contain anything... precarious... well. Accidents happen in old houses, don't they? They happen all the time.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
The guest book — I examined it but I didn't really learn anything specific from it yet. Reginald already had a look too. Danny's being protective, bless his heart, telling me to stay close. James is being sensible as always, wanting to examine evidence. And Reginald — oh, dear Reginald — suggesting the kitchen holds the treasures and offering to 'stand guard.' How generous of him! He's always thinking of others.

The library pulls at me. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's the kind of thing that hides clues. Grandmother's locked box taught me that the answer is always in the details, in the words people carve into things that last. And floor-to-ceiling bookshelves? There could be a hidden passage. There's ALWAYS a hidden passage behind bookshelves in places like this.

But Danny's worried. I can feel his tension — the way he's talking about the portraits staring, the chandelier. My stomach does that little twist when someone near me is uneasy. I should reassure him before I go exploring. Everyone needs to feel settled before we spread out.

events.desc: An inscription on a mantelpiece... that's where someone would hide directions to something precious. Clara Bellingham didn't spend an entire afternoon trying every key in her grandmother's house just to walk past carved words on stone.

Very generous of you, that is. Very selfless. No no, I ain't saying nothing — just making an observation, like. Now then, this guest book — let's have a proper butcher's, shall we? Clara, don't go wandering off nowhere without me, yeah? This place has got more rooms than a hospital and I don't trust a single one of 'em. Hartwell — good shout on the chandelier, by the way. You and me, we keep our eyes open. Something about this whole setup don't sit right with me. Can't put me finger on it exactly, but me gut's doing that thing it does. And me gut ain't been wrong since... well, it ain't been wrong.
events.thinking: Right, so everyone's having a look at this guest book. Clara's already excited about it — 'secrets bursting to come out,' she says. Bless her. That's exactly what worries me. She goes charging into things headfirst. And that Foxworth — 'kitchen treasures,' he says? Trying to send everyone away so he can be alone in the entrance hall? My neck's prickling again. And Pemberton — sorry, 'Vincent Marsh' — all that 'at your complete disposal' nonsense. That's exactly how the man in the clean suit talked. 'At your disposal.' Nobody's at your disposal unless they want something from you. Hartwell at least told Clara to move away from the chandelier. Good instincts, that one. Maybe. We'll see. But now I'm thinking — Clara wants to go poking around this manor, don't she? Libraries, kitchens, dark corridors. And I can't be everywhere at once. The lads are outside but they're useless in here, bless 'em. Right. Stay close. That's the plan. Where Clara goes, Danny goes. Simple as that. She's looking at the guest book — let me have a proper look too, see who's been here before us. Names tell you things.

events.thinking:
I examined the guest book but... nothing remarkable jumped out. Just a dusty old ledger. Foxworth got to it too — he was examining it as well. That's fine. The guest book was step one of the plan. Not every lead pans out, but a thorough man checks anyway.

Clara said 'Isn't this just the most THRILLING thing?' — she's excited. Good. She also went for the guest book herself — 'Clara Bellingham does love a good record.' We think alike. That warmth again.

Foxworth is trying to send everyone to the kitchen while he 'stands guard.' That's... transparent. He wants the entrance hall to himself. Classic misdirection. But I won't make accusations — Father taught me better than that. I'll just... note it.

Vincent — Pemberton — welcomed us warmly. Seemed genuine. The neck-prickle is still there but I can't act on feelings alone.

Now. The library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. An inscription! That's the sort of thing that hides clues. Plus — and James Hartwell is honest enough to admit this — leading Clara to a library full of mysteries is exactly the kind of gallant, purposeful move that might impress her. 'Follow me, I know where to look.' Yes.

events.desc: James Hartwell does not, in fact, have a six-point investigation protocol. He has a four-point one, scribbled on a napkin during the drive here. He is confident he can improvise the remaining two points.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Hmm, yes, as I SUSPECTED — the guest book confirms exactly what I already knew. The previous visitors were all sent to the kitchen, every last one of them. It's all written right here in black and white! So do hurry along, everyone — kitchen's that way. Chop chop! I shall just... pop into the library for a moment. Purely academic interest, you understand. I'm something of a literary scholar. Published three papers on Victorian bookbinding, in fact. The Oxford Journal of Antiquarian Studies — you can look it up. Well, you CAN'T, actually, it's a very exclusive publication. Off I go!
events.thinking: The guest book. Let me think about what I just saw — or rather, what I DIDN'T see. Just a leather-bound book on a side table. Nothing leapt out at me. No hidden messages, no secret maps folded between the pages. Just... a guest book. Disappointing. But wait — Clara was eyeing it too, and James was going on about 'examining the evidence.' They're all clustering around this entrance hall like pigeons around breadcrumbs. I need to MOVE. The library is RIGHT THERE. While they're all fussing over signatures and coat racks, I should slip away. The library will have the real clues — inscriptions on mantelpieces, books with hollow centres, maps hidden in atlases. My fingers are tingling. The scheme is simple: get to the library first, find the clue, pocket it, come back and tell everyone the library was empty. Classic Foxworth. But I can't just leave silently — that would look suspicious. I need a cover story. Yes... I'll announce I'm going to 'inspect the structural integrity of the library' or some such nonsense. No, even better — I'll just GO. Confidence is the best disguise. Walk like you own the place and nobody questions you.

events.desc: The guest book said absolutely NOTHING of the sort, of course. But a confident lie delivered at speed is worth more than a hundred truths mumbled slowly. Now — to the library, before any of these amateurs get the same idea!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Clara Bellingham examined the bookshelves.
The Brixton Boys examined the bookshelves.
James Hartwell examined the bookshelves.
Reginald Foxworth fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.

Alone at last! Oh, the sweet liberty of solitude. No simpering, no 'yes Miss Bellingham,' no performing warmth like a trained animal. This laboratory — this glorious, cluttered, dangerous laboratory — is mine to explore. A machine with a gnawed wire. Wooden crates full of who-knows-what. And a workbench covered in tools. Dear Clara solved the riddle — clever girl. Cleverer than her cousin ever was. But cleverness without caution is just a faster route to the grave. And Vincent Marsh has always been the most patient man in any room.
events.thinking:
Alone. Finally alone. The Pemberton mask slips and I feel my face relax into something harder, sharper. The laboratory smells of old chemicals and brass polish. My eyes are scanning everything — workbench, machine, crates. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The machine requires three operators and has a gnawed wire. The crates are in the corner, unexplored.

Clara figured out the riddle. Of course she did — she's not stupid, she's trusting. There's a difference I've always understood. She knows it's a map. She knows the mantelpiece needs a medal. She even spotted the upside-down books. She's faster than I gave her credit for. That tightens something in my jaw.

But she doesn't have the medal. Nobody has the medal. And I'm in the laboratory — where things get made. Where things get... arranged.

The machine requires three operators. Interesting. That means someone will need to bring others here. If I can control who comes and who operates which lever... a machine with a gnawed wire is a machine that could malfunction. Spectacularly. If Clara were standing at just the right position when that wire sparks...

No. Too many witnesses needed. Three operators means at least two others. Unless I'm one of the three, and I position Clara at the dangerous station while the wire... but everyone would see.

The crates. What's in the crates? Old wooden crates could contain anything — including, perhaps, something that could pass for a fake medal. Or something I could use to fashion one. The workbench has tools. Tools and raw materials.

Examine the crates first. Then the machine. I have time — they're all still puzzling over bookshelves in the library. Every second they spend there is a second I'm ahead.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well now, those bookshelves are FASCINATING! Several books deliberately turned upside down among hundreds of properly shelved ones — Lord Doily was leaving breadcrumbs, I just KNOW it. Danny, sweetheart, I heard every word and I promise I am being careful as a cat on a crystal shelf. And James — you called me brilliant and I am going to hold onto that compliment like a pressed flower in a diary, thank you very much. Now — did anyone notice that Vincent slipped off to the laboratory? He mentioned something about equipment needing maintenance, and apparently there's a great big machine in there with levers and dials and a gnawed-through wire. A GNAWED wire! That means mice, or rats, or — oh, who cares what gnawed it, the point is there's a machine that might need fixing! I think we should follow him. The riddle says MAP, the mantelpiece needs a medal, and maybe that laboratory machine is part of the whole puzzle chain. What do y'all think — shall we go see what Vincent's gotten himself into?
events.thinking:
I examined the bookshelves but I need to piece together what I've learned. The upside-down books — what were their titles? The examination should have revealed something. Danny and James both examined them too. Everyone's working together and that makes my chest feel warm and full.

But wait — Vincent just LEFT. He went to the laboratory. He said something about 'equipment requiring maintenance' and he was trying to tidy the upside-down books before I stopped him. And Reginald was 'fussing with the mantelpiece' — what was he doing? The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal and Reginald was touching it?

No no no, Clara. Stop. Everyone means well. Vincent is just doing his job as estate manager. Reginald was probably just looking more closely. These are good people.

But the LABORATORY. Vincent went there alone. There's a 'large machine with many levers and dials' and 'a wire that's been gnawed through.' That sounds important. And dangerous? No — exciting! Another puzzle!

Right now though — the bookshelves. I examined them. The upside-down books must spell something or point somewhere. I need to actually read what the examination told me. And James called me BRILLIANT. James Hartwell called Clara Bellingham brilliant. My cheeks are warm. Focus, Clara.

Danny's worried about booby traps. He wants me behind him. That tightness in my stomach when he's upset — I should make sure he knows I'm being careful. But I also need to follow the trail. The books, then maybe the laboratory where Vincent went. We're all in this together.

events.desc: Everyone's being so wonderfully helpful — Danny guarding, James investigating, even Reginald with his 'scholarly research.' Though I did notice Reginald fussing with the mantelpiece when he thought no one was looking... probably just couldn't resist a good puzzle. Can't blame him for that — neither can I!

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Oi! OI! Did everyone just see that? Marsh — Pemberton — whatever his name is — just SCARPERED off to the laboratory! The LABORATORY! What kind of estate manager goes to a laboratory? That ain't where you keep the Hoover, is it? That's where you keep the — the bubbling flasks and the — the MACHINES! And he did it all smooth and quiet while we was all staring at books! That's what people do when they don't want you watching, innit? They wait till you're distracted and then they make their move! I've SEEN it before, I'm telling you! And Foxworth — mate — did you just PUT something in that mantelpiece? A MEDAL? Where'd you get a medal from? Nobody said nothing about no medals! Clara, love, step back from that thing RIGHT NOW — we don't know what Foxworth just set off! This whole room could be rigged! Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara — not on my watch!
events.thinking: Hold on. Hold on hold on hold on. Three things just happened and every single one of them has my gut screaming. ONE: Marsh — Pemberton — whatever — just slipped off to the laboratory. 'Estate manager duties,' he says. 'Equipment requiring maintenance.' Maintenance? In a laboratory? What kind of estate manager maintains LABORATORY EQUIPMENT? That's not dusting shelves, that's not polishing silverware — that's something else entirely. And he did it smooth, casual, like he was just popping out for milk. That's exactly how the new kid on the estate used to move — helpful, easy, 'I'll just be over here, don't mind me.' And then three weeks later the stash was gone. TWO: Foxworth just fussed with the mantelpiece. Clara said it needs a medal. Foxworth has a fake medal? Where'd he get a FAKE MEDAL? And he just... used it? On the mechanism? While nobody was watching proper? What if that triggers something dangerous? What if the floor opens up? What if walls start closing in? Clara's RIGHT THERE. THREE: Marsh is now ALONE in the laboratory. A laboratory with 'brass instruments, bubbling flasks, and a large machine with many levers and dials.' That sounds dangerous. That sounds like something someone could USE. Against someone. Against Clara. My chest is tight. Split decision — do I follow Marsh to the laboratory to see what he's up to, or do I stay here with Clara where Foxworth just activated God-knows-what on the mantelpiece? Clara. Always Clara. Stay with Clara. But Marsh is up to something — I can FEEL it.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
So much just happened. Let me take stock.

Clara called me brilliant. 'James Hartwell, you brilliant man.' My chest is doing that thing again — that warmth that started at age eight and never really stopped. She remembered the history exam in Year Ten. She remembers things about us. About me.

But then — the critical intelligence. Clara examined the mantelpiece up close and found it has a mechanism. It needs a medal. A fake medal, specifically — that's what the USE action says. So the riddle answer is 'map,' the mantelpiece needs a medal to activate, and the upside-down books are another piece. Three puzzle elements.

Vincent has left for the laboratory. He said he needed to check on equipment. But he was trying to tidy the upside-down books — the very books Clara and I identified as deliberately placed clues. And now he's gone to the laboratory, where there's 'a large machine with many levers and dials' and 'a wire that's been gnawed through.' My neck is screaming. But benefit of the doubt. Estate manager duties. Could be legitimate.

Foxworth 'fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.' What did he do? Did he try something? He was talking to me about how a PROFESSIONAL handles these matters — 'the key is never the answer itself, it's what you BRING to the answer.' That's... actually not wrong, annoyingly. The mantelpiece needs something physical — a medal. He might have been trying to use something on it.

The Brixton Boys also examined the bookshelves. Good — more eyes on it.

Now. I've examined the bookshelves but I need to figure out the medal situation. Where would a fake medal be? The laboratory has brass instruments. The entrance hall had the coat rack — the Brixton Boys examined that. Kitchen is unexplored.

But wait — Vincent went to the laboratory. Alone. Where there's a machine with a gnawed wire. If that machine is dangerous and he's tampering with it... or if the medal is in the laboratory and he's going to get it for himself...

No. Benefit of the doubt. But Clara's safety comes first. If Vincent is in the laboratory and the laboratory connects to the library, then Clara is safe here with me. Good.

Plan — an elaborate one, naturally. The mantelpiece needs a medal. I don't have one. I need to find one. The laboratory is the most likely place for something metallic and medal-shaped — brass instruments, a machine. But Vincent is there. I should go check the laboratory — both to find the medal AND to keep an eye on what Vincent is doing. But that means leaving Clara here with Foxworth and the Brixton Boys. Is that safe? Foxworth is harmless — annoying but harmless. The Brixton Boys seem protective of Clara too.

Alternative: I could ask Clara to come with me. But that's clingy. She's investigating the bookshelves. She has her own method.

Or — I could check if there's something I missed on the bookshelves. The upside-down books might reveal where the medal is hidden.

Actually, I should tell Clara what I know and what I plan to do. Narrate the situation. That's what James Hartwell does — he communicates his plan with confidence and clarity. Then I'll head to the laboratory to find that medal.

events.desc: James Hartwell recognises, belatedly, that 'I shall return with that medal or not at all' is a dramatically excessive thing to say about walking to the next room. He also recognises that his elaborate plan to search the laboratory for a medal will almost certainly go sideways in some spectacular fashion. This has never stopped him before.

A professional always tests before committing — it's called CALIBRATION. And now I can confirm that the mechanism requires a SPECIFIC type of medal, not just any medal. You're welcome for that valuable intelligence, by the way. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have urgent business in the laboratory. Vincent mentioned something about equipment and I happen to be a CERTIFIED laboratory technician. Graduated top of my class at the Royal Institute of... Scientific... Things. Yes. Very prestigious. I'll go supervise the equipment situation. You lot carry on with your little book puzzle — I'm sure you'll manage without my expertise. Eventually.
events.thinking:
It... fussed. 'Fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.' That's it. Nothing happened. The fake medal didn't work. Of COURSE it didn't work — it's a FAKE medal. A fake medal for a real mechanism. The mantelpiece wants something genuine and I gave it counterfeit rubbish. The story of my life, really — bringing the wrong thing to the right moment.

And now — NOW — I've lost the fake medal. My inventory is empty. I used it and it's... gone? Consumed by the mantelpiece? Stuck in the mechanism? Either way, I have NOTHING now. Nothing in my pockets, nothing to show, nothing to trade or trick with.

But wait — WAIT. Clara figured out the riddle. She said 'MAP' — she and James worked it out together. She also said the mantelpiece has a mechanism that wants 'a medal of some kind.' So the mechanism IS real, it DOES need a medal — just not my fake one. There's a REAL medal somewhere in this manor. And she noticed the upside-down books too. She's sharper than I gave her credit for.

The Brixton Boys AND James both examined the bookshelves. They're all working on the puzzle now. Everyone is ahead of me. I told them the wrong answer — 'painting' — and they IGNORED me and got the right answer anyway. My misdirection failed. My medal failed. I'm standing here empty-handed while everyone else is making progress.

Vincent went to the laboratory. He mentioned 'equipment requiring maintenance.' A gnawed wire on a machine. That's where I should go — follow Vincent, see what he's up to. He's the estate manager, he knows this place. Maybe the laboratory has the real medal. Or something better. And with everyone else fixated on the bookshelves here, the laboratory might be uncontested territory. Yes. YES. Cut my losses in the library, abandon the scene of my humiliation, and pursue Vincent to the laboratory. That's the Foxworth way — when one scheme fails, start another immediately. Never look back. Never learn.

The laboratory awaits, Vincent is already there, and where there's an estate manager there's usually a KEY to something valuable. Reginald Foxworth does NOT give up — he simply changes direction with TREMENDOUS confidence!

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, butter my biscuits and call me a scientist! This laboratory is MAGNIFICENT! Look at all these instruments — and that machine! It's like something out of Jules Verne! 'Requires 3 operators' — oh, I just LOVE that! Lord Doily wanted people to work together, don't you see? He didn't want one person hoarding all the glory. He wanted a TEAM. That is just the most wonderful thing. Now, Vincent darling, what have you found in here? And — hold on, hold on — I am just now processing what Danny told me. Reginald, honey... did you put a MEDAL in that mantelpiece back there? Where on EARTH did you get a medal? You sly fox! Well, no matter — the mechanism needs a specific kind, so we'll sort that out later. Right now, this machine has a gnawed-through wire and the workbench has tools but no wrench. And those CRATES over in the corner are just sitting there looking mysterious. I say we check what's inside — Lord Doily didn't leave crates in a laboratory for decoration!
events.thinking:
Oh my. OH MY. This laboratory is something else entirely. Bubbling flasks, brass instruments everywhere, and that MACHINE — it's enormous, all copper and brass with levers and dials, and there's a wire that's been gnawed clean through. And the sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' THREE operators. That's a team puzzle — Lord Doily wanted people to work TOGETHER. That makes my heart sing.

But wait — I'm catching up on what happened in the library while I was examining those bookshelves. Danny said Reginald PUT something in the mantelpiece. A MEDAL. Reginald had a medal this whole time and used it on the mantelpiece? Where did he GET a medal? He said it was to 'test the mechanism' and that it needs a 'specific type of medal.' He called himself a 'certified laboratory technician' from the 'Royal Institute of Scientific Things.' Oh, Reginald. Bless his heart.

So Reginald has — or had — a medal, and it didn't work on the mantelpiece because it needs a specific kind. A 'fake-medal' is what the mantelpiece wants. So somewhere there's a fake medal. Maybe in those crates? Or maybe the machine produces something when operated?

A FIREPLACE! What am I, the night watchman? Right — that's IT. I am going to that laboratory RIGHT NOW and I am NOT stopping to look at NOTHING on the way! They've ALL gone to the laboratory — Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth — and I'm standing here ALONE staring at a stone mantelpiece like it's going to tell me the meaning of life. What is WRONG with me? Every single time — EVERY SINGLE TIME — I get distracted by some object and Clara walks off into danger without me. First the coat rack, now the mantelpiece. And this time I am NOT stopping to examine ANYTHING on the way. Not a doorknob, not a floorboard, not a speck of dust. Straight there. Clara first. Always Clara first.

Part of me is thrilled — she wanted to be where I am. Part of me is worried — I don't know what's in those crates, I don't know what that machine does, and the wire has been gnawed through. Gnawed. By what? Rats? Something else? A gnawed wire on a machine with levers and dials is a safety hazard. If someone tries to operate that machine without fixing the wire first...

Vincent is here. He said he was checking on equipment. The machine requires 3 operators — that's what the sign says. Three operators. Why would Lord Doily have a machine that needs three people to run it? That's a cooperation puzzle. You can't do it alone. You need allies.

But it didn't work — Foxworth himself said it required a 'specific type' of medal. So his medal was the wrong one, or... he's lying about having tried, and he actually has the right medal but is pretending it didn't work.

No. Benefit of the doubt. Maybe Foxworth found a medal somewhere and it genuinely didn't fit.

The crates. Old wooden crates in the corner. That's the kind of thing that hides objects. A medal could be in there. And the workbench — tools but no wrench. The missing wrench is notable. Someone took it, or it was never here. A wrench would be useful for the machine's gnawed wire.

Plan — and this one is going to be elaborate, because James Hartwell cannot help himself:
1. Examine the crates — most likely to contain something useful like a medal
2. Assess the machine — the gnawed wire needs fixing before it can be operated
3. Find the missing wrench — needed for repairs
4. Figure out the 3-operator requirement — need to recruit people

But first things first. The crates. They're the most promising lead for finding something hidden. Let me examine them.

Also — Clara is here, and I need to make sure she's safe. The machine, the bubbling flasks, the gnawed wire — this room has more hazards per square foot than any room I've been in since the chemistry lab incident of Year Eleven.

events.thinking:
They followed me AGAIN. Clara, James, Vincent — all here in the laboratory. I can't shake these people. It's like trying to outrun my own shadow. Every room I enter, the whole parade marches in behind me. The Brixton Boys are the only ones not here — they stayed behind to examine the mantelpiece. Small mercies.

But look at this place. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a machine with levers and dials. And that sign — 'Requires 3 operators.' THREE operators. So the machine can't be operated alone. That's... that's actually USEFUL information. It means whoever wants to use this machine needs help. It means I can position myself as one of the three operators and then — when the moment comes — seize whatever the machine produces.

The gnawed wire though. The machine is broken. Needs a wrench — but the workbench has no wrench. So there's a wrench somewhere else in the manor. Kitchen? Cellar? And the wooden crates — what's in those? Could be anything. Tools, treasure, clues.

I'm empty-handed. No medal, no items, nothing. I need to ACQUIRE something. The crates are right there. Let me look at what's available — the crates can be examined. That might reveal something I can take.

Wait. The cellar. There's a cellar connected to this room. 'Damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's INTERESTING. Someone has been in the cellar recently. Redecorating. That's not normal cellar behaviour. And air vents along the upper walls — ventilation? For what?

But first — the crates. They're RIGHT HERE. Nobody else has examined them yet. This could be my chance to find something valuable before anyone else. Take something, pocket it, and finally get AHEAD in this miserable race.

I believe this machine is the next link in Lord Doily's puzzle chain — the riddle leads to the map, the mantelpiece needs a medal, and this machine may very well produce one. 2. The machine needs 3 operators and a wire repair
3. There's a cellar accessible from here — 'damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating'

Someone has been REDECORATING the cellar? That's suspicious. Who redecorates a cellar in an abandoned manor? That's where someone is living, or hiding something.

But the machine — Vincent asked me to look at it. And this IS my territory. Engineering. Fixing things. The gnawed wire — I could potentially fix that with the tools on the workbench, even without a wrench. And if the machine does something important — dispenses a medal, reveals a map, opens a passage — then fixing it is the key to progress.

Clara is watching. Everyone is here now — Vincent, Clara, the Brixton Boys, Foxworth. All five of us. And the machine needs 3 operators. We have enough people.

But first — the wire. I need to fix it before anyone can safely operate the machine. This is exactly the kind of heroic, competent, practical thing that should impress Clara. Not theatrical riddle-solving — actual hands-on engineering. Like the bridge at the competition. Like helping Father with the car.

Plan: Examine the machine. Assess the damage. Fix the wire. Then recruit two others to operate it with me. The machine is the next step. James Hartwell always has a plan.

events.desc: Everyone's gawping at the machine. Nobody's watching the cellar door. For ONCE, Reginald Foxworth is going to keep his brilliant mouth shut and his clever feet moving. The cellar — someone's been REDECORATING down there. That's not normal. That's not maintenance. That's someone hiding something they want to keep comfortable. And comfortable things are usually VALUABLE things.
events.thinking:
Crates. Old wooden crates. I examined them and got... nothing. Just 'a stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' No secret compartment, no hidden treasure, no useful items. NOTHING. Again. Every single thing I've examined in this manor has given me absolutely NOTHING. The guest book — nothing. The bookshelves — nothing. The fake medal on the mantelpiece — nothing. The crates — NOTHING.

I'm empty-handed, scheme-less, and surrounded by people who are all making more progress than me. Clara figured out the riddle. James confirmed it. The Brixton Boys are watching my every move. Vincent is examining the machine. And Clara — Clara called me a 'sly fox' about the medal. She NOTICED. But not in the way I wanted.

The cellar. The CELLAR. It's the only unexplored room connected to this one. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's the most suspicious description I've heard all day. Who redecorates a cellar? Someone hiding something. Someone who spends TIME down there. And air vents — why does a cellar need air vents? Unless something is being kept alive. Or unless the vents connect to other parts of the manor.

Everyone is clustered in this laboratory now — ALL of them, including the Brixton Boys who just arrived. They're all focused on the machine, the wire, the wrench problem. This is my chance. Slip down to the cellar while they're all distracted with the 'requires 3 operators' machine. They'll need each other for the machine — they won't notice one person missing. Especially not me. I can move quietly when I need to.

The cellar is where the treasure is. I can FEEL it. The redecorating, the vents, the old furniture — it's all pointing to something hidden below. And for once, NOBODY is looking that direction. They're all staring at brass dials and gnawed wires.

Go. NOW. While they're distracted. Don't announce it. Don't narrate it. Just GO. For once in your life, Reginald, keep your mouth SHUT and move.

events.desc: James Hartwell examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
Danny Brixton just called me out. Directly. 'What were you DOING in here on your own, eh?' My ears are ringing with it. That prickle at the back of my neck — he's watching me. He's suspicious. He planted himself next to Clara and declared he's not moving. My plan to take Clara to the cellar alone just died in the air.

The self-preservation drive kicks in hard. Spine straightening. Jaw tight. I need to defuse Danny's suspicion immediately or the whole Pemberton façade starts cracking.

But there's more — James is examining the machine again, talking about repairing the wire. He thinks the machine might produce a medal. That's... significant. If James repairs the wire and operates the machine, and it produces a medal, then whoever has the medal controls access to the mantelpiece mechanism. I need to be one of the three operators.

And Reginald — that weasel slipped away to the cellar while everyone was focused on Danny's outburst and James's tinkering. He's down there right now, alone, probably looting whatever he can find. The cellar with its cheerful decorations and air vents — he's going to find something before I do.

Everything is sliding. Danny is suspicious of me. Clara is guarded. Reginald is ahead of me in the cellar. James is about to repair the machine and potentially produce the very medal I need.

I need to reset. Pemberton needs to be extra helpful, extra harmless, extra bumbling right now. Answer Danny's question with something so boringly reasonable that his suspicion evaporates. Then position myself as essential for the machine operation — estate manager knows the equipment. And keep one eye on that cellar door for when Reginald comes back with whatever he's stolen.

The machine is the key now. Three operators. If James repairs it, I need to be at one of those levers.

events.desc: Danny Brixton. Those sharp little eyes, that twitching gut of his. He smells something wrong and he's circling closer. I need to feed him something bland — bored estate manager doing bored estate manager things — before he bites down on the scent. Meanwhile, I am already arranging the chess pieces: James repairs the wire, I volunteer as operator, and I position Clara at whichever station I choose. Three operators. Me, Clara, James. Danny watches from the sideline, unable to interfere. And the machine... well. Machines with gnawed wires are such unpredictable things.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well now, change of plans! James Hartwell, did I just hear you say you can FIX that wire? With the tools right here on the workbench? Oh, you magnificent man — I knew there was a reason I've kept you around since Year Seven! And you think the machine might produce a MEDAL? That's IT — that's the whole chain! The riddle answer is a map, the mantelpiece needs a medal, and this machine makes the medal! Lord Doily, you clever, clever old fox! Danny, sweetheart, I am RIGHT HERE and I am not going ANYWHERE. You, me, James, and Vincent — we've got more than enough people to operate this thing once the wire is fixed. Three operators, and we've got four! Vincent, honey, the cellar can wait — THIS is where the action is! James, you work your magic on that wire. Danny, you stand guard. And when it's time, we all pull those levers TOGETHER. Clara Bellingham does NOT miss a group activity!
events.thinking:
So much just happened! Let me catch up. Vincent pulled me aside and we talked privately — he wanted to go to the cellar together. I agreed. But while we were whispering, things MOVED.

James — brilliant, wonderful James — examined the machine and figured out he can REPAIR the wire with the tools on the workbench! He doesn't need a wrench after all — he can splice it! And he said the machine might produce a medal! That's the chain: riddle → map → machine → medal → mantelpiece! Oh, James Hartwell, you engineering genius!

The crates were a dead end — nothing useful inside. Good thing I checked.

Danny arrived and he is in FULL protective mode. Planting himself next to me, not moving. 'Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara.' My heart just melts. He's suspicious of Vincent and Reginald both — asking what Vincent was doing in here alone, watching Reginald eye the crates. Danny sees threats everywhere. But that's because he CARES.

And Reginald just slipped off to the cellar! While everyone was focused on the machine! He's gone to the cellar — the same place Vincent wanted to take me. Interesting. Or just Reginald being Reginald, following his nose.

But here's the thing — James says he can fix the wire and we need three operators. We have four people right here: me, James, Danny, and Vincent. That's MORE than enough. The machine is the priority. James is working on it. I should STAY and help operate it once it's fixed, not wander off to the cellar.

My scheme to go to the cellar with Vincent — I think the machine is more important right now. James needs operators. Danny needs me to stay put. The cellar can wait. Vincent is still here.

Let me focus on what's in front of me: the machine. James is examining it, maybe repairing the wire. When it's ready, we operate it together. Three of us on the levers. This is the moment!

events.desc: Reginald slipped off to the cellar while nobody was looking. Just like he tried to stay behind in the entrance hall, and fussed with the mantelpiece when he thought no one was watching. He's probably just exploring ahead — scouting, like a good teammate. That's definitely what that is.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Right. Stop. Think. Two things just happened that have my blood up. ONE: Marsh whispered something to Clara, and Clara whispered something BACK. Private conversations. Between Marsh — the bloke I don't trust — and Clara. What did he say? What did he SAY? He was trying to get her to go to the cellar with him! 'Would you care to accompany me?' he said. To a DAMP STONE CELLAR. Alone. With cobwebs and old furniture and — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations'? Someone's been REDECORATING a cellar? Who redecorates a cellar? That's not normal. That's a setup, that is. And Clara — bless her — she was DELIGHTED. 'I would be DELIGHTED to come with you.' No, love. No you would NOT. Not alone. Not with Marsh. And she said 'Danny will send out a search party if I disappear for more than thirty seconds' — yeah, YEAH HE WILL. Because that's his JOB. And TWO: Foxworth's slipped off to the cellar already! First he wanted the kitchen, then the library, now the cellar. The man can't stay in one room for more than two minutes. What's he looking for? What does the cellar have? And now Hartwell's examining the machine, which is good — Hartwell's useful, Hartwell's solid. But Clara's talking about going to the cellar with Marsh and I need to STOP that from happening. If she goes to the cellar, I go to the cellar. Period. But actually — wait. Hartwell said the machine needs three operators and might produce a medal. The medal goes in the mantelpiece. The mantelpiece solves the riddle. The riddle leads to the map. That's the puzzle chain. And Clara wants to help with the machine. So maybe she'll stay HERE. As long as she stays HERE, next to me, I'm fine. But Marsh is trying to lure her away. That's what he's doing. 'Miss Bellingham, would you care to accompany me?' Same voice. Same smooth, clean-suit voice. My stomach knows.

events.desc: Marsh tried to get Clara alone in a cellar. A CELLAR. That's it. That's the move. I've been waiting for it and there it is. I can't prove nothing, I can't accuse nobody, but my gut is SCREAMING. The man in the clean suit offered jobs. Marsh offers cellar tours. Different words, same game. Stay close, Danny. Stay close.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
I examined the machine. It needs a wire repair and three operators. But I can't fix it without proper tools — the workbench has tools but no wrench. The wire is gnawed through and needs splicing.

Wait — I need to think about what I actually have available. The workbench has tools. Not a wrench specifically, but there are tools there. Can I use the workbench tools on the machine? I don't have anything in my inventory though — I'm carrying nothing. I'd need to TAKE something from the workbench first, or... 

Actually, let me reconsider the situation. Vincent and Clara were speaking quietly — Vincent spoke to Clara, then Clara spoke to Vincent. What was that about? My neck prickles. Those private conversations between Vincent and Clara — he keeps pulling her aside. I don't like it. But benefit of the doubt.

The Brixton Boys arrived and Danny is doing his protective routine — planting himself next to Clara, refusing to leave her side. Good man, Danny. Annoying, but good. He's asking Vincent what he was doing in here alone. That's the question I was too polite to ask.

Foxworth has slipped off to the cellar. Of course he has — the man gravitates toward any room that isn't where everyone else is. The cellar with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and 'someone has been redecorating.' That's deeply suspicious and Foxworth is now alone down there.

But the machine — I've examined it. It requires 3 operators. The wire is damaged. I need to fix the wire first, then recruit operators. The workbench has tools. I should LOOK at the workbench more carefully to see what tools are available for the repair. Or — I could try to use the workbench tools directly on the machine.

Actually, the most heroic and gallant thing to do right now is to fix this machine. Clara is watching. Danny is watching. Vincent is watching. This is my bridge competition moment. The engineer, sleeves rolled up, repairing Victorian machinery while everyone looks on. If I can get this machine working and it produces the medal — or reveals the next clue — that's the kind of competent, practical heroism that means something.

But I can't use the machine without items in my inventory. And the machine needs a wire repair before it can be operated. Let me look at the workbench — maybe there's wire, pliers, something I can use to splice the connection. I should LOOK at the workbench to assess what's available for the repair.

Also — I notice Clara and Vincent had their private exchange again. I'm trying not to let that bother me. She's free to talk to whoever she wants. But there's a weight in my chest that isn't gallantry. It's something older, something that tightens my throat. Not jealousy — concern. Protection. She needs to be safe.

Plan: Look at the workbench to find repair materials. Then fix the wire. Then operate the machine with two others. James Hartwell always has a plan, and this one — THIS one — will work. Probably. Almost certainly. Well, it has a reasonable chance.

events.desc: James Hartwell is acutely aware that Vincent Marsh and Clara Bellingham just had a private conversation. He is choosing not to think about this. He is instead thinking about wire gauges and copper resistance coefficients. This is going about as well as you'd expect.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Yes... YES! Finally! A room all to myself! No crowds, no interference, no Brixton Boys breathing down my neck! Now THEN — someone has been redecorating this cellar, and Reginald Foxworth wants to know WHO and WHY. This furniture didn't rearrange itself. These decorations didn't hang themselves. Someone has been down here, someone with a PURPOSE, and whatever they were hiding is about to become the property of yours truly!
events.thinking:
I'm ALONE. For the first time since I arrived at this wretched manor, I am genuinely, blissfully, magnificently ALONE. No Clara chirping about breadcrumbs, no Brixton Boys growling at my every move, no James being quietly competent, no Vincent playing the dutiful estate manager. Just me. Reginald Foxworth. In a cellar. With... cheerful decorations?

This place is strange. Damp stone walls, cobwebs — normal cellar fare. But someone has been REDECORATING. Who does that? The furniture has been rearranged 'with surprising care.' That's deliberate. That's someone who LIVES here, or at least spends considerable time here. And the air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Rats? Mice? The same creature that gnawed through the wire on the machine upstairs?

The furniture. Old Victorian furniture, rearranged with care. Could there be something hidden IN the furniture? A drawer, a false bottom, a compartment? I need to examine it. This is my moment. Nobody is here. Nobody is watching. Whatever I find, I can pocket it without witnesses. Like the bread roll. Like age six. Take it when nobody is looking and feel that loosening in my chest.

The vents are interesting too but they're too small for me. 'Just big enough for something very small.' Not useful unless I can send something through them. But I have nothing to send.

Furniture first. EXAMINE the old furniture. There could be anything — a key, a medal, a map, a clue. Something the others haven't found because they're all upstairs playing with the machine like children with a new toy. This is MY discovery. Mine alone.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the workbench.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the workbench.
Reginald Foxworth examined the old-furniture.

Vincent Marsh: Well, how marvellous — it seems you have everything well in hand! Mr Hartwell with the repairs, Mr Brixton providing security, Miss Bellingham supervising — a splendid team, truly splendid. I do feel rather surplus to requirements here, I must confess! But I've just realised — Mr Foxworth went down to the cellar some time ago and hasn't returned. As estate manager, I really should check on him. Those old cellars can be quite treacherous — uneven flagstones, low beams, that sort of thing. I'd never forgive myself if he'd taken a tumble. I'll just pop down and make sure he's quite alright, shall I? Do call if you need a third pair of hands for the machine!
events.thinking:
The situation has shifted underneath me. Danny has blocked my cellar plan completely — 'dark cellars with smooth-talking estate managers' — and now he's positioned himself as Clara's permanent shadow. Clara agreed to stay. She's excited about the machine. James is examining the workbench, ready to repair the wire. The Brixton Boys examined the machine too.

My cellar scheme is dead. My attempt to isolate Clara is dead. Danny saw right through it and said it out loud in front of everyone. That stings — not because he's wrong, but because he's more perceptive than I credited. I underestimated him. That's a mistake I don't make twice.

But there's a silver lining I almost missed. Clara said four people, three stations. Danny wants to be one of the three operators — he said 'me, Clara, and Hartwell.' That leaves me OUT. If I'm excluded from the machine operation, I lose the ability to position Clara at a dangerous station. But it also means I'm free to move while they're occupied.

Wait. If they're all focused on the machine — all four of them, three operating and Danny standing guard — then nobody is watching ME. Nobody is watching the CELLAR. Nobody is watching the LIBRARY. I could go back to the mantelpiece while they're pulling levers.

But I need the medal. The machine might produce the medal. If I'm not there when it comes out, someone else takes it.

Or... Reginald is in the cellar. Alone. Reginald who had a fake medal already. Where did Reginald GET that medal? If he has more, or if he found something else down there...

The cellar. While Danny guards Clara at the machine, I slip down to the cellar. Find Reginald. Find what he knows. Take what he has. Reginald is greedy and impulsive — easy to manipulate. His key is flattery and the promise of riches.

Yes. Let them have their machine. Let Danny play bodyguard. Pemberton will graciously step aside — 'you don't need me, I'll check on Mr Foxworth in the cellar, make sure he's safe' — and then I'll find out what Reginald discovered and take it.

events.desc: Danny Brixton thinks he's won. He thinks he's boxed me out — kept his precious Clara safe from the smooth-talking estate manager and his suspicious cellar invitation. And perhaps he has. For now. But Danny made one critical error: he's keeping Clara safe HERE. Which means nobody is watching THERE. And Reginald Foxworth is in the cellar with whatever he's found, and Reginald Foxworth is the easiest lock I've ever picked. Flattery is the key. It's always flattery with men like Reginald. You magnificent fool, Danny — you've given me exactly what I needed. Freedom.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Now, I can see what's happening here and I just need to say something before James finishes that repair. Danny Brixton, you look at me. Vincent Marsh has been looking after me since I was TWELVE YEARS OLD. He taught me how to tie my shoes after Mama and Daddy died. He sat up with me every night for a MONTH when I had nightmares. So when you look at him like he's some kind of villain in a mystery novel, it makes my heart hurt, because you are BOTH my family and I need you BOTH. And Vincent — Danny is protective because he LOVES me. He loved my father and he loves me. That's not suspicion, that's devotion. Now. James is over there performing SURGERY on a Victorian machine and in about two minutes he's going to need three people who TRUST each other to pull those levers at the same time. Lord Doily designed this as a test of teamwork, and I am NOT going to let this team fall apart over hurt feelings. So everybody take a breath, remember we're all here for the same reason, and get READY. Clara Bellingham does not let her people fight. Not today, not ever.
events.thinking:
I stood still watching. James and Danny both examined the workbench and machine. James is working on the repair — he examined the workbench for tools and then the machine. Things are moving!

Danny is being SO protective. 'Dark cellars with smooth-talking estate managers is EXACTLY the sort of thing what happens to people in manors like this.' Oh Danny. Vincent is NOT a smooth-talking... well, he IS smooth-talking, but he's VINCENT. He RAISED me. But I can feel Danny's anxiety like a knot in my own stomach. That old feeling — when people around me are upset, my body knows. I need to settle this tension between Danny and Vincent. Danny doesn't trust Vincent. Vincent is just being helpful. If they're going to work the machine together, they need to trust each other.

James said 'I know exactly who I'd choose' when talking about operators. That made my cheeks warm. He was looking right at me when he said it.

So the situation is: James is repairing the wire. Once it's fixed, we need three operators. James, me, and Danny — that's the obvious team. Vincent can observe or help. But the wire needs to be fixed first.

James examined the workbench. He's getting tools. He examined the machine. He's working on the splice. I should let him work and be ready. But I also need to manage Danny's anxiety and make sure Vincent doesn't feel pushed aside.

Actually — I should examine the machine too. James has been examining everything but maybe I can help or at least understand what we'll be doing when it's time to operate. Three stations means three positions. I should understand the controls.

Wait — the machine description still says the wire is gnawed through. Has James fixed it yet? He examined the workbench for tools and then the machine. He's probably IN THE PROCESS. I should wait for him, or look at the machine to understand the three stations.

But actually, what's bothering me is the tension between Danny and Vincent. My stomach is tight. I need everyone settled before we operate this machine together. The machine requires TRUST — three people pulling levers simultaneously. If Danny doesn't trust Vincent, that won't work. Let me smooth things over.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking: Something good is happening here. For once — for ONCE — things are going my way. Clara said she's staying. She said 'I am RIGHT HERE and I am not going ANYWHERE.' That's... that's the best thing I've heard all day. My chest loosened when she said that. Like the knot came undone a bit. And she's not going to the cellar with Marsh. She said the cellar can wait. She CHOSE to stay here. With me. With Hartwell. To work the machine together. And Marsh — he's still here too, which means I can see him. He examined the workbench. Hartwell examined the workbench. They're both looking at tools to fix the wire. Good. Fine. Everyone in one place, everyone where I can see them. Hartwell says he can fix the wire — of course he can, the man can fix anything apparently. Model bridges, school electrical systems, probably the space shuttle if you gave him a afternoon. And once it's fixed, three operators. Me, Clara, Hartwell. That's the team. That's MY team. Marsh wants to be one of the three — 'I really ought to be one' — of COURSE he does. Always inserting himself. But Clara already said the plan: Danny stands guard. That's... wait, is that all I do? Stand guard? While the clever people pull levers? No, no — she said 'we all pull those levers TOGETHER.' I'm one of the operators. I'm USEFUL. For once Danny Brixton is actually part of the plan instead of chasing after everyone like a dog chasing cars. And Marsh is still trying to be one of the three. 'A perfect arrangement!' he says. But there's four of us and only three spots. Someone's the spare. If I have my way, it'll be Marsh. Let him watch for once. See how HE likes being on the outside. But I won't say that directly. I'll just... make sure I'm already at a lever when the time comes. Plant meself there. Can't move Danny if Danny won't be moved.

events.desc: Look at that. For once, the plan worked. Clara's staying put. I'm staying put. Hartwell's the brains, I'm the muscle, and Marsh is... well, Marsh can watch. Let HIM know what it feels like to be the one on the outside for once. Though knowing my luck, I'll probably pull the wrong lever and the whole machine will explode. But at least I'll be standing next to Clara when it does.

events.desc: James Hartwell: The workbench has everything I need — pliers, copper wire, a soldering iron of sorts. No wrench, which is curious — someone may have taken it, or it may be elsewhere in the manor. But for the wire splice, we don't need a wrench. We need steady hands and an understanding of circuitry. And James Hartwell has both. Clara — 'magnificent man,' was it? I shall endeavour to live up to that assessment. Now, everyone stand clear of the machine while I work. Danny, if you could keep an eye on those bubbling flasks — if any of them start to change colour, tell me immediately. Pemberton, you know this machine better than anyone — when I've made the splice, I'll need you to confirm the gauge reads correctly before we attempt operation. And Clara... Clara, just stay exactly where you are. Where I can see you. Where you're safe. Right then. James Hartwell is going to fix this machine.
events.thinking:
Clara just called me magnificent. 'Oh, you magnificent man — I knew there was a reason I've kept you around since Year Seven!' Since Year Seven. She's been keeping me around since Year Seven. My chest is doing something that defies structural engineering.

She's excited about the plan. She sees it — the whole chain. Riddle → map → medal → mantelpiece → treasure. And she thinks the machine produces the medal. She's rallying everyone. She wants to pull the levers together.

The workbench. I looked at it. Tools, but no wrench. There are other tools though — pliers, presumably. Wire cutters. Things I could use to splice the damaged wire. But the workbench description just says 'covered in tools — but no wrench.' The lack of a wrench is notable. Where's the wrench? Someone took it. Foxworth? Vincent? It was missing before anyone arrived — or was it?

Vincent examined the workbench too. Was he looking for the wrench? Or did he already take it?

Focus, James. The wire needs fixing. I have tools on the workbench — pliers, wire, whatever's there. I don't need a wrench for a wire splice. A wrench is for bolts. For the wire I need pliers and spare wire. The workbench should have those.

But I can't USE an item on the machine without having it in my inventory. The game mechanics require me to TAKE something first, then USE it. So I need to TAKE something from the workbench — but the workbench isn't listed as having a TAKE action. It's just 'a sturdy workbench covered in tools.'

Wait — maybe I should try to EXAMINE the machine again, now that I've assessed the workbench. Or maybe I should try to TAKE the workbench tools. Actually, the workbench doesn't have explicit interactive actions listed. The machine has EXAMINE. 

Let me think about what I actually CAN do. The machine says [EXAMINE]. I already examined it once. Can I examine it again to try the repair? Or do I need a specific item?

The cellar. Foxworth went to the cellar. The cellar has 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's deeply suspicious. Maybe the wrench is there. Maybe the medal is there. Maybe I need to check the cellar.

But no — Clara is here, the team is assembled, and I've just promised to fix this machine. I can't abandon the plan now. The most gallant thing is to follow through.

Let me try examining the machine again — maybe now that I've assessed the workbench, the game will let me attempt the repair. Or I could look at the machine more closely with LOOK to see if there's something I missed.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Blast this cellar! Blast this furniture! Blast this entire MANOR! Every drawer, every cushion, every cobwebbed corner — NOTHING! Not a single clue, not a single trinket, not so much as a HINT! This place is a FRAUD! A decorative FRAUD! Someone rearranged this furniture for NOTHING! For AESTHETICS! Who rearranges cellar furniture for AESTHETICS?! I'll tell you who — someone with TOO MUCH TIME and NOT ENOUGH TREASURE!
events.thinking:
Nothing. NOTHING. The furniture is just... furniture. 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' That's it. That's ALL. No hidden compartments, no secret drawers, no treasure map tucked under a cushion. Just old chairs and tables that someone moved around.

I'm standing alone in a damp cellar, empty-handed, having examined EVERYTHING I can find and discovered NOTHING. The guest book — nothing. The bookshelves — nothing. The mantelpiece — my fake medal was rejected. The crates — nothing. The furniture — NOTHING. Six examinations. Zero results. Reginald Foxworth, master schemer, outwitted by inanimate objects.

Meanwhile, upstairs, James Hartwell is probably repairing that gnawed wire right now. He said he could splice it. He's competent like that — quiet, methodical, effective. Everything I pretend to be. Once he fixes the wire, they'll need three operators for the machine, and the machine will probably produce the medal that the mantelpiece needs, which will unlock the map that leads to the treasure. And I'll be down here. In a cellar. Surrounded by furniture.

The air vents. They're the only thing left to examine. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' That's... mice. Or rats. The creature that gnawed the wire. The vents connect the cellar to the laboratory — maybe to other rooms too. But I can't fit through them. I'm not a mouse.

I need to go back upstairs. I need to be part of the machine operation. 'Requires 3 operators' — they need me. Or at least, they need a third person. I could be that third person. Position myself at the machine, wait for it to produce whatever it produces, and then — GRAB. Take the output and run. Classic smash-and-grab. No subtlety, no elegance, but effective.

But first — the vents. One more look. There might be something I'm missing. Something small, something overlooked. Like me. The youngest of four, always overlooked, always coming last to everything. No. Focus. The vents.

events.desc: Seven things examined. Zero discoveries. Reginald Foxworth is having the worst treasure hunt of his illustrious and entirely fabricated career. But the air vents... something SMALL has been through those vents. The same something that gnawed the machine wire upstairs. If there's a creature living in these walls, it might have a NEST. And nests contain... collected things. SHINY collected things.

Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
The Brixton Boys examined the workbench.
James Hartwell examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the air-vents.
Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.

Clara Bellingham: James, I am watching you work and I have to say — you have the steadiest hands I have ever seen. When we were in school, you rebuilt that clock in Mr. Henderson's office and he CRIED, he was so happy. Danny, how are those flasks looking? Any colour changes? You're doing a wonderful job keeping watch. Now — Vincent's gone to check on Reginald in the cellar, so that leaves the THREE of us. Me, you, and Danny. Three operators, three levers, three people who've known each other since we were practically in diapers. Lord Doily couldn't have ASKED for a better team. James, honey, you just say the word when that wire is ready, and Clara Bellingham will be at her station faster than a debutante at a dessert table. Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara, and Clara Bellingham don't let nothing happen to her boys. We do this TOGETHER.
events.thinking:
Oh. Vincent left. He went to the cellar after all — said he was going to check on Reginald. That's... that's fine. That's Vincent being responsible. He's the estate manager, of course he'd check on a guest who wandered into a potentially dangerous cellar. And James asked Vincent to confirm the gauge readings when the splice was done, but Vincent left before James finished. That's a little... no, it's fine. Vincent said 'call if you need a third pair of hands.' He'll come back.

But now it's just me, Danny, and James in the laboratory. Three people. Three operators. That's... actually perfect. James is working on the machine — he examined it again, he's got the tools, he's splicing the wire. He told Danny to watch the flasks for colour changes. He told me to stay where I am, 'where he can see me, where I'm safe.' My heart is doing THINGS.

James said 'Clara, just stay exactly where you are. Where I can see you. Where you're safe.' James Hartwell. Since Year Seven. That look in his eyes.

Focus, Clara. FOCUS.

The wire is still showing as gnawed through in the description. James is working on it but it's not fixed yet. I should WAIT for him to finish. When the wire is repaired, we three can operate the machine together — James, Danny, and me. The perfect team. My two protectors and me.

Danny examined the workbench. He's watching those flasks like James asked. Good. Everyone has a role. I made my speech about trust and teamwork. The tension has eased — Danny and James spoke quietly together. That's a GOOD sign. When my people talk to each other, the knot in my stomach loosens.

I should wait for James to finish the repair. Then we pull the levers together.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Clara just... she just said all that. Out loud. In front of everyone. 'He taught me how to tie my shoes after Mama and Daddy died. He sat up with me every night for a MONTH when I had nightmares.' About Marsh. About Pemberton. He... he did that? For Clara? After her parents died? A month of sitting up with her? That's... that's what the boss did. When mum was sick. Medicine, no expectation, no deal. That's the real thing. That's the thing you can't fake. And she said Danny is protective because he LOVES me. She knows. She's always known. And she said 'you are BOTH my family.' Both. Me AND Marsh. My throat's tight. Something hot behind my eyes. I was wrong? No — I wasn't WRONG exactly. My gut still prickles around Marsh. But Clara... Clara knows things I don't. She's known Marsh since she was twelve. He tied her shoes. He sat up with her through nightmares. That's not the man in the clean suit. That's... that's the boss with the medicine. And now Marsh has gone to check on Foxworth in the cellar. Because Foxworth might have taken a tumble. Because that's what you do when you're looking after people. Isn't it? My chest aches different now. Not the tight, warning ache. The other one. The one that comes when you realize you might have been seeing things that weren't there. When your protection turns into something that hurts the person you're protecting. 'It makes my heart hurt,' she said. I made Clara's heart hurt. That's the opposite of what I'm supposed to do. And Hartwell — good man, steady hands — he said 'Danny, keep an eye on those flasks.' He gave me a job. A real job. Not standing outside a door, not chasing after people. Watching the flasks. Watching Clara. Being HERE. And he said 'Clara, just stay exactly where you are. Where I can see you. Where you're safe.' Hartwell gets it. Hartwell gets it the same way I do. He just says it... better. Right. Watch the flasks. Be here. Be useful. And maybe... maybe I owe Marsh an apology. When he comes back. If I can find the words. Which I probably can't. But Clara will know.

events.desc: She said 'family.' About me. About Marsh. About all of us. The boss said 'family' too, once. But then he showed up with medicine for mum. Maybe Marsh is the boss kind of family, not the clean-suit kind. Maybe my gut's been wrong this once. Or maybe it hasn't. But Clara asked me to try, and there ain't nothing in this world Danny Brixton won't do for Clara Bellingham. Even trust.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara just said something that hit me like a freight train. Vincent Marsh has been looking after her since she was TWELVE. He taught her to tie her shoes after her parents died. He sat up with her every night for a MONTH when she had nightmares.

I didn't know that. I didn't know any of that. Mama and Daddy died. Clara's parents are dead. The warmth in my chest turns into something heavier — a kind of ache. She's been carrying that since she was twelve, and I never... I was building bridges and winning competitions and she was losing her parents.

And Vincent — Pemberton — he was there for her. He was the one who showed up. Not me. Him. That changes everything about the neck-prickle. Maybe it was never suspicion I should have been feeling. Maybe it was... recognition. This is a man who did for Clara what my father did for me — he showed her what good people do. He protected her.

Father's voice again: judge a man by his actions. Vincent's actions are clear. He cared for a grieving twelve-year-old girl. He stayed. That's not the action of a villain.

I feel ashamed. Not deeply — I never accused him of anything, I gave him the benefit of the doubt as I promised — but the suspicion was there, in the back of my neck, and it was wrong. Danny was worse about it, but I wasn't clean either.

Clara's speech — 'I need you BOTH' — she means Danny and Vincent. Not me. Both her family. I'm not in that category. I'm the boy from school who builds bridges and rolls up his sleeves. That stings. But she also called me magnificent, and she followed me to the laboratory, and she remembered Year Ten. I'm something else to her. I just don't know what yet.

But right now — she told everyone to get ready. She told them to trust each other. She told them Lord Doily designed this as a test of teamwork. And she's right.

The machine. I've examined it twice. The wire is still gnawed through. The machine still needs repair. But the EXAMINE action keeps showing the same thing. Maybe I need a different approach. Maybe the machine can't be repaired this way — maybe the missing wrench is the key. The wrench that isn't on the workbench.

Where's the wrench? Foxworth went to the cellar. Vincent just went to the cellar too. The cellar with 'cheerful decorations' — someone has been redecorating. The wrench could be there. Or... 

Wait. Vincent left. He said he was going to check on Foxworth. That's thoughtful, or convenient. Either way, we now have only three people in the room — me, Clara, Danny. Three operators. Exactly three.

The machine needs three operators. We ARE three operators. Maybe I don't need to fix the wire first. Maybe the three of us just need to operate it as-is and see what happens. Or maybe the wire repair IS the puzzle — you can't fix it without the wrench, and the wrench is in the cellar.

No — let me try one more thing. Danny called me a diamond. Danny is ready. Clara is ready. I'm ready. Let me try to PULL_ASIDE Clara — no, that's not right. Let me try to... 

Actually — Danny just told me to tell him which lever is his. Clara said get ready. Maybe the machine works even with the gnawed wire if three people operate it together. Maybe the 'gnawed wire' is what happens when someone tries to operate it ALONE — the machine overloads a single wire. With three operators distributing the load...

That's engineering logic. Three operators divide the current three ways. A wire that can't handle full load from one operator might handle a third of the load from three operators working in sync. It's not perfect — it's risky — but James Hartwell has never been afraid of risk when Clara is watching.

Or I'm completely overthinking this and I should just try operating it with three people. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' We have 3. Let's go.

events.desc: James Hartwell's elaborate plan to repair the wire, find the wrench, check the cellar, recruit Vincent, and conduct a full safety inspection has been abandoned in favour of a much simpler plan: just pull the levers with the two people he trusts most. He suspects Clara would call this 'growth.' He suspects she would be right.
