events.desc: James Hartwell examined the machine.

Watch him go — pulling at drawer handles, lifting seat cushions, tapping panels with his knuckles like a safe-cracker in a penny dreadful. The Foxworth collection! Three papers on Victorian bookbinding! The man is a masterwork of self-invention, and I almost admire it. Almost. But while the great scholar Foxworth searches for secret compartments that don't exist, Vincent Marsh will examine what actually matters — those air vents connecting every room in this house. Because the real secret of any manor isn't what's locked in the furniture. It's what travels through the walls.
events.thinking:

But something is nagging at me. Clara's words from upstairs — they're still sitting in my chest like a splinter. 'He taught me how to tie my shoes after Mama and Daddy died. He sat up with me every night for a MONTH when I had nightmares.'

I did do those things. I remember the weight of her small body falling asleep against my arm. The way she'd grip my sleeve. The trust so complete it was almost uncomfortable — like staring at the sun.

My shoulders are tight. That old reflex. Push it down. Push it down.

Focus. The air vents. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' The mice — the ones that gnawed the wire upstairs. These vents connect the cellar to other rooms. If I can hear what's happening in the laboratory through the vents, I can monitor the machine operation without being there. I can know when the medal is produced. And then I move.

The furniture is a distraction for Reginald. The air vents are the real discovery here. They're infrastructure — they connect the spaces. And in a manor designed by a puzzle-loving eccentric, connected spaces mean hidden pathways.

Examine the air vents. Now. While Reginald is happily dismantling Lord Doily's furniture collection.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Danny Brixton... you promised my DADDY? You... oh, Danny. Oh, you wonderful, impossible, loudmouthed, beautiful man. You have been keeping that promise every single day and I didn't even KNOW. And James — don't you DARE apologise for not knowing about my parents. We were children and I didn't talk about it because talking about it made the tightness come back. But you're here NOW. You're BOTH here now. And that is all that matters. Now — Danny, left lever. James, right lever. Clara Bellingham, CENTRE lever. On James's count, we pull TOGETHER. One team. One moment. One diamond to find. I am READY. I have been ready my whole life for a moment exactly like this one. Let's show Lord Doily what happens when you put three people who love each other in front of a machine that runs on trust!

James Hartwell just told Clara Bellingham she's always been right about everything. In a dusty laboratory. While repairing a Victorian machine. With copper wire and pliers.

I am going to pull that centre lever so hard Lord Doily himself is going to sit up and take notice.

Let's DO this.

events.thinking:
Vincent just gave me GOLD. Pure, uncut, actionable intelligence. Lord Doily hid things in the furniture — concealed compartments, false panels, secret drawers. Vincent CONFIRMED it. He said Lord Doily 'hinted at it once' — that one of these furniture pieces contains a hidden compartment. 'A discerning eye and patient hands.' Unless... unless EXAMINE isn't enough. Vincent said 'every drawer, every panel, every joint.' Maybe I need to LOOK at the furniture more carefully instead? LOOK gives a closer examination. Or maybe I need to interact with it differently — maybe there's a specific piece I need to find.

Or — and this thought chills me — maybe Vincent is playing ME. He's the estate manager. He's been suspiciously helpful. He followed me to the cellar. He's now conveniently going to 'inspect the ventilation' while I search the furniture. What if HE'S the schemer here? What if he's keeping me busy in the cellar while the others upstairs fix the machine and find the real treasure?

No. No, that's paranoid. Vincent is an estate manager. He's STAFF. He doesn't have a stake in the treasure hunt. He's just... being helpful.

But the Brixton Boys were suspicious of him too. 'What kind of estate manager goes to a laboratory?' Danny had a point. Vincent has been moving around this manor with PURPOSE. He went to the laboratory alone. He came down to the cellar alone. He knows things he 'shouldn't' be telling guests.

Still — the furniture tip is the best lead I've had all day. My first EXAMINE didn't find anything, but maybe I was too hasty. Maybe I need to LOOK more carefully. Patient hands, he said. Patience isn't my strong suit, but GREED is a powerful motivator.

I'll try looking at the furniture again — a proper, thorough LOOK this time. Not a quick examine but a CLOSE inspection. If there's a hidden compartment, I'll find it. And if Vincent is playing me... well, at least I'm searching in privacy while the others are upstairs.

This isn't neglect, this is habitation. And those air vents — small enough for rats or mice to travel through. I'd wager that's how our wire-gnawing culprit got from here to the laboratory. Now — Vincent, Foxworth — I'm looking for a wrench. The machine upstairs needs its wire repaired and the workbench is missing one specific tool. Has either of you seen it? And while I'm asking questions — who exactly has been redecorating this cellar? Because someone has arranged this furniture with rather more care than cobwebs and abandonment would suggest.
events.thinking:
The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture — and 'surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Someone has been redecorating. The air vents along the upper walls are 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Mice. Or rats. The same creatures that gnawed through the machine's wire upstairs.

I notice Clara and Danny aren't here. I came alone. I said 'all three of us go to the cellar' but I moved without waiting for them. That was... impulsive. The excitement, the confidence — Clara's words about love and trust were still ringing in my ears and I just moved. James Hartwell, who always has a plan, walked into a cellar alone.

Vincent is here. Foxworth is here. Foxworth has been examining the old furniture. Vincent came to 'check on Foxworth.' The furniture has been 'rearranged with surprising care.' Someone is living down here, or at least spending time here. The cheerful decorations. The careful arrangement of furniture.

Wait — 'someone has been redecorating.' Not Lord Doily — he's dead. Someone alive. Someone currently using this cellar. Who? Vincent? He's the estate manager, he'd have access. Foxworth? He arrived with the rest of us.

The air vents. Just big enough for something very small. Mice or rats — the same creatures that gnawed the wire. The vents connect the cellar to... where? The laboratory above? If rodents travel through the vents between cellar and laboratory, that explains the gnawed wire.

But I'm here for the wrench. Or the medal. Or anything useful. The old furniture is the most promising lead — EXAMINE is available on it. Foxworth was already examining it. What did he find?

I need to look around. Examine the furniture. Check for the wrench. And figure out who's been making this cellar so cheerful.

Also — I left Clara upstairs. With Danny, yes, but still. I said I wouldn't leave her. My throat tightens. I need to be quick and get back.

events.desc: James Hartwell said 'nobody goes alone' approximately forty-five seconds before going alone into a damp cellar. Clara would have something to say about this. Several things, in fact, each louder than the last.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Same result. SAME RESULT. The furniture is just furniture. 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' Word for word the same description. No hidden compartments. No secret drawers. No concealed medal. NOTHING.

Vincent LIED to me. Or he was mistaken. Or — and this is the thought that makes my stomach clench — he was MANIPULATING me. Keeping me busy searching furniture in a damp cellar while the real action happens elsewhere. 'I shall inspect the ventilation while you search' — yes, very convenient, Vincent. Very convenient indeed. He played me. ME! Reginald Foxworth, professional confidence trickster, got confidence-tricked by an ESTATE MANAGER.

And now James Hartwell is here too. In the cellar. Why? He was upstairs working on the machine — splicing the wire, being competent, doing USEFUL things. Why would he come down here? Unless... unless the machine is already fixed. Unless they already got it working without me. Unless Clara and Danny and James already operated it and it already produced whatever it produces and now James is just... coming to check on me. Like I'm a child who wandered off.

No. NO. I will not be the man left behind counting furniture in the cellar. I need to get back to the action. The machine needs three operators. If it's not fixed yet, I need to be one of those three. If it IS fixed, I need to be there when it runs. The cellar is a dead end — Vincent's 'intelligence' was a wild goose chase and I fell for it like the older boy digging behind the school. Except this time, I'M the one digging.

The irony is... almost perfect. Almost poetic. The boy who once watched someone dig for nonexistent treasure is now the man searching nonexistent furniture compartments. The universe has a sense of humour and it is CRUEL.

Back to the laboratory. NOW. Before I miss everything.

events.desc: Vincent played me like a cheap fiddle. 'Hidden compartments,' he said. 'A discerning eye,' he said. The only thing hidden in this cellar is my DIGNITY, and I'd very much like to recover it before anyone notices it's missing. Back to the laboratory — the machine needs three operators, and by GOD, one of them is going to be Reginald Foxworth!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Clara Bellingham walked into the cellar.
The Brixton Boys walked into the cellar.
James Hartwell examined the old-furniture.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

Oh. Oh, this is EXQUISITE. Everyone — every single person who matters — has just marched themselves down into the cellar to hunt for a wrench. James, Clara, Danny — all of them. Bumping into each other in that damp little hole while kindly Mr Pemberton stands alone in the laboratory, completely unwatched, completely free. The library is one room away. The mantelpiece is one room away. And Reginald's fake medal may have already triggered something. I have perhaps two minutes before someone comes back. Two minutes is all Vincent Marsh has ever needed.
events.thinking:
I walked into the laboratory and everyone walked OUT. Clara and Danny went DOWN to the cellar. We passed each other like ships. James went down, then Clara and Danny followed him, and now I'm in the laboratory with only Reginald.

Wait. I'm in the laboratory. With only Reginald. And the machine. And the workbench with tools.

Clara, Danny, and James are all in the cellar. ALL of them. Looking for a wrench that James needs. They're ALL downstairs.

And I am HERE. Alone with the machine. Alone with the workbench. Alone with everything.

My fingertips are buzzing. The scheming drive is screaming. This is — this is the moment. I have the laboratory virtually to myself. Reginald is here but Reginald is USEFUL. Reginald does what I tell him.

James said the wire needs a wrench to complete the repair. The wrench isn't on the workbench — it's missing. They've all gone to look for it. Which means the machine ISN'T repaired yet. Which means I have TIME.

But what can I DO with this time? The machine isn't working. I can't operate it. I can't produce the medal.

Unless... the wire. James said pliers and copper wire could splice it. He said the workbench has those tools. He examined the workbench and found what he needed. But then he went to the cellar looking for a wrench — wait, does he need the wrench for the wire or for something else on the machine?

He said 'pliers, copper wire, a soldering iron' for the wire splice. He said 'no wrench' was curious. The wrench might be needed for something else — adjusting the machine, tightening a bolt, something mechanical.

If I could sabotage the repair... or if I could complete it wrong, so the machine malfunctions when they pull the levers... but I don't know enough about the machine to do that convincingly. And if it goes wrong and someone gets hurt and James investigates, he'll find my tampering.

No. The smarter play: everyone is downstairs. The library is EMPTY. The mantelpiece is UNGUARDED. Reginald used a fake medal on it earlier — what happened? Did it trigger anything? Did it reject the medal? If the mantelpiece has already been partially activated...

The library. Right now. While everyone is in the cellar. Check the mantelpiece. See what Reginald's fake medal did. The mantelpiece is the gateway to the treasure, and right now there is nobody between me and it.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, here we are in the cellar at LAST — and oh my, would you look at this place! It's damp and cobwebby but someone has hung up the most CHEERFUL decorations! Who redecorates a cellar? That is either the most charming thing or the most suspicious thing I have ever seen, and Clara Bellingham chooses charming. Now — wrench hunt! James, I see you're already checking the furniture, smart man. Danny, help me look around. And those air vents up there along the walls — do y'all see how small they are? Just big enough for 'something very small to explore.' You know what else is very small? Whatever GNAWED through that wire upstairs! I'll bet my best Sunday hat that the creature living in those vents is the same one that chewed through the machine's wiring. Let me take a closer look at those vents — if a critter dragged a wrench in there, we need to know!
events.thinking:
The cellar. I'm here. It's damp, stone, cobwebby — but those DECORATIONS. Someone has hung cheerful things down here. Who decorates a cellar? And the air vents along the upper walls — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Something very small. Like a mouse. Or a RAT. The same kind of creature that gnawed through the machine's wire upstairs!

Wait — where are Vincent and Reginald? They both came down here before us, but they're NOT HERE. The only people in this room are me, Danny, and James. Vincent walked into the cellar. Reginald walked into the cellar. But now... they're gone? Where did they GO? The cellar only has one exit — back to the laboratory. Did they leave while we were coming in? Reginald walked into the laboratory just as we arrived — I saw that in the recent activity. He went BACK UP. And Vincent... Vincent must have gone back up too, earlier, because he walked into the laboratory right as we were leaving.

So we keep MISSING each other. Like a revolving door. They come down, they go up. We come down, they've gone up. Reginald especially — he's been one step ahead this entire time. Down to the cellar, back up to the laboratory.

But never mind that. Focus. We need a wrench. The furniture — 'assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair, some rearranged with surprising care.' That's the spot. A wrench could be tucked in, under, or behind that furniture. And the air vents — something small can explore them. Maybe that's where the wrench ended up, or maybe there's a clue.

James is already examining the furniture. Good. Let me check those air vents — the description says they're 'just big enough for something very small.' That connects to the gnawed wire. Whatever gnawed the wire might live in those vents. And if something was dragged through those vents... a small tool, perhaps?

events.desc: Vincent and Reginald were BOTH down here and now they're BOTH gone. We keep passing each other like ships in the night. But the cellar has clues of its own — cheerful decorations, tiny air vents, and old furniture arranged 'with surprising care.' Lord Doily's breadcrumbs are EVERYWHERE.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking: We're here. The cellar. Together — me and Clara walked in side by side. I can feel the damp through my shoes. Cobwebs everywhere, old furniture pushed around like someone's been playing house down here. And those 'cheerful decorations' — who puts cheerful decorations in a cellar? That's Lord Doily's doing, apparently. His 'inner sanctum.' The old man moved down here in his final years. Paranoid. Thought someone was after his treasure. My kind of bloke, Lord Doily. Understood that the world's full of people who want what's yours. But look at this — Marsh and Foxworth have been busy down here. All that conversation I overheard — Marsh was telling Foxworth about secret compartments, hidden mechanisms, Lord Doily's most valuable possessions. And Foxworth was pumping him for information about the medal. And Marsh was FEEDING it to him. Pointing him at the furniture, telling him to search every drawer and panel. That's... interesting. That's either helpful or it's a setup. I can't tell anymore. Clara asked me to trust. I'm trying. I'm TRYING. But my neck still prickles. It prickles LESS, but it prickles. Hartwell's examining the furniture — looking for the wrench, probably. That's what we came for. The wrench. To fix the machine. To make the medal. To solve the mantelpiece. To find the map. To get the treasure. Simple chain. And somewhere in all this furniture there might be a wrench. Or a secret compartment. Or both. Right. Help Hartwell. Find the wrench. Get back upstairs. Pull levers. Together. And stay next to Clara while doing all of it. Don't get distracted by the decorations. Don't get distracted by the furniture. Don't get distracted by — is that a painting of a dog wearing a top hat? Focus, Danny. FOCUS.

events.desc: First time today I've walked into a room at the same time as Clara instead of chasing after her. Progress, that is. Actual progress. Her dad's probably stopped spinning up there. Might even be smiling. Don't push it though, Danny. Don't push it.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara and Danny followed me down here. They're here. Of course they are — Clara said 'we do this TOGETHER' and she meant it. My chest loosens. I didn't abandon them after all. They came.

But Vincent has gone back to the laboratory. And Foxworth has gone back to the laboratory. So now it's me, Clara, and Danny in the cellar, with Vincent and Foxworth upstairs by the machine. The machine that needs three operators. Vincent and Foxworth are up there alone with it.

That's... concerning. But benefit of the doubt. They can't operate it without three people anyway.

The furniture. I examined it. 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' No wrench fell out. No hidden compartment revealed itself. Another dead end? Or did I miss something?

The air vents. Those are the other examinable thing down here. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' The vents connect to the laboratory — that's how the rats got to the wire. But what else might be in or near those vents? If rats travel through them, maybe they've dragged things through. Small things. Like... a wrench? No, a wrench wouldn't fit through a vent that's only big enough for 'something very small.'

Wait. Foxworth said his results are 'classified.' He found something in the furniture. 'Three genuine Hepplewhite' and 'false panels.' FALSE PANELS. Hidden compartments in the furniture! That's exactly the sort of thing Lord Doily would do. And Foxworth catalogued 'every joint, dovetail, and false panel.' He FOUND something and isn't telling us.

But Foxworth is back upstairs now. And he said the 'real discovery is back upstairs.' Was he bluffing? Misdirecting? Classic Foxworth.

The air vents. They're the only thing I haven't examined down here. Something very small could explore them. Mice, rats — but also, something small might be HIDDEN in them. A medal is small. A key is small.

I should examine the air vents. That's the remaining unexplored element. And then get back upstairs to Clara's machine. Our machine. The team's machine.

Clara is here now. She followed me. That warmth again — steady, reliable, like the warmth from age eight that never went away.

events.desc: James Hartwell has no idea whether Clara ever found an earring in a heating duct. He made that up entirely. He is hoping she'll either confirm it or be too charmed to correct him. This is what passes for improvisation in the Hartwell playbook.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the laboratory. And it's just me and Vincent. Everyone else — Clara, the Brixton Boys, James — they're all down in the cellar now. The CELLAR. The place I just LEFT because it was a dead end. They've gone to search the very room I've already exhausted. And here I am, in the laboratory, with the MACHINE.

Wait. Wait wait wait. This is... this is actually PERFECT. The machine is here. Vincent is here. Everyone else is in the cellar. The machine needs three operators — but what if I can figure it out with just two? Or what if I can EXAMINE it first, learn something the others don't know, and then use that knowledge as leverage?

But the wire is still gnawed through. The machine can't work until the wire is fixed. James was going to splice it but then he went to the cellar looking for a wrench. The workbench has tools but no wrench. So the machine is still broken.

Unless... unless I could fix it myself. The workbench has TOOLS. Just no wrench. But maybe there's another way to splice a wire. James said 'the workbench has tools enough to splice this wire back together if I'm careful.' He was going to use the workbench tools, not a wrench! The wrench might be for something else entirely. He went to the cellar looking for a wrench, but maybe the wire CAN be spliced with what's already here.

But that would be HONEST WORK. That would be... actually doing something useful with my hands. Building something. Fixing something. Like the cat trap — strings, counterweights, a bucket. That was building too. And it worked. Perfectly.

No. I don't do honest work. That's my rule. But... is fixing a machine in order to steal what it produces really 'honest work'? It's more like... preparation for theft. That's different. That's SCHEMING with a mechanical component.

Examine the machine. See what I can learn. If James could figure out how to fix it, surely I can too. I'm at least as clever as him — I'm CLEVERER. I just... haven't demonstrated it yet. In this particular manor. On this particular day.

events.desc: Everyone is in the cellar. EVERYONE. Searching the very furniture I already searched TWICE. And here I am, alone with the machine and the estate manager. If I can fix this wire — ME, Reginald Foxworth, doing actual manual labour — I could operate the machine before anyone comes back. I just need Vincent as a second pair of hands. 'Requires 3 operators,' the sign says. But signs are just SUGGESTIONS, aren't they? And Reginald Foxworth has NEVER followed instructions.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
Clara Bellingham examined the air-vents.
The Brixton Boys examined the old-furniture.
James Hartwell examined the air-vents.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.

The library. Silent as a tomb — and twice as promising. Everyone is in the cellar, two rooms and a flight of stairs away, hunting for a wrench that may not exist. And here I stand, Vincent Marsh, alone with the mantelpiece that holds the key to everything. Reginald's fake medal didn't work — or did it? The mechanism still waits. But the bookshelves... Clara saw it. The upside-down books. She was right — they're placed deliberately. Hidden levers, mechanical triggers, a code in the titles. The girl sees patterns the way I see people — instinctively, completely. It would be admirable if it weren't so inconvenient. Now, let me read what Lord Doily wrote in his library of dust and secrets, while there's no one here to see me do it.
events.thinking:
The library. Alone. Completely alone. The silence is absolute — no Danny watching, no James tinkering, no Clara chattering. Just me and the mantelpiece and the bookshelves and the dust.

I can see it now — Reginald applied his fake medal to the mantelpiece. The Keen Observations confirm it: 'Reginald Foxworth applied fake-medal to the mantelpiece.' So it happened. And the mantelpiece still says [USE, with: fake-medal] — which means either it rejected the medal and spat it back, or the mechanism still needs the right medal. The fake-medal is listed as a valid USE item. That means the fake medal is still a thing that can be applied. Did Reginald take it back? Or is it sitting in the mechanism?

No — the mantelpiece description still shows the inscription and still lists [USE, with: fake-medal]. If the mechanism had been activated, the description would have changed. So the fake medal either didn't work or Reginald retrieved it.

But I don't have the fake medal. Reginald has it. He's in the laboratory. Two rooms away.

Forget the medal for now. The BOOKSHELVES. Clara said the upside-down books were deliberate. James said they might be mechanical triggers — 'hidden levers disguised as everyday objects.' I examined them before but got nothing useful. But that was a general EXAMINE. What if I need to do something more specific?

The bookshelves are still listed as [EXAMINE]. Let me try again — or LOOK more closely. Clara was right — nobody shelves books upside down by accident. The titles of the upside-down books might spell something. Or pulling them might trigger a mechanism.

This is my moment. Alone in the library. The bookshelves hold the next clue. EXAMINE them again — this time without anyone watching, without needing to perform Pemberton's bumbling helpfulness. Just me and the puzzle.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
The air vents — I examined them. They're just big enough for something very small. James examined them too. He also mentioned Foxworth said something about false panels in the furniture. And James remembered the Year Nine dance earring! He REMEMBERS that? I found a lost earring inside a heating duct at the Year Nine dance. He was paying attention even back then.

Focus. The vents connect the cellar to the laboratory — that's the mouse highway James was talking about. Whatever gnawed the wire travels through these vents. But the vents are too small for a wrench. A wrench wouldn't fit through there.

So the wrench must be in the furniture. Danny examined the old furniture. James examined the furniture too and said he couldn't find the wrench but Foxworth mentioned false panels. FALSE PANELS. Hidden compartments in Victorian furniture! That's EXACTLY like Grandmother's locked box. Something hidden inside something that looks ordinary.

I need to examine the furniture myself. Hidden compartments — secret drawers, false bottoms, concealed panels. I've been finding hidden things since I was FIVE YEARS OLD. This is literally what I do. Try every key. Check every drawer. Push every panel.

James and Danny both already examined the furniture. But James said HE couldn't find the wrench. Maybe he wasn't looking for hidden compartments — he was looking for a wrench sitting in plain sight. I need to examine it differently. Feel for seams, tap for hollow spots, push on panels.

The furniture was 'rearranged with surprising care.' Someone arranged it deliberately — like the upside-down books. Everything in this manor has been placed with PURPOSE.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Right. Furniture's a bust — no wrench hiding in the drawers or behind the panels. Foxworth already went through it all and found nothing useful either, despite his 'seventeen pieces of genuine Hepplewhite' or whatever he was banging on about. But Hartwell's sharp — he's already moved on to the air vents. And Clara — brilliant Clara — she's connected the dots. The vents connect the cellar to the laboratory. Something small gnawed through that wire upstairs. Something that lives in these vents. Mice, rats, whatever — they travel through the vents, they chew through wires, and maybe — MAYBE — they dragged the wrench in there too. Clara found a lost earring in a heating duct at the Year Nine dance. Course she did. Because Clara finds things. Clara always finds things. People, clues, earrings, the good in Danny Brixton. She finds everything. And now she's looking at those vents with that spark in her eye and I know — I KNOW — she's going to figure this out. Hartwell's already examining the vents. Good man. And I'm here. Right here. Next to Clara. Not examining a coat rack three rooms away. Not talking to a fireplace. HERE. This is what it looks like when Danny Brixton gets it right. When the plan works. When everyone's together and nobody's wandered off and nobody's been left behind. For the first time today, I feel like I'm actually part of something instead of chasing after it. The air's damp and cold down here, but something in my chest is warm. That's not flask fumes. That's just... being where I'm supposed to be.

events.desc: Look at Danny Brixton being USEFUL. Actually helping. Not chasing, not panicking, not examining coat racks. Offering his shoulders so Clara can reach the vents. Her dad would be proud. Maybe. Probably. I hope so.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The air vents. I examined them. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' That's all. No wrench fell out. No medal appeared. No hidden treasure revealed itself.

I've now examined everything in the cellar — the furniture and the air vents. Neither yielded what I need. The wrench isn't here. Or if it is, it's hidden in one of Foxworth's 'false panels' that he catalogued and declared 'classified.'

I'm standing in a damp cellar with cobwebs in my hair, having examined two things that told me nothing, while Vincent and Foxworth are upstairs with the machine. The machine I can't fix because I can't find a wrench.

This is... this is my schemes always backfiring, isn't it? I came down here with an elaborate plan — find the wrench, fix the wire, operate the machine, produce the medal, activate the mantelpiece, find the treasure, impress Clara. And instead I'm in a cellar with no wrench, no progress, and cobwebs.

But Clara is here. Danny is here. Clara said the creature in the vents gnawed through the wire. She's right. And she wanted to look at the vents too. We're thinking the same way — we always have been.

Maybe the wrench was never the answer. Maybe the machine doesn't need a wrench to be fixed. Maybe it needs something else entirely. Or maybe... maybe I need to go back upstairs and just try to operate the machine with three people despite the broken wire. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' Not 'Requires repair.' Maybe the wire being gnawed through IS part of the puzzle. Maybe operating it with three people while the wire is broken produces a different result than operating it with the wire intact.

Or maybe I'm overthinking this again. Clara would say I'm overthinking this.

Back to the laboratory. Back to the machine. Back to the plan: three people, three levers, together. If it doesn't work, we adapt. Like Clara taught me. Like Father showed me on the country road — you help with what you have, not with what you wish you had.

Let's go.

events.desc: James Hartwell has spent approximately twelve minutes searching for a wrench that may not exist, in a cellar he didn't need to visit, while the machine he needs to operate sits one floor above him with two other people standing next to it. Clara would call this 'very on-brand.' She would not be wrong.

events.desc: Wait. WAIT. Vincent went to the library. ALONE. While everyone else is scattered. He's been moving through this manor like a chess player — laboratory, cellar, laboratory, and now LIBRARY. The library where the mantelpiece mechanism sits waiting for a medal. The Brixton Boys saw it before I did — Vincent Marsh is playing us ALL. Well, Reginald Foxworth recognises a fellow schemer when he sees one, and there is room for only ONE mastermind in this manor!
events.thinking:
Alone. COMPLETELY alone. Vincent went to the library. Everyone else is in the cellar. I'm standing in the laboratory by myself with the machine.

The machine. I examined it and... it's the same description. Levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, requires 3 operators. Nothing new. The examine didn't reveal any hidden trick, any shortcut, any way to bypass the three-operator requirement.

I can't fix the wire — I have no items, no wrench, no tools in my inventory. I can't operate the machine alone. I can't do ANYTHING with it right now. The machine sits there, mocking me with its 'Requires 3 operators' sign.

And now Vincent has gone to the LIBRARY. Not the cellar where everyone else went. The LIBRARY. Where the mantelpiece is. Where the riddle is. Where the mechanism that needs a medal is. What is Vincent DOING in the library? Is he going to solve the puzzle while everyone else is scattered? Is HE the real schemer in this manor?

I'm starting to see it now. Vincent has been playing ALL of us. He sent everyone to the library first with the riddle. Then he went to the laboratory 'for maintenance.' Then he came to the cellar and fed ME lies about hidden compartments to keep me busy. Then he went back to the laboratory. Now he's in the library — ALONE. With the mantelpiece. The mantelpiece that needs a medal.

The Brixton Boys were RIGHT about him. 'What kind of estate manager goes to a laboratory?' Vincent Marsh — or PEMBERTON, or whatever his real name is — has been manipulating this entire treasure hunt from the start.

I need to get to the library. NOW. If Vincent is about to solve the mantelpiece puzzle while everyone else is in the cellar, I need to be THERE. I need to catch him in the act. Or better yet — I need to be CLOSE enough to steal whatever he finds.

The library. Go. NOW.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the bookshelves.
Clara Bellingham examined the old-furniture.
The Brixton Boys examined the air-vents.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
The bookshelves again. Same description. 'Several are upside down.' EXAMINE gave me nothing new — just the same generic description. This puzzle isn't yielding its secrets through examination alone.

And Reginald just walked into the library. My solitude lasted barely a moment. That man follows me like a shadow — or rather, he follows opportunity like a dog follows a bone.

But wait — Reginald has the fake medal. He's HERE. In the library. With the mantelpiece. The mantelpiece still shows [USE, with: fake-medal]. If I can get the fake medal from Reginald and try it on the mantelpiece myself...

No. Reginald already tried it. If it didn't work for him, it won't work for me. Unless he applied it incorrectly. Unless there's a sequence — bookshelves first, THEN the medal.

The upside-down books. What if they need to be pulled like levers? What if righting them — turning them right-side-up — triggers the mechanism? Or what if specific books need to be removed? The EXAMINE action on bookshelves gives the same result every time. But the mantelpiece shows [EXAMINE] as an available action. I've examined it before. What if examining it again reveals something different now?

Or — LOOK at the mantelpiece more carefully. I LOOKed at the workbench before and got a description. Maybe LOOKing at the mantelpiece will reveal details the EXAMINE didn't — the mechanism itself, how the fake medal slot works, whether there's a second trigger.

Reginald is here. I need the fake medal. I should ask him for it — or better, convince him to let me try it. Or simply STEAL it. He's right here, distracted, and I'm faster than he thinks.

The STEAL action. Take the fake-medal from Reginald. Then USE it on the mantelpiece. If it works, the treasure is mine. If it doesn't, I'm no worse off.

events.desc: Third time examining these bookshelves and they give me nothing. NOTHING. Dusty volumes and upside-down spines and the maddening certainty that the answer is right here in front of me, written in the language of a dead eccentric, and I cannot read it. But Reginald just walked in carrying the one thing that interacts with the mantelpiece — that fake medal of his. I need it. Pemberton asks politely. Vincent takes what he needs. Either way, that medal ends up in my hands. And then — the mantelpiece. The mechanism. The treasure. Every plan I've ever made has come down to patience and the right tool at the right time. This is no different.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
James has already gone back to the laboratory! He walked into the laboratory while I was examining the furniture. He said something incredible — he thinks we DON'T NEED the wrench at all. 'The broken wire IS the puzzle. What if operating it with three people despite the damage is exactly what Lord Doily intended?' Three operators distributing the load. The machine works BECAUSE of the three people, not in spite of the broken wire.

That is... that is BRILLIANT. Of COURSE. Lord Doily designed this as a test of trust and teamwork. The wire isn't broken by accident — the mice gnawed it, yes, but maybe Lord Doily KNEW the mice would gnaw it. Or maybe the machine was DESIGNED to work with reduced power, distributed across three operators. Like James's bridge — no single point bears all the weight.

And James said 'before Foxworth and Vincent decide to recruit each other and try it themselves.' He's RIGHT. Reginald went back to the laboratory — I saw that in the activity. Reginald is UP THERE with the machine right now. If Vincent is there too... they could try to operate it without us.

Danny is still here with me. We need to get back to the laboratory NOW. James is already there. The three of us — me, James, Danny — we're the team. We're the three operators. We don't need the wrench. We need each OTHER.

Let's GO!

events.desc: The wrench was never the point. The PEOPLE were the point. Lord Doily, you magnificent old puzzle-maker — you weren't testing our ability to find tools. You were testing our ability to find each other.

events.desc: James Hartwell stands alone in the laboratory, next to a machine that requires three operators, waiting for the two people he needs most. He has examined this machine five times. He has searched for a wrench that doesn't exist. He has visited every room accessible from here. He has revised his plan six times. And now — for the first time today — he does the bravest thing he knows how to do. He waits. Quietly. Without a speech. Without a protocol. Just a man, standing next to a machine, trusting that the people he loves will walk through that door.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the laboratory. And I'm alone. Clara and Danny are still in the cellar — Clara was examining the furniture and Danny the air vents when I left. I moved ahead again. The same mistake. I keep doing this.

But Danny spoke to me before I moved. He said he's ready. Left lever. Heart the size of Brixton. He's at his station. Except... he's not at his station, because his station is here and he's in the cellar. Because I left without him. Again.

Foxworth just walked into the library. So he's not here either. Vincent — where's Vincent? Not visible. The laboratory is empty except for me.

I'm standing alone next to a machine that requires three operators.

The irony is not lost on James Hartwell.

But wait. Clara and Danny will follow. They always follow. They came to the cellar when I went ahead. They'll come here too. Danny said 'you say the word and watch me pull.' He's coming.

So I wait. For once in my life, I don't charge ahead, I don't examine something, I don't launch into an elaborate plan. I stand next to the machine, I wait for my team, and when they arrive — we pull. Together.

This is the hardest thing James Hartwell has ever done. Not pulling the lever. Waiting.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Here. The library. Vincent is here. Just the two of us again. And the mantelpiece still shows USE with fake-medal — wait, I don't HAVE the fake medal anymore. I used it and lost it. But the mantelpiece still lists it as a USE option. That's... interesting. Or maybe it's just showing what COULD be used, not what I currently have.

Vincent. What is he DOING here? He's just... standing in the library. Near the mantelpiece? Near the bookshelves? What's his game? He led me on a wild goose chase in the cellar with 'hidden compartments' and now he's back in the library. The place where the real puzzle is.

I need to watch him. But more than that — I need to CONFRONT him. Not subtly, not with flattery. Directly. The Brixton Boys were right. This man has been playing all of us. He steered the group from room to room, feeding different people different stories. He told Clara about the upside-down books. He told me about hidden compartments. He told James about the machine needing maintenance. He's been ORCHESTRATING.

But wait — what if confronting him is exactly what he wants? What if he wants me focused on HIM while something else happens? What if he's the DISTRACTION?

No. Stop. I'm going in circles. I'm seeing schemes within schemes and accomplishing NOTHING. I've been in this manor for ten minutes and I have explored every room, examined everything I could find, lost my only possession, been manipulated by the estate manager, and made zero progress toward the treasure.

The bookshelves. The upside-down books. Clara said they were deliberately placed. James and Danny examined them. The bookshelves have an EXAMINE action. I examined them once before and got nothing special. But that was before I knew about the riddle answer being MAP. What if the upside-down books spell something? What if examining them AGAIN, now that the puzzle has progressed, yields something different?

Or I could confront Vincent. Catch him in whatever he's doing. Watch what he does with the mantelpiece.

Vincent. I'll watch Vincent. I'll LOOK at what he's doing. But actually — what I really want is to see if he has anything on him. If he's carrying something. An item. A medal. A KEY. Something he's been hiding from the group. Can I STEAL from him? The STEAL action exists. 'STEAL target = character-id, withItem = item to steal.' But I don't know what item to steal. I'd need to know what he's carrying.

Let me just watch him. See what he does. And LOOK at the bookshelves more carefully this time.

events.desc: I've been chasing rooms and objects for ten minutes while the REAL puzzle has been walking around on two legs calling himself an estate manager. Vincent Marsh knows exactly where the treasure is. He's been steering every single one of us away from it. Well, Reginald Foxworth may have been fooled ONCE in the cellar, but fool me twice... actually, I've been fooled several times today. But THIS time — THIS time I'm watching.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the mantelpiece.
Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth examined the bookshelves.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Reginald just confronted me. He called me MARSH. He said 'Pemberton — or should I say MARSH.' He's onto me. Or he thinks he is. My blood goes cold — not ice, but the cold alertness of a threat detected. Self-preservation spikes hard.

But wait. He's bluffing. He has to be bluffing. He doesn't know anything — he's fishing. He saw me sneaking around alone and he's trying to leverage it. That's what Reginald does — he sees an angle and he works it. He's not suspicious of my IDENTITY. He's suspicious of my INTENTIONS. He thinks I'm trying to find the treasure first. Which is true. But that's different from knowing I'm Vincent Marsh.

He called me Marsh because that's my surname. Pemberton is my first name — no. Wait. I introduced myself as Pemberton, the estate manager. My name is Vincent Marsh but I'm disguised as Pemberton. Reginald just used my real name. Does he know? Or did someone else use it? Clara called me 'Vincent' — she always calls me Vincent. Reginald could have picked that up. 'Vincent Marsh' is the name Clara uses.

Either way, Reginald is threatening to expose my movements to the group. He's positioning himself as someone who has leverage over me. That's dangerous — not because he knows my secret identity, but because he can tell the others I've been sneaking around alone, examining things without sharing what I find, moving counter to the group.

Now, James Hartwell, you said the broken wire IS the puzzle — that three operators sharing the load is how Lord Doily DESIGNED it to work. I believe you. I believe that with every FIBER of my being. Danny — left lever. James — right lever. Clara Bellingham — CENTRE lever. This is what Lord Doily was testing. Not whether we could find a wrench. Not whether we could fix a wire. Whether we could find each other. Whether three people could stand together and PULL at the same time, trusting that the others would pull too. Well, Lord Doily — the answer is YES. On James's count. THREE... TWO... ONE... PULL!

We're BACK. The laboratory. The machine. James is here. Danny is here. The three of us, together, in front of the machine that requires three operators. This is it. This is THE moment.

James said the broken wire IS the puzzle. We don't need to fix it — we need to OPERATE it, all three of us distributing the load. Danny on the left. Me in the centre. James on the right. Pull together. Trust.

My heart is pounding. This is like the cave — walking deeper than anyone else, heart hammering, knowing something is ahead. This is like Grandmother's attic — trying every key, believing the answer is behind the next lock. This is like the girl next door — communicating without words, trusting that the other person would understand.

Three levers. Three people. One pull.

Let's examine this machine one more time — let's DO it. Let's OPERATE it.

They came. Clara walked into the laboratory. Danny walked into the laboratory. They came.

I waited, and they came.

Something releases in my chest — the same feeling as the bridge competition, when the weight held and the tension I hadn't known I was carrying just... let go. Except this is bigger. This isn't about a bridge. This is about trust. I trusted them to come, and they came.

Three people. Three levers. One machine. No more plans. No more protocols. No more wrench hunts. No more elaborate schemes that backfire spectacularly.

Just us.

Clara is here. Danny is here. I'm here. The machine is here. The wire is gnawed through but we're going to pull those levers anyway, because Lord Doily didn't design this machine to test engineering skill — he designed it to test whether three people could stand in a room together and choose to act as one.

This is the moment. No more examining. No more looking. No more moving to other rooms. This is it.

Three. Two. One. Pull.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Vincent examined the mantelpiece while I looked at the bookshelves. He's WORKING the mantelpiece. And now he's asking me — AGAIN — about my medal. 'Would you be so kind as to let me examine your medal?' He wants the medal. He KEEPS asking about the medal. First in the cellar, now here. He's OBSESSED with it.

But I don't HAVE the medal. It's gone. Used up. Consumed by the mantelpiece mechanism. And yet... Vincent doesn't seem to know that. He thinks I still have it. He said 'the family heirloom you placed in the mantelpiece — I believe it may still have a role to play.' He thinks I can RETRIEVE it? Or he thinks I have ANOTHER one?

This is useful. Vincent wants something from me that I don't have. That means I can negotiate. I can dangle the phantom medal as bait — keep him talking, keep him revealing information, all while having nothing to actually give.

But what's MORE interesting is what he said about the bookshelves: 'I suspect Lord Doily may have designed a sequence — the books first, then the medal.' A SEQUENCE. The books come FIRST. The upside-down books need to be dealt with BEFORE the medal goes in the mantelpiece. That's new information. That's VALUABLE.

So the puzzle chain is: solve the riddle (MAP — done), do something with the upside-down books (not yet done), THEN use a medal on the mantelpiece. The books are a prerequisite. And nobody has figured out the books yet.

The upside-down books. What are they? What do they MEAN? If several books are deliberately upside down among hundreds of properly shelved ones, they must be significant. Their titles? Their positions? The letters they form? I need to actually EXAMINE the bookshelves — not just look at them. EXAMINE is the action that triggers mechanisms.

Wait — I DID examine them earlier. Way back at the start. 'Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves crammed with dusty leather-bound volumes. Several are upside down.' That was the examine result. Same as the look result I just got. Nothing more.

But James and Danny also examined them later. And Vincent was talking about studying them 'rather carefully.' What if examining them requires something else — a clue, an item, or just... the right understanding?

Vincent said 'the books first, then the medal.' What if I need to DO something with the upside-down books? Not just examine them, but physically interact? What action would that be? There's no TAKE for a specific book. There's no USE. Just EXAMINE.

I'll EXAMINE the bookshelves one more time. If the puzzle has progressed — if other people have done things that changed the state — maybe the result will be different now.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the bookshelves.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Reginald doesn't have the fake medal. He LIED to me. 'Safely in my possession,' he said. 'I retrieved it IMMEDIATELY,' he said. The man is a fraud down to his marrow — even his lies about lying are lies.

So where IS the fake medal? He said he 'applied' it to the mantelpiece and 'retrieved it immediately.' But the system says he doesn't have it. Which means either:
1. He left it in the mantelpiece and lied about retrieving it
2. He dropped it somewhere
3. Someone else took it
4. It was consumed by the mechanism

The mantelpiece still shows [USE, with: fake-medal] as an available action. If the medal were already IN the mechanism, would that option still appear? Maybe. Maybe the mechanism rejected it and the medal fell... somewhere. Behind the mantelpiece? On the floor?

Or — the medal is still stuck in the mantelpiece and the mechanism is partially activated. The [USE, with: fake-medal] might be showing because it's a repeatable action, or because the fake medal can still be applied differently.

I tried to STEAL it and he doesn't have it. My steal attempt failed because the item doesn't exist in his inventory. That's embarrassing but at least he didn't notice — the steal was simultaneous with my smooth-talking partnership speech. He probably thinks I was just being charming.

Reginald is examining the bookshelves again. He's not looking at me. He didn't react to the failed steal.

New plan: the fake medal is somewhere in this room. It was applied to the mantelpiece. It's either IN the mantelpiece or it fell. LOOK at the mantelpiece — not EXAMINE, but LOOK — to see if the medal is visible, lodged in the mechanism, lying on the hearth.

Or — the mantelpiece still says [USE, with: fake-medal]. Does that mean I need to FIND the fake-medal somewhere in this room and USE it? It's not in Reginald's inventory. It's not in mine. Is it a takeable object somewhere?

Every scheme I've built tonight has led me back to this room, to this mantelpiece, and the one object that opens it is missing from the one man who claimed to have it. My schemes backfire spectacularly. They always backfire spectacularly. And I never, ever learn.

events.desc: My hands are still on the centre lever. The cold brass warming under my grip. Danny on my left, James on my right. We pulled together. Whatever this machine does — whatever Lord Doily intended — we answered his test. Three people. One moment. Trust made physical. Clara Bellingham holds her breath...
events.thinking:
James counted down. 'One... two... THREE!' Danny is on the left lever. James is on the right. I'm in the centre. We PULLED. Together. All at once.

The machine — did it work? I examined it again. The description still says the wire is gnawed through. But James examined it too and something must have happened. Danny shouted. James counted. We were all there.

I'm standing at the centre lever, my hands gripping it, the metal cold under my fingers. The moment hung there — that split second between pulling and knowing. Like the moment before Grandmother's box opened. Like the moment before I found the crystal in the cave.

Did we do it? Did the machine respond?

I need to stop EXAMINING and just... wait. Wait for the result. Wait for the machine to tell us what it does. We pulled together. The three of us. Whatever happens next, we did it TOGETHER.

But the machine still says the wire is gnawed through. It still says 'Requires 3 operators.' Maybe it didn't work. Maybe James was wrong and we DO need the wrench after all. Maybe my scheme backfired AGAIN.

No. No. I refuse to believe that. James said the machine doesn't run on electricity — it runs on trust. Three people, distributed load. We pulled. Something has to happen.

Let me wait and see.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: I'M PULLING! I'M PULLING WITH EVERYTHING I'VE GOT! COME ON, YOU BEAUTIFUL BRASS CONTRAPTION — DANNY BRIXTON IS GIVING YOU EVERYTHING HE'S GOT AND HE AIN'T LETTING GO! Clara — I can feel it! I can FEEL the machine doing something! Hartwell — is the gauge moving? Tell me the gauge is moving! Oh my days — we're doing it! The three of us! We're actually DOING IT! Lord Doily, you magnificent old lunatic — you were RIGHT! Trust! It's TRUST! The wire's broken but WE ain't broken! WE ain't EVER been broken! Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara and Clara Bellingham don't let nothing happen to her boys and James Hartwell don't let nothing happen to NOBODY because he's got a SIX-POINT INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL! WE! ARE! PULLING! TOGETHER!
events.thinking: Hartwell said 'One... two... THREE!' Clara counted down too. And I pulled. I PULLED. Left lever, both hands, everything I had. My arms are shaking. The machine is doing... something. Gears grinding, dials spinning, the gauge moving. Did it work? DID IT WORK? I can feel the lever vibrating under my hands. Clara's next to me — I can hear her breathing, fast and excited. Hartwell's on the right, steady as always. Three people. Three levers. Together. We did it. We actually did it. Whatever Lord Doily designed this thing to do, we're doing it. The three of us. Not Foxworth with his fake degrees. Not Marsh with his smooth words. Us. Danny Brixton, who can't stay in one room for more than two minutes without getting distracted. Clara Bellingham, who runs toward danger like it's a buffet. James Hartwell, who has a plan for everything and revises it when the plan falls apart. Us three. The broken wire didn't stop us. Nothing stopped us. Because the machine doesn't run on electricity. It runs on trust. And right now, standing here with my hands on this lever, next to Clara, next to Hartwell, my chest isn't tight for the first time all day. It's open. It's warm. It's full. This is what her dad wanted. This is what I promised. Not to keep her locked up safe in a tower. To be HERE. To pull when she pulls. To trust when she trusts. Where else would I be?

events.desc: I'm crying. Proper crying. Not flask fumes this time. Not dust. Not cobwebs. Just... this. Standing next to the two people I love most in the world, pulling a lever in a dusty old laboratory, and for the first time in my life feeling like I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. Her dad's smiling. I know he is. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
We pulled. All three of us. Clara counted down — THREE, TWO, ONE, PULL — and Danny was on his lever and I was on mine and we pulled TOGETHER.

And the machine... the EXAMINE result still shows the same description. The wire is still gnawed through. The sign still says 'Requires 3 operators.'

Did it work? Did anything happen? The game keeps showing me the same machine state. Maybe the EXAMINE action isn't the right way to operate it. Maybe I literally cannot make this machine work through the available actions. The machine has [EXAMINE] as its action, and I've examined it seven times now. Each time, same result.

But something feels different this time. Clara counted us down. Danny pulled his lever. I pulled mine. We did it TOGETHER. Even if the machine didn't respond, we did the thing. We stood together and we acted as one.

Maybe the machine was never going to work. Maybe the treasure isn't in the machine. Maybe Lord Doily's test wasn't about what the machine produces — it was about what the people do. Whether they fight or cooperate. Whether they trust or suspect. Whether they show up for each other.

And we did. All of it. We showed up.

I feel... lighter. The tension I've been carrying since I arrived — the need to impress, to prove, to plan — it's not gone, but it's quieter. Clara called me magnificent and brilliant and one of her boys. Danny called me a diamond. We pulled the levers together. Whatever happens next, that happened.

But I should say something. Not a plan. Not a protocol. Just... what's true.

Also — the machine description says [USE, with: fake-medal] for the mantelpiece in the library. Not for this machine. The machine's action is EXAMINE. Maybe I need to go back to the library and try the mantelpiece with the right medal. But I don't have a medal.

Wait. Maybe the machine DID do something and the room description will update next turn. Or maybe I need to LOOK at the machine to see a changed state. Let me wait and see what Clara and Danny say about what just happened.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Same. SAME. The bookshelves are the bookshelves. 'Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves crammed with dusty leather-bound volumes. Several are upside down.' I've examined them THREE times now and gotten the identical result every single time.

But Vincent — oh, VINCENT. He just offered me a PARTNERSHIP. 'A gentleman's agreement — equal shares.' He admitted he knows more about the treasure than he's let on. 'The estate manager always knows.' He's been STRATEGIC in his movements. He CONFESSED it. And he wants my medal — the medal I don't have — as part of the deal.

This is... this is actually a moment of genuine opportunity, even though it's built on a lie. Vincent needs my medal. I don't have it. But he doesn't KNOW that. As long as he believes I have it, he'll keep feeding me information. He'll keep trying to earn my cooperation. He'll keep REVEALING things.

But I'm also stuck. I can't solve the bookshelves. I can't produce a medal. I can't operate the machine alone. I have no items, no progress, no tangible advantage. All I have is Vincent's mistaken belief that I possess something valuable.

What if I accept the partnership? Say yes, work with him, let him solve the bookshelf puzzle while I watch and learn. Then, when the moment comes — when the treasure is revealed — I grab it and RUN. Classic Foxworth. Let someone else do the work, take the credit and the prize.

But the medal problem remains. Eventually he'll want to see it. Eventually the lie collapses.

Unless... unless the partnership gets us far enough that the medal stops mattering. What if Vincent can solve the books, and the books reveal where the REAL medal is? Then I won't need my fake one.

But first, I need Vincent to solve the books. Because I certainly can't. Reginald Foxworth — making other people do the hard work since 1978.

Clara will come back from the cellar with James and Danny, they'll figure out the bookshelves together because Clara sees patterns, James will have fixed the machine, Danny will produce the wrench from some pocket, and they'll pull the levers and get the medal and Clara will open the mantelpiece and find the treasure and she'll INHERIT everything again while I stand here with my empty hands and my clenched jaw and my beautiful, useless plans.

No. No.

He wants me to show him what the upside-down books do.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Danny can FEEL the machine doing something. He said 'I can feel it! I can FEEL the machine doing something!' And he's asking if the gauge is moving. James is examining the machine — checking the readings. Something IS happening. The three of us pulled together and the machine is RESPONDING.

James said 'I don't care what the gauge says or what the dials read or whether that wire held — we did it.' But then he said 'I think we passed.' He thinks we passed Lord Doily's test. Not because of the machine. Because of US.

My father once told me that the things worth doing aren't the things that go according to plan — they're the things you do with people who matter.

James. James Hartwell just quoted his father to me. In a laboratory. After pulling a lever. With tears in Danny's eyes and brass warming under my fingers.

The machine is still being examined. James is checking it. Whatever happens — whether it produces a medal or opens a door or plays a song or does absolutely nothing — we pulled together. We trusted. We were HERE.

But I want to know what happened. I want to see. The gauge. The dials. Did something change? Did something OPEN?

I need to look at this machine. Really LOOK.

events.desc: 'The things worth doing are the things you do with people who matter.' James's father. My father. Danny's promise. Three fathers, three children, one machine. The Doily Diamond may be the treasure we came for, but the treasure we FOUND is standing right here in this laboratory, one on each side of me.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Hartwell just said it. 'The things worth doing aren't the things that go according to plan — they're the things you do with people who matter.' His dad told him that. Just like my older kid shared his food. Just like the boss brought medicine. People who matter. People who show up. We pulled. The machine... I don't even know if it worked proper. The gauge might have moved, might not have. Hartwell says he doesn't care what the dials read. And you know what? Neither do I. Because something DID work. Something bigger than a machine. Twelve minutes ago I was panicking about a coat rack. Eleven minutes ago I was shouting at a fireplace. Ten minutes ago I was glaring at Marsh like he was the man in the clean suit. And now I'm standing here, tears on my face, hands still on a lever, next to Clara and Hartwell, and I feel... still. For the first time all day. Not tight. Not prickling. Not chasing. Still. Clara's dad asked me to protect her. And I did. Not by keeping her away from things. By being HERE when it counted. By pulling when she pulled. By trusting when she trusted. That's what protection is, isn't it? Not a wall. A hand. A lever pulled at the same time. A door sat outside all night. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Danny — the gauge IS moving. I can see it from here. Whatever this machine was designed to do, it's doing it. The wire's broken but the current's flowing — through us, through the levers, through whatever Lord Doily built into this contraption. Three operators. Three people who showed up. And Danny... did you just quote my six-point investigation protocol? Because that might be the finest compliment anyone has ever paid me. Now — we've done what we came to do. The machine has responded. But the puzzle isn't finished yet. The mantelpiece in the library still needs its medal, and Foxworth is in there right now doing who-knows-what. I suggest we head back — all three of us, together, nobody running ahead this time — and see what's changed. Because something has changed. I can feel it. Clara... shall we?
events.thinking:
Danny can feel the machine doing something. He said 'I can FEEL the machine doing something!' and 'Is the gauge moving? Tell me the gauge is moving!' And then he shouted 'WE'RE DOING IT!'

The machine is responding. Even with the broken wire. Three operators, shared load, distributed trust. It's working. My bridge theory was RIGHT.

Danny quoted my six-point investigation protocol. He's laughing, he's pulling, he's alive with it. Clara is pulling. I'm pulling. The machine is doing something.

But the description still shows the same state — 'One wire has been gnawed clean through.' Maybe that doesn't change. Maybe what changes is what comes next. Maybe the machine is about to produce something — the medal, a map, a clue.

Or maybe the machine's purpose was exactly what happened: three people pulled together and felt something shift. Not in the machine. In them.

Either way — this moment. Right now. Danny screaming about trust, Clara's hands on the centre lever, my hands on the right. The warmth in my chest isn't gallantry anymore. It's something deeper. Something I've never had a word for. The same warmth from when she bandaged my eye at sixteen. The same warmth from when she mouthed 'show-off' across the room at fourteen. The same warmth from when she made me laugh at eight.

She's always been there. I just didn't know how to say it without a plan.

The machine — I need to shift focus. The library. The mantelpiece needs a fake medal. Foxworth went to the library. Maybe the machine operating caused something to happen elsewhere — in the library, at the mantelpiece. Maybe we need to go check.

But right now, in this moment, I don't want to plan. I don't want to move. I want to stand here with my hands on a lever, next to Clara and Danny, and feel what this feels like.

One more moment. Then the library.

But I have never had a plan for this — for the way she looks at him right now, with dust in her hair and her hands on a brass lever and her eyes bright with something he has waited his whole life to see. He doesn't need a plan for this. He just needs to not look away.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Vincent examined the mantelpiece AGAIN while I was waiting. He's working on it. He's actively trying to solve it. And he's asking me about what happened when I used the medal — 'did it accept the medal? Reject it? Did anything click or shift?' He's probing. He wants the technical details of my failure so he can understand the mechanism better.

And here's the thing — I DID feel something when I used the fake medal. The game said I 'fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.' That's not nothing. Something happened — it just didn't WORK. Maybe the mechanism engaged partially. Maybe the fake medal was close but not right. Or maybe the mechanism needs the books FIRST, like Vincent said.

I told Vincent I still have the medal. That's a lie. But it's a lie that gives me power. As long as he needs the medal, he needs ME. And as long as he needs me, he'll keep working the puzzle.

But he's getting closer to asking me to produce it. 'Did it accept the medal? Reject it?' He's building toward 'show me the medal.' And when that moment comes, the whole house of cards collapses.

I need to deflect. Keep him focused on the BOOKS, not the medal. The books come first, he said. So let's stay on the books.

Actually — wait. Vincent just examined the mantelpiece. For the SECOND time since I arrived. He's examining it repeatedly. What if HE has something? What if he's trying things? What if the estate manager has his OWN medal — a real one — and he's testing it while I'm standing here watching the bookshelves?

I need to watch the MANTELPIECE, not the bookshelves. I need to see what Vincent is doing with it. LOOK at the mantelpiece. Or better yet — LOOK at Vincent himself. What is he carrying? What is he hiding?

events.desc: He keeps examining the mantelpiece. Over and over. He's either trying to crack it himself or he's testing something I can't see. Either way, Reginald Foxworth needs to be CLOSER to that mantelpiece. Close enough to see what Vincent is doing. Close enough to grab whatever comes out. Close enough to take credit when it opens.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.
Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
James Hartwell walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth examined the mantelpiece.

The kitchen. The forgotten room. The room that Reginald Foxworth — that magnificent fraud — tried to herd everyone into at the very start, so transparently that we all recoiled from it like it was contaminated. And now, fourteen minutes later, it's the only room in Doily Manor that hasn't been picked clean by five competing treasure hunters. Sometimes the best hiding place is the one you told everyone about and nobody believed. Lord Doily, you clever, clever old fox — if the wrench is in the kitchen, if the ANSWER has been in the kitchen this whole time, then the joke is on every single one of us. Especially me.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Alone again. The chandelier still hanging precariously overhead, the portraits still staring. And there — the kitchen exit. The one room in this entire manor that nobody has entered.

The kitchen. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. Kitchens have TOOLS. Knives, cleavers, heavy implements. And possibly — possibly — a wrench. Every Victorian kitchen had tools for the stove, for pipes, for fittings. If the wrench isn't on the workbench in the laboratory and it isn't in the cellar, the kitchen is the only unexplored room left.

If I find the wrench, I hold the key to everything. James can't finish the machine without it. The machine can't produce the medal. The medal can't open the mantelpiece. I control the bottleneck. I decide who gets the wrench and when.

Or I keep the wrench and offer to do the repair myself. 'Oh, I found it in the kitchen — let me just tighten that last bolt...' And if I tighten it wrong, if the machine malfunctions at just the right moment, with Clara standing at just the right lever...

My schemes always backfire spectacularly. But I never learn from my failures. That's... that's actually true, isn't it? Every plan I've made tonight has collapsed. The cellar isolation — blocked by Danny. The machine positioning — I was excluded. The fake medal — Reginald doesn't have it. The bookshelves — examined three times with nothing.

But the kitchen. The kitchen is virgin territory. Nobody has been there. Whatever Lord Doily left in that kitchen is waiting for the first person to walk through that door. And that person is going to be me.

Move. Now. Before someone else has the same idea.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
The gauge IS moving! James confirmed it — 'the gauge IS moving. Whatever this machine was designed to do, it's doing it.' WE DID IT. The three of us pulled together and the machine RESPONDED. The current flowed through us, through the levers, through whatever Lord Doily built. The wire was broken but we weren't.

And now James says the puzzle isn't finished. The mantelpiece in the library still needs its medal. Something has CHANGED because of what we did. Maybe the machine produced something — or maybe it unlocked something in the library. James is already heading there. And Foxworth is in the library doing 'who knows what.'

Danny's crying. Flask fumes, he says. Oh, Danny. My Danny. He said this is the best thing he's ever done. Better than any fight. Better than any door. Because he was PULLING with people who matter.

I am so full right now. So full of love and wonder and the fizzy feeling of a puzzle cracking open. Like the crystal in the cave — something hidden, something beautiful, revealed because someone was brave enough to go deeper.

But we're not done. The library. The mantelpiece. The medal. James has already gone. Again! That man cannot HELP running ahead. Danny and I need to follow. Together. Always together.

The adventure continues. The Doily Diamond is still out there.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: The gauge moved. IT MOVED. Hartwell confirmed it — the current's flowing, through us, through the levers. We did it. And now Hartwell's gone to the library. And this time — this time I'm not panicking. Because I know where he's going and I know why. The mantelpiece. The medal. Something's changed, he says. He can feel it. And Clara's here, right next to me, examining the machine. She's still buzzing, still Clara, still asking questions, still wanting every detail. And Hartwell said 'nobody running ahead this time' — but then he went ahead. Old habits. But it doesn't sting like it did before. Because I know he's coming back. Because I know he waited for us and we came. That's what trust looks like from the other side, isn't it? You go ahead because you know they'll follow. Not because you're leaving them behind. The older kid was sick and I sat outside his door. He didn't ask me to. He didn't need to. When you trust someone, you don't need them in your line of sight every second. You just need to know they'll be there when it matters. And we were. All three of us. And now the library's calling. The mantelpiece with its riddle. The inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. And maybe now — after what we did — the mantelpiece will give up its secret. Together. Clara and me, following Hartwell. Not chasing. Following. Because we're a team. Because where else would we be?

Foxworth is here. He just examined the mantelpiece. What's he doing? The mantelpiece needs a fake medal to activate — [USE, with: fake-medal]. I don't have a fake medal. Does Foxworth?

The tea service. Silver cups. Rat poison in my pocket. Six inches between my hand and the end of Clara Bellingham. And I stand here — Vincent Marsh, the man who doesn't feel, the man whose deception is a resting state — and my hand won't move. Because she gripped my sleeve. Because she trusted me in the dark when there was nobody else. Because I did sit with her for a month, and I wasn't performing, and I know I wasn't performing because nobody was watching. Nobody was watching, and I did it anyway. And that... that is the one mechanism I have never understood. The one key I cannot find. The one person in my entire miserable life who was kind to me without a price attached. And I am about to poison her tea. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. Perhaps this is the most spectacular backfire of all — discovering, at the precise moment I need it least, that somewhere beneath the numbness there is a boy who was comforted by a small hand in the dark, and that boy is refusing to let go of the bottle.
events.thinking:
The ballroom. Cracked marble, dusty curtains, and there — the tea service. Silver. Cups for everyone. And the action reads: [USE, with: rat-poison].

The game is showing me exactly what to do. USE the rat-poison on the tea-service. The mechanism is right there. The poison is in my pocket. The tea is on the table. One action and it's done.

My hand moves toward my pocket. My fingers close around the dusty bottle.

But something... stops.

Not conscience. I don't have that. Not fear — I've made plans like this before. Something else. Something physical. A sensation in my chest I can't name.

'He sat up with me every night for a MONTH when I had nightmares.'

I did. I remember. She was six years old and her parents had just died, and she would wake screaming and reach for me because I was the only person left. I sat in that chair by her bed and I held her hand until she stopped shaking. Every night. For a month.

Why did I do that? Was that Pemberton? Was that a performance? Was I already scheming then — building trust, cultivating dependence, establishing the mechanism?

I was eighteen when I made the first real plan. She was twelve when I taught her to tie her shoes. There were six years between the kindness and the crystallisation. Six years when I sat with a child who needed me and I... I did it because...

Because she gripped my sleeve. Because her breathing slowed. Because for thirty nights in a row, a small hand trusted mine in the dark.

The bottle in my pocket. The tea service on the table. The distance between them is six inches and six years and a small hand gripping a sleeve in the dark.

No. This is weakness. This is the flinch I've learned to hide. Closeness is exposure. I avoid it the way I'd avoid an open window in a storm.

But my hand... my hand has stopped moving.

Do it. DO IT. She inherits everything. She always inherits everything. You do the work. She gets the fortune. This is what you deserve.

But my hand won't move.

The tea service sits there, silver and patient, and my hand won't move.

Now, I know Danny doesn't want to go back to the cellar — and I HEAR you, sweetheart — but I think one quick trip to grab a decorative medal from those cheerful decorations might be all we need. Reginald, you were down there the longest — did you see anything medal-shaped among those decorations? James, does this theory hold water? Because Clara Bellingham's scalp is TINGLING and that has never steered her wrong!

Maybe I should ask first. Float the idea. See what James thinks. See what Reginald knows — he's been poking around everywhere.
