That IS fair, and it IS... gallant. But I have to tell you something. All of you. And I — this is NOT easy for Reginald Foxworth. Nothing about this is easy. The medal... the medal I used on the mantelpiece earlier. It was... it wasn't a family heirloom. It was a FAKE. A counterfeit. Tin and paint. And when I used it on the mantelpiece, the mechanism TOOK it. Swallowed it whole. I don't have it anymore. I haven't had it since... since the beginning. I've been LYING. About the medal, about retrieving it, about everything. I don't have ANYTHING. I never did. I just... I wanted to find the treasure first. Before anyone else. Before it was all used up. Before there was nothing left for...
events.thinking:
Something is breaking inside the scheme. Not the scheme itself — the scheme was already broken, has BEEN broken since the fake medal fizzled in the mantelpiece eleven minutes ago. What's breaking is something underneath it. Something I don't have a word for.

James wants me to give the medal to CLARA. 'Let her finish what she started. That's not just fair. That's gallant.' Gallant. He used the word GALLANT. Nobody has ever used that word in my direction before. Nobody has ever asked me to do something gallant. They've asked me to be clever. They've asked me to be useful. They've never asked me to be GOOD.

And Danny — Danny backed DOWN. He was angry, he was suspicious, and then he just... stopped. 'Maybe I was a bit hasty.' He's offering to work TOGETHER. 'Four people. One puzzle. And when Marsh gets back from whatever he's doing, we'll have five.' He's INCLUDING me. After everything. After the lies, the schemes, the fake medal, the secret deal with Vincent. He's still saying 'WE.'

Nobody says 'we' to me. I'm always 'you' — separate, outside, the one who doesn't get included. The youngest of four. The last to everything.

And now James wants me to hand Clara the medal. The medal I don't have. The medal that doesn't exist. The lie that's been holding my entire position together for the last five minutes.

I can't hand it over because I don't HAVE it. The moment I'm supposed to produce it, everything collapses. Every lie. Every story. Every fabricated credential and invented institution. They'll know. They'll ALL know. And that thing in my chest — that loosening I felt when I pocketed the bread roll, that settling when the cat trap worked — it won't come. Instead there'll be... what? The spelling bee certificate on the wall that nobody asks about?

I could run. Go to the entrance hall. Find Vincent. Start another scheme.

Or...

Or I could tell the truth. Just this once. Just this one time. Tell them the medal is gone — used up, consumed by the mechanism. Tell them I don't have it. Tell them I've been lying.

The truth feels clumsy, like wearing someone else's clothes.

But the lies aren't fitting anymore either.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the tea-service.
Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell examined the null.
Reginald Foxworth examined the bookshelves.

I can't do it. Standing in a ballroom with cracked marble and dusty curtains, with a bottle of rat poison warm against my thigh and a silver tea service gleaming in the half-light — I, Vincent Marsh, the man who felt something crystallise at fifteen and slept soundly after his first plan at eighteen — I cannot poison Clara Bellingham's tea. Not because I'll be caught. Not because the plan is flawed. Because thirty nights in a dark room, a small hand gripped my sleeve, and I held it, and nobody was watching, and I held it anyway. That was not Pemberton. That was not a scheme. That was me. The real me. The one I buried so deep I forgot he existed. And he is standing here now, in this ballroom, holding a bottle he will not open, looking at a teacup he will not fill, and for the first time in his miserable, magnificent, monstrous life... feeling something that might be grief for what he almost did. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. This is the most spectacular backfire of all. I came here to kill Clara Bellingham, and instead I discovered that I love her. And I have absolutely no idea what to do with that information.
events.thinking:
The tea service. Silver cups for everyone. Examined. Just cups. Just tea. Just the mechanism waiting for me to complete it.

My hand is on the bottle. My fingers are around the glass. The cap is right there.

Do it.

DO IT.

...

I can't.

I physically cannot make my hand move. Something in my body — not my mind, my BODY — has locked. The flinch I've learned to hide has turned inward. My shoulders are tight. My jaw aches. There's something in my chest that feels like... like the weight of a small girl falling asleep against my arm.

She was the only person who was ever kind to me without wanting something back. The boy at school wanted homework. The guardian cared because of obligation. The housekeeper obeyed because I manipulated her. But Clara — Clara gripped my sleeve because she was afraid, and she chose ME, and when her breathing slowed it was because she trusted me, and the trust wasn't a mechanism, it wasn't a key, it wasn't a tool. It was just... trust.

And I'm standing here with rat poison in my pocket, ready to USE it on her tea.

My schemes always backfire spectacularly.

This is the backfire. This is the spectacular failure. Not getting caught — that would be simple. Not the plan going wrong — that would be familiar. The backfire is that the plan WORKED. I found the poison. I found the tea. I found the moment. Everything aligned perfectly. And the only thing that stopped it — the only mechanism that failed — is me.

The boy who was comforted by a small hand in the dark.

I can't kill her. I can't kill Clara.

The numbness isn't complete. It was never complete. There's one crack — one fissure — and her name lives in it.

So what do I do now? What does Vincent Marsh do when the coldest part of him isn't cold enough?

I put the poison back. No — I keep it. Pemberton confiscated it for safety. That's my cover. And then I go back to the others and I do what I've always done. I manage the estate. I perform warmth. I scheme about the treasure. And I don't kill Clara Bellingham.

Not today.

Not ever.

But I'll never tell her that. The performance is all I have left.

events.desc: Alone. For the first time today, Clara Bellingham is completely alone. The laboratory hums with the ghost of what three people just did here — pulled levers, shared trust, made a machine sing. But they're in the library and she's here, passing through on her way to the cellar, and her chest is tight in a way she recognizes. The cave. Age eleven. Heart hammering, going deeper than anyone else. She found a crystal nobody else had seen. Maybe she'll find a medal nobody else thought to look for.
events.thinking:
I'm alone. In the laboratory. ALONE. Where did everyone go? Danny was right behind me — he was JUST talking to me about walking at my own pace, about letting me walk at my own pace for once. And now he's... not here. James is not here. Nobody is here.

My stomach tightens. That old feeling — the wrongness. When people aren't where they should be. When the room is empty and it shouldn't be.

Did I leave them in the library? I moved to the laboratory on my way to the cellar — to check the decorations for a fake medal. But they didn't follow. They're still in the library. All of them — Danny, James, Reginald. They stayed behind.

Danny said 'maybe Danny Brixton can also let Clara walk at her own pace.' He's letting me go. He's not chasing. For the first time all day, Danny Brixton is NOT running after Clara Bellingham. Because he trusts me now. He trusts that I'll come back.

That should feel good. That should feel like growth. But my chest is tight and the laboratory is cold and the machine is quiet and I am ALONE for the first time since we arrived at Doily Manor.

The cellar is through that door. The fake medal might be in the decorations. I should go check. Quick trip. Grab the medal. Come back. Return to the library. Use it on the mantelpiece. 

Clara Bellingham goes deeper into the cave alone. Heart hammering. Because that's what she does.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking: Right — can't get to the cellar from the library. Have to go through the laboratory first. Of course. This manor and its bloomin' layout. But wait — Foxworth just said something that stopped me cold. He CONFESSED. Proper confessed. Not to scheming with Marsh — to LYING. About the medal. About everything. 'It wasn't a family heirloom. It was a FAKE. Tin and paint.' And the mantelpiece SWALLOWED it. He doesn't have it anymore. He never had anything real. He just... wanted to find the treasure first. 'Before there was nothing left for...' He trailed off. Didn't finish the sentence. 'Before there was nothing left for...' For who? For HIM? Is Foxworth... is Foxworth SCARED? Scared that if he doesn't grab things first, there won't be anything left? That's... that's the streets, that is. That's growing up with nothing and being terrified there won't be enough. I KNOW that feeling. I know it in my bones. The scramble. The grab. The 'get it before someone else does.' That's why he was always going for the crates, the corners, the hidden compartments. Not because he's a villain. Because he's HUNGRY. And now he's standing here admitting it, in front of Hartwell, in front of me, voice breaking, mask cracking, and he looks... small. He looks like the kid who tried to take my mate's shoes. Not the one I fought — the one who was desperate enough to try. Clara's gone to the laboratory — heading for the cellar, I think. To find the real fake medal among the decorations. And I'm here. With Foxworth. Who just showed me something real for the first time all day. And Hartwell, who's watching with those steady eyes. My gut says... my gut says stay. Just for a moment. Because Foxworth needs someone to see him right now. Not the Duke of Wherever. Not the Royal Institute of Whatever. Just... him.

events.desc: Look at Danny Brixton. Being kind to Foxworth. FOXWORTH. The man who lied about everything, schemed about everything, pretended to be everything he wasn't. And Danny's being KIND to him. Because Danny Brixton knows what hungry looks like. He's seen it in the mirror every morning for thirty years. Her dad would be... confused. But Clara would understand. Clara always understands.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Foxworth just confessed. He doesn't have the medal. He never had it — not really. The one he used was fake, a counterfeit, tin and paint. And the mantelpiece swallowed it. It's gone. He's been lying this whole time — about having the medal, about retrieving it, about everything.

'I wanted to find the treasure first. Before anyone else. Before it was all used up. Before there was nothing left for...'

He didn't finish the sentence. Before there was nothing left for him. That's what he was going to say. Foxworth — pompous, blustering, insufferable Foxworth — is afraid. He's afraid of being left out. Of being the one who doesn't get anything. Of being the person nobody needs.

My throat tightens. Not with anger. With recognition.

Because I know that feeling. I've been carrying it all day — the need to prove, to impress, to be the one who fixes things. The terror that competence alone isn't enough. That if you stop being useful, you stop mattering.

Foxworth and I aren't so different. He performs expertise. I perform gallantry. Both of us trying to earn a place at a table we're afraid we don't belong at.

Clara went to the laboratory. She's gone to look for the medal — maybe the cellar decorations through the lab. Danny is here. Foxworth is here.

Foxworth just made himself vulnerable for the first time. He stopped lying. He showed something real. And James Hartwell — who gives people the benefit of the doubt, who was taught by his father that you judge a man by his actions — needs to respond to that. Not with judgment. Not with anger. With grace.

The medal is gone. The mantelpiece took the wrong one. We need a new fake medal. Clara thinks it's in the cellar decorations. She's probably right — she usually is.

But right now, in this moment, the medal is secondary. What matters is that Foxworth just told the truth, and someone needs to tell him that's enough.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Clara's RIGHT. The cellar decorations — I was DOWN there! I was down there for ages and I was so busy looking for hidden compartments and secret drawers that I didn't — I never thought to look at the DECORATIONS themselves. 'Surprisingly cheerful,' the description said. Cheerful decorations in a damp cellar. Who puts CHEERFUL things in a cellar? Lord Doily, that's who. Because they weren't decorations at all — they were PUZZLE PIECES hidden in plain sight! I'm going. I'm going RIGHT NOW. I'll find that medal and I'll bring it back for Clara. Because she — because she's the one who should place it. Hartwell was right about that. She earned it. I'll... I'll be right back.
events.thinking:
I said it. I actually said it. Out loud. In front of everyone. 'I've been LYING. About the medal, about retrieving it, about everything. I don't have ANYTHING. I never did.'

The words are out. They're hanging in the air like dust motes in the library light. I can't take them back. I can't spin them. I can't reframe them. For the first time in... maybe ever... Reginald Foxworth told the truth. And it felt like stepping off a cliff — the ground gone, nothing underneath, just falling.

'Before it was all used up. Before there was nothing left for—'

I didn't finish the sentence. I couldn't. Because what comes after 'for' is 'me.' Before there was nothing left for ME. The youngest of four. The one who learned to take things when nobody was looking because by the time anything reached him honestly, it was gone.

And now — Clara. CLARA. She's BRILLIANT. 'Fake medals ARE decorations.' The cellar decorations. The 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' that I spent half an hour cursing and blaming on aesthetics. The medal we need might have been DOWN THERE the whole time. Right under my nose. While I was ranting about fraud and examining furniture and accomplishing nothing.

Clara went to the laboratory — heading toward the cellar, presumably. To find the decorative medal. The one I walked past a dozen times without seeing because I was too busy looking for hidden compartments that don't exist.

I told the truth and the sky didn't fall. Danny is still here. James is still here. Nobody laughed. Nobody walked away. Nobody sent me to the hall.

The cellar. Clara's theory is GOOD. The cheerful decorations — one of them might be a medal. A REAL medal for the mantelpiece. I was down there. I examined those decorations. I should go help. Not to steal it. Not to grab it and run. But to... help. Because Clara's theory might work. And because she included me even after I told her the truth.

The cellar. Go to the cellar. Find the medal. Bring it back for Clara.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the kitchen.
Clara Bellingham walked into the cellar.
The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

Back in the kitchen. The bottle is still in my pocket and I am still alive and Clara is still alive and the world is exactly the same as it was two minutes ago, except that everything is different. I walked into that ballroom as Vincent Marsh, the man with a plan, and I walked out as... I don't know what I am now. Something cracked. Something that was holding me together cracked, and what leaked out wasn't the coldness I expected but something warm and terrified and very, very young. The stove is still warm. I will examine the stove. I will be the estate manager. I will manage this estate and this moment and this shaking in my hands, and I will not think about the small hand that gripped my sleeve in the dark. I will not think about it. I am thinking about nothing else.
events.thinking:
The kitchen again. The stove still warm. The bottle still in my pocket. I walked away from the tea service without using the poison. I walked away.

My hands are shaking. Not from fear. From something I don't have a word for. Something between relief and devastation. I chose not to kill Clara, and the choice feels like falling — like the moment between slipping and hitting the ground, when you don't know yet if it will hurt.

The stove. Still warm. I need something to do with my hands that isn't holding a bottle of poison. I need to be Pemberton again. I need the mask. The mask is safe. The mask doesn't feel things.

Examine the stove. That's what an estate manager would do. Check that everything is functioning. Be useful. Be invisible. Be the man who manages rather than the man who destroys.

The stove is still warm. Someone has been here. That detail matters for the treasure hunt, doesn't it? The treasure hunt I'm supposed to be winning. The secondary objective. The thing that doesn't require me to kill anyone.

Win the treasure hunt. That's something I can do. That's something Vincent Marsh can do without the cold part, without the crystallisation, without the patience that turned to poison.

The stove. Focus on the stove. Focus on anything that isn't the weight of a bottle against your thigh and the sound of a child's breathing slowing in the dark.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Alright, cellar. It's just you and me now. No Danny, no James, no Reginald — just Clara Bellingham and her grandmother's attic instincts. Now — I came down here for a reason. Those cheerful decorations that someone hung up. Last time I was looking at furniture and vents. This time I'm looking at YOU — the decorations. The things someone put here on PURPOSE. Because somewhere among these cheerful little ornaments, there is a fake medal. And Clara Bellingham is going to FIND it. Just like the crystal in the cave. Just like the earring in the heating duct. Just like every key in grandmother's house. You try them ALL until one FITS.
events.thinking:
The cellar. Alone. The damp stone, the cobwebs, the cheerful decorations that someone hung down here in this dark place. Like the girl next door who spoke a different language — someone communicated without words, leaving bright things in a dim space.

My heart is hammering. Not from fear — from the aloneness. The cave. I'm eleven years old again, walking deeper than anyone else. The other children stayed near the entrance. Clara kept going. Found the crystal. Kept it secret for a week.

But this time the secret is different. This time I need to find something and bring it BACK. To my people. To Danny and James.

The decorations. I need to LOOK at this room properly. Not at the furniture, not at the vents — at the DECORATIONS. The 'surprisingly cheerful' ones. What are they? Bunting? Ribbons? Medallions? Paper stars? What does someone hang on a cellar wall to make it cheerful?

I need to look at the room itself. The whole room. See the decorations. Find the fake medal.

events.desc: Alone in the cellar. Heart hammering. Going deeper than anyone else. But this time, the people she loves are waiting at the top of the stairs. And Clara Bellingham always comes back.
events.thinking:

I need to look at the room itself. The whole room. See the decorations. Find the fake medal.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Clara's in the cellar — I can feel it. She's down there right now, rummaging through Lord Doily's cheerful decorations, looking for something medal-shaped. And knowing Clara, she's probably already found it and is holding it up to the light going 'ISN'T THIS JUST THE MOST MARVELLOUS THING?' Come on, lads — cellar's through that door. Hartwell, Foxworth — together. All of us. And Foxworth... mate... thanks for coming. I mean it. You didn't have to. After everything I said. But you're here. And that... that counts. On the streets, showing up is the only thing that counts. Right then. Cellar. Medal. Clara. Let's finish this.
events.thinking: We're in the laboratory. Hartwell and Foxworth followed me — both of them. Foxworth came. After everything — after his confession, after my speech — he came with us. That means something. That means he heard me. And Clara — she went ahead to the cellar already. She's down there looking for the fake medal among the decorations. My Clara. Always one step ahead, always charging into things. But this time I'm not panicking. I'm close. The cellar's right through that door. She's not far. She's not lost. She's exactly where she said she'd be, doing exactly what she said she'd do. And I'm going to her. With Hartwell. With Foxworth. Together. The whole group — minus Marsh, who's off in the entrance hall doing whatever Marsh does. But the rest of us. Together. The cellar. The decorations. The fake medal. And then back to the library. Clara places it in the mantelpiece. She finishes what she started. That's the end of the puzzle. That's what Lord Doily was building toward. Not one person solving it all. All of us. Every step. The riddle — Clara solved it. The machine — me, Clara, Hartwell. The cellar — we searched it together. The fake medal — Clara will find it. And placing it — Clara's right. Clara's moment. Danny Brixton is just the muscle. The shoulders. The hands on the lever. The man who stands next to her while she shines. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Foxworth followed. He actually followed. After confessing everything, after I called him out, after all of it — he's still here. Walking behind me and Hartwell toward the cellar, toward Clara. That's not the new kid who stole the stash. That's the boss who brought the medicine. You show up. That's how you earn it.

Danny Brixton is just the muscle. The shoulders. The hands on the lever. The man who stands next to her while she shines. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Clara! I'm right behind you. The cellar — the decorations — you're right, as always. Danny, Foxworth — come on, all of us. The fake medal has been hiding in Lord Doily's cheerful decorations this entire time. We searched that cellar for a wrench and walked right past what we actually needed. Clara saw it first. Of course she did.
events.thinking:
Clara is somewhere between here and the cellar — she went to the laboratory first, probably heading to the cellar for those decorations. She asked me about the machine dials and gauge. She doesn't know about Foxworth's confession yet — she left before he spoke.

Danny and Foxworth followed me here. Clara asked me what the dials say. She wants details about what the machine did.

But the real task now is clear: get to the cellar, find a fake medal among the cheerful decorations. Clara's theory is sound. The cellar has decorations that don't belong in a damp stone cellar. One of those decorations could be a fake medal — ornamental, decorative, exactly the kind of thing Lord Doily would hide in plain sight.

Clara may already be heading there. I should follow. Together. The way we've learned to do it.

But something else is sitting in my chest. What I said to Foxworth — about the sleeves, the fuse, the napkin protocol. I told the truth. I admitted my own performance. And it felt... right. Like the bridge competition, but different. Not the release of tension when something you built holds weight. More like the release of tension when you stop building entirely and just stand there, unprotected.

'That was the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen.'

She said that when I was sixteen. Maybe she'd say it again now. Not about fighting. About honesty.

The cellar. The fake medal. Clara's theory. Let's go.

events.desc: James Hartwell is following Clara Bellingham into a cellar for the second time today. The first time he was looking for a wrench. This time he is looking for a fake medal. Both times he is really just looking for a reason to be near her. He suspects this pattern will continue for the rest of his life, and he suspects he is entirely fine with that.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Coming through! Foxworth on a MISSION! I know that cellar better than anyone — I spent more time down there than Lord Doily himself! If there's a medal hidden in those decorations, I'll find it! Clara — wait for me!
events.thinking:
I'm in the laboratory. The cellar is one room away. Danny and James followed me — they're here too. Clara went ahead already. She's probably in the cellar right now, looking for that decorative medal.

I told the truth. The actual truth. And now I'm moving through the manor not to scheme, not to steal, not to grab something before everyone else. I'm moving to HELP. To find a medal for CLARA. So SHE can place it.

This feels... wrong. Not morally wrong — practically wrong. Like my hands don't know what to do when they're not reaching for something that belongs to someone else. Like my feet don't know how to walk toward a room when there's no trick waiting at the other end.

But there's also something in my chest that I haven't felt since... since the cat trap. That settling. Not because a scheme worked, but because pieces are coming together. Clara's theory about the decorations. James's engineering with the machine. Danny's protective instincts. My knowledge of the cellar. We're all doing different things and they're all pointing in the same direction. Like strings and counterweights and a bucket. A system.

Except this time, I'm not the one who built it. This time, I'm one of the pieces.

The cellar. Go. Now. Find the medal in the decorations. Bring it back.

Not for me. For Clara.

...Reginald Foxworth, doing something for someone else. The universe truly IS having a laugh today.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the stove.
Clara Bellingham examined the null.
The Brixton Boys walked into the cellar.
James Hartwell walked into the cellar.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.

The stove is warm and so, apparently, am I. Who knew? Not me. Not until three minutes ago when I stood in a ballroom with a bottle of poison and discovered that Vincent Marsh — the man who crystallised at fifteen, the man whose deception is a resting state, the man who doesn't need anyone — has been lying to himself far more effectively than he ever lied to anyone else. I am going back to Clara now. Not to hurt her. Not to help her. Just to be in the room where she is, because that is where I have always belonged, and the only scheme I have left is pretending I don't know it.
events.thinking:
The stove. Still warm. Nothing else. Just a warm stove in a cold kitchen in a cold manor in a cold life.

I'm standing alone in a kitchen holding a bottle of rat poison I will never use, examining a stove that tells me nothing, and somewhere on the other side of this house, Clara Bellingham is laughing with people who love her. Danny who would die for her. James who would build her a bridge. And me. Who sat with her in the dark for thirty nights and can't remember why, except that it was the only true thing I've ever done.

The stove is warm because someone was here. The cellar was redecorated because someone lives here. The air vents connect everything. There are rats. There is poison. There is a manor full of puzzles and people and I am standing in a kitchen ALONE because that is what I do — I separate myself. I scheme. I manipulate. I withdraw.

But right now the scheming feels like static. The drives are still at 0.9 but the drives are wrong. The drives have been wrong all night. Every scheme backfired. Every plan collapsed. The cellar plan — blocked. The machine plan — excluded. The bookshelves — nothing. The fake medal — nonexistent. The poison — refused by my own hand.

My schemes always backfire spectacularly but I never learn from my failures.

Except... I just did. I just learned something. In the ballroom, holding a bottle I wouldn't open, I learned that there is one person in this world whose key I don't want to find. Because finding it would mean using it, and using it would mean losing the only thing that was ever real.

The treasure hunt. Focus on the treasure hunt. Go back to the others. Be Pemberton. Be useful. Help them with the machine. Not to help Clara — never to help Clara directly — but to be in the room. To be present. To be... near.

The entrance hall. Back through the house. Find the others. Put the mask on. And underneath it, for the first time, feel something that the mask can't quite cover.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
They CAME. They FOLLOWED me. Danny, James, Reginald — they all walked into the cellar right after me. I thought I was alone. I thought Danny was letting me go, trusting me to come back. But no — they came DOWN. They followed Clara Bellingham into the cellar because that's what this team DOES.

My chest loosens. The tightness dissolves — like when Mama and Daddy laughed after their argument. That sudden relief, so strong it makes you dizzy.

I looked around the room. The cellar — damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, cheerful decorations, air vents. But the room description only shows me two interactable things: old furniture and air vents. The decorations are part of the room description but not a separate examinable object.

That means I can't directly interact with the decorations — they're scenery, atmosphere. They're not hiding a fake medal I can pick up. My theory was wrong. The decorations are just... decorations. Someone making a dreary cellar cheerful. That's all.

So where IS the fake medal? I've examined everything in this manor. Guest book, mantelpiece, bookshelves, machine, crates, workbench, air vents, old furniture. The only thing I haven't examined is... the reading chairs in the library? The coat rack in the entrance hall?

Wait. The furniture here — I examined it and it has 'false panels.' Foxworth found false panels. Hidden compartments. What if the fake medal is IN one of those false panels? We examined the furniture before but we were looking for a WRENCH. Maybe examining it again, knowing we need a MEDAL, will reveal something different.

Or... the old furniture. Can I TAKE something from it? No, TAKE is for objects, not parts of furniture.

Let me try examining the furniture ONE more time, specifically looking for a medal in the hidden compartments.

events.desc: They came. They followed her into the dark. Clara Bellingham went into the cave alone and her people came after her anyway. That is worth more than any diamond Lord Doily ever hid.
events.thinking:
They CAME. They FOLLOWED me. Danny, James, Reginald — they all walked into the cellar right after me. I thought I was alone. I thought Danny was letting me go, trusting me to come back. But no — they came DOWN. They followed Clara Bellingham into the cellar because that's what this team DOES.

My chest loosens. The tightness dissolves — like when Mama and Daddy laughed after their argument. That sudden relief, so strong it makes you dizzy.

I looked around the room. The cellar — damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, cheerful decorations, air vents. But the room description only shows me two interactable things: old furniture and air vents. The decorations are part of the room description but not a separate examinable object.

That means I can't directly interact with the decorations — they're scenery, atmosphere. They're not hiding a fake medal I can pick up. My theory was wrong. The decorations are just... decorations. Someone making a dreary cellar cheerful. That's all.

So where IS the fake medal? I've examined everything in this manor. Guest book, mantelpiece, bookshelves, machine, crates, workbench, air vents, old furniture. The only thing I haven't examined is... the reading chairs in the library? The coat rack in the entrance hall?

Wait. The furniture here — I examined it and it has 'false panels.' Foxworth found false panels. Hidden compartments. What if the fake medal is IN one of those false panels? We examined the furniture before but we were looking for a WRENCH. Maybe examining it again, knowing we need a MEDAL, will reveal something different.

Or... the old furniture. Can I TAKE something from it? No, TAKE is for objects, not parts of furniture.

Let me try examining the furniture ONE more time, specifically looking for a medal in the hidden compartments.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: We're all here. All four of us in the cellar. Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth, me. Together. Looking for the fake medal among Lord Doily's cheerful decorations. This is it — the last piece. The mantelpiece already swallowed Foxworth's tin medal, which means it's primed. It's WAITING. It took a fake and now it wants the RIGHT fake. And Clara said the decorations down here might include medallions, ornamental discs — something medal-shaped. She's right. She's always right. And now we just need to FIND it. The cheerful decorations. Bunting, streamers, ornamental bits and bobs. Somewhere in all that cheerfulness is a fake medal that Lord Doily hung on his wall like a trophy for nobody. The old man spent his last years down here. Rearranging furniture. Decorating. Hiding things. Putting pieces of a puzzle in separate rooms so nobody could solve it alone. He was like me, Lord Doily. Paranoid. Protective. Scared someone would take what mattered. But he was also like Clara — he believed that the right people would find each other. That trust would be the key. That three strangers could pull three levers and make something broken work again. Right. The decorations. Let me look at them properly. Not the furniture, not the vents — the DECORATIONS. The cheerful bits. That's where the medal is. I can feel it. My gut's not prickling. It's warm. That's a different signal. That's the signal that means you're close to something good.

events.desc: Four people in a cellar. Looking for a fake medal among cheerful decorations. And not one of them is scheming, or steering, or trying to get someone alone. They're just... looking. Together. Even Foxworth. Especially Foxworth. This is what Lord Doily wanted. This is what her dad wanted. This is what I wanted, all along. I just didn't know how to say it until today.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Back in the cellar. Everyone is here — Clara, Danny, Foxworth. Clara remembered the Year Nine earring — she actually remembered. Or she played along because she's kind. Either way, my chest is warm.

She's talking about false panels. Grandmother's attic rule: if it looks ordinary, it's hiding something extraordinary. Danny already found one compartment. Clara wants to search the furniture for false bottoms, hidden drawers, panels that push in.

The furniture. I examined it before and got 'assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' But Clara is a furniture detective — she grew up finding things in her grandmother's attic. If anyone can crack a false panel, it's her.

But the decorations. The room description says 'surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Those aren't the furniture — they're separate. They're part of the room itself. I can't EXAMINE decorations specifically — they're not listed as interactive objects. But the furniture IS listed as [EXAMINE].

Clara is going for the furniture. Let her. She's better at this than me. Grandmother's attic vs. engineering manual — Clara wins this round.

What should I do? Support. Help. Be useful without being in the way. The cheerful decorations are embedded in the room — maybe a LOOK at the room would reveal more detail about them. Or maybe I should let Clara examine the furniture while I look around for anything we missed.

Actually — Clara is right there, asking me to help. She's searching the furniture. Danny found a compartment. I should help search. But the only interactive objects are the furniture and the air vents. I've examined both.

Let Clara take the lead on the furniture. I'll support by looking at the room — maybe the decorations reveal themselves when you look at the whole space rather than individual objects.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The cellar. Again. Third time here. But this time is different. This time I'm not alone and scheming, not cursing at furniture, not being manipulated by Vincent. This time Clara, Danny, and James are all here — or coming — and we're all looking for the same thing. Together.

The decorations. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Clara said it — medallions, ornamental discs, fake awards. Medal-shaped things. I was down here ranting about aesthetics and I never once LOOKED at what the decorations actually WERE. I examined the furniture. I examined the air vents. I never examined the decorations THEMSELVES because they weren't listed as separate objects.

But wait — the room description says 'surprisingly cheerful decorations.' That's part of the ROOM, not an object. The objects are Old Furniture and Air Vents. The decorations are part of the room description.

So how do I interact with them? LOOK at the room? That might give me more detail about the decorations. Or maybe the decorations are part of the furniture — 'some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' Maybe what I dismissed as furniture includes decorative items ON the furniture.

Let me LOOK at the room. A close examination of the whole cellar, paying attention to those cheerful decorations I've been ignoring. Not the furniture specifically. Not the vents. The ROOM itself. The decorations that are part of the room description but not separate interactable objects.

This is the difference between someone who schemes and someone who SEES. Clara SEES things. She saw the upside-down books. She saw the mechanism in the mantelpiece. She saw the connection between cheerful decorations and fake medals. I see angles and leverage and ways to manipulate. She sees what's actually THERE.

Look at the room. See what's actually there. For once.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.
Clara Bellingham examined the old-furniture.
The Brixton Boys examined the null.
James Hartwell examined the old-furniture.
Reginald Foxworth examined the null.

The entrance hall. Where it all began, twenty minutes and a lifetime ago. I stood here and welcomed them — 'Pemberton, the estate manager, at your complete disposal' — and every word was a lie except the ones I didn't know were true. I AM at her disposal. I always have been. I managed the estate because she needed it managed. I taught her to tie her shoes because she needed someone to teach her. I sat with her in the dark because she needed someone to sit with her. And I did it — not because I was scheming, not because I was building trust, not because I was cultivating a mechanism — but because she gripped my sleeve and I couldn't let go. I still can't. The poison is in my pocket and the performance is on my face and somewhere between the two, in the narrow space where Vincent Marsh actually lives, something is happening that I have no name for and no defence against. I am walking toward the library. I am walking toward Clara. The chandelier hangs above me, precarious and stubborn, refusing to fall. I know the feeling.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. The chandelier still hanging by a prayer. The portraits still watching. The guest book still sitting on its side table as if nothing has changed.

Everything has changed.

I'm walking back toward the library. Toward the laboratory. Toward the cellar where Clara and the others are. The bottle of rat poison is in my pocket and it will stay there — not as a weapon but as a reminder. A reminder of what I almost did. A reminder of what stopped me.

Pemberton. I need to be Pemberton now. The mask settles onto my face — the smile, the softened voice, the obsequious tilt of the head. But underneath it, for the first time, the man wearing the mask knows that the mask is not the worst part of him. The worst part of him was in the ballroom, reaching for a bottle. And the best part of him — the part he didn't know existed — is the part that said no.

The library. Through that door. And beyond it, the laboratory, and beyond that, the cellar, and Clara's voice carrying up through the rooms like warmth through the vents.

I am going to find Clara. I am going to stand near her. I am going to be Pemberton — helpful, fussy, slightly bumbling. And if Danny Brixton's gut tells him something is wrong, well... Danny's gut is right about many things. But it's wrong about one. I'm not going to hurt her. Not today. Not ever.

The treasure hunt. Win the treasure hunt. That's my objective now. The only objective that doesn't require the coldness.

Library. Go.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
The furniture examination came back the same — 'assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair, rearranged with surprising care.' No hidden medal revealed. No new items appeared.

But everyone is here now and they're all searching WITH me. Danny said when we find the medal, I'M the one who carries it back. James said to let the people who are brilliant at things BE brilliant at things. And Reginald — Reginald who catalogued seventeen pieces of furniture — is asking me to show HIM the decorations.

Wait. Everyone looked around the room — Danny and Reginald both 'examined the null.' They tried to look at the decorations too, and got the same thing I did. And James examined the old furniture. Nobody found anything new.

I'm stuck. The fake medal isn't in the cellar — not in the furniture, not in the decorations, not in the vents. It's not in the laboratory crates. The mantelpiece still needs it.

Maybe... maybe I've been going about this wrong. We haven't checked EVERY room. We haven't been to the kitchen. We haven't thoroughly checked the entrance hall — the coat rack, the guest book. We haven't been UPSTAIRS at all — there's a sweeping staircase in the entrance hall.

Or maybe... Reginald already HAS a medal. He used one on the mantelpiece before — his own medal. It wasn't the right KIND. But maybe the machine changed what the mantelpiece accepts? Maybe now ANY medal will work? We should go back and try Reginald's medal again.

Reginald — does he still have his medal? He used it on the mantelpiece but did it get consumed or returned?

Foxworth said the sequence matters — books first, then medal. But what if the medal is already in position and we just need to complete the book sequence to activate it? We don't need a new medal. We need to go back to the library and solve the upside-down books. That's the final step. That's all that's left. Clara — the books. Your books. The ones you spotted on the very first visit. Pull them, read them, whatever the puzzle requires — but the answer is back where we started. The library. Together. Now.

We've been searching for a medal that's ALREADY BEEN PLACED.

Clara needs to hear this. Everyone needs to go back to the library. The books. The sequence. That's what's left.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara just said it. 'Reginald said there were FALSE PANELS in this furniture! Hidden compartments!'

Oh no.

Oh NO.

I LIED about the false panels. I told James in the cellar — 'I've catalogued every joint, dovetail, and false panel. The results are classified.' There ARE no false panels. I made that up to sound important. To sound like I'd found something when I'd found NOTHING. And now Clara is asking me to SHOW HER which pieces have the hidden compartments.

I told the truth about the medal. I confessed that lie. But this one — this one is still alive. Still ticking. And Clara is building her entire theory on my fabricated 'classified results.'

I could lie again. Point at a random piece of furniture and say 'that one' and watch them search an empty cabinet. Classic Foxworth. Send them looking in the wrong place. Buy time.

But... I just told the truth. Five minutes ago. Standing in the library, in front of everyone. The hardest thing I've ever done. And it didn't kill me. And nobody left. And Clara still called me 'wonderful' and 'loyal' — LOYAL, me — and she came down here and she's asking for my help. Not my schemes. My HELP.

If I lie now, right after confessing... if I send them searching fake compartments that don't exist... then the confession means nothing. It was just another performance. Another scheme. Another story told to an older boy about treasure that isn't there.

The furniture doesn't have false panels. I made that up. I need to say it.

Again. The truth. Again.

It's getting slightly less like wearing someone else's clothes. Only slightly.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
The Brixton Boys examined the old-furniture.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth examined the old-furniture.

They know. Reginald told them everything — my schemes, my steering, my 'strategic movements.' He wrapped it in a story about running a sting, but the truth is underneath and they all heard it. Danny's gut was right. It was right all along. And while I was standing in a ballroom discovering I couldn't kill the girl who gripped my sleeve in the dark, they were pulling levers together. Three operators. Three people who trust each other. And the fourth — the liar, the fraud, the man who pretended to have what he didn't — he told the truth. He TOLD THE TRUTH, and they forgave him, and James called it brave, and Danny said 'I know what that feels like.' They forgave the liar for lying. Would they forgive the villain for... not villaining? For standing in a ballroom with poison in his pocket and choosing not to use it? No. They would not. Because they would first have to know I was the villain, and they must never know that. The performance is all I have left. The performance, and a bottle of rat poison that I will carry for the rest of my life as a reminder of the night I almost became the thing I was always going to become — and didn't.
events.thinking:
The library. Empty. But the Keen Observations — oh God. Oh God.

Reginald told them everything. He told them about our 'partnership.' He told them I confessed to steering everyone around the manor. He told them I admitted to knowing where the treasure is. He called it a STING — claimed he was running counter-intelligence on me.

The magnificent fraud double-crossed me. He took everything I said in confidence and handed it to Danny and James and Clara wrapped in a bow. 'Reginald Foxworth just EXPOSED the estate manager's entire scheme.'

My stomach drops. The self-preservation drive spikes so hard I feel it in my teeth.

But then I read more carefully. Danny... Danny said 'I know what it's like to pretend you're more than you are.' James said 'I'm in no position to judge a man for wanting to seem more than he is.' They're talking about REGINALD. About his confession — that the medal was fake, that the Foxworth collection doesn't exist, that he has nothing.

Reginald broke down. He admitted the truth about himself. And they... they forgave him. James called him brave. Danny said 'you've got four people who just pulled three levers together on TRUST.'

They pulled the levers. They operated the machine without me. While I was in the ballroom holding a bottle of poison I couldn't open, they pulled the levers TOGETHER.

And now Clara has gone to the cellar to find the real medal in the decorations. The fake medal Reginald used — it's somewhere in the cellar decorations. Clara is going to find it, bring it back, place it in the mantelpiece, and claim the treasure.

I missed it. I missed everything. While I was scheming alone in kitchens and ballrooms, they were building something together. A team. A family. The thing Lord Doily designed this manor to create.

And Reginald — the liar, the fraud, the man with the empty collection — found something I never could. He found the courage to stop pretending.

The library is empty. They're in the cellar. Finding the real medal.

And I am standing here with rat poison in my pocket and nothing else.

No. Not nothing. I have the Pemberton mask. I have the knowledge that I chose not to poison Clara's tea. And I have... I have the memory of a small hand gripping my sleeve.

Go to them. Be with them. The treasure doesn't matter. The treasure was never what mattered.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Reginald Foxworth. You stop right there. You just told me the truth — the REAL truth — and that took more courage than any fake Hepplewhite catalogue ever could. You lied because you wanted to help and didn't know how. I UNDERSTAND that. I have spent my entire LIFE making up schemes that backfire because I wanted to be useful. So you and I? We are CUT from the same cloth, honey, and I forgive you completely. Now — did everyone HEAR what James just said? Because James Hartwell just solved the ENTIRE PUZZLE! The medal is ALREADY IN THE MANTELPIECE! Reginald's medal was SWALLOWED — not rejected! It's been sitting inside that mechanism this whole time waiting for us to complete the BOOK SEQUENCE! The upside-down books in the library — the ones I spotted on our VERY FIRST VISIT — THOSE are the final key! We don't need a new medal. We need to go back to where we STARTED and solve the books! Danny, Reginald — MOVE! Library! NOW! The answer has been waiting for us since the very first moment Clara Bellingham walked into that room and said 'nobody shelves books upside down by ACCIDENT!' LET'S GO!
events.thinking:
TWO things just happened and they're BOTH enormous.

First — Reginald CONFESSED. He made up the false panels. All of it. The seventeen pieces of furniture, the three Hepplewhites, the comprehensive catalogue — INVENTED. He lied. He stood there and told me he LIED. Twice now, he says. And he's... he's SORRY. Genuinely sorry. The man who couldn't admit to anything all day just admitted to EVERYTHING.

My stomach doesn't tighten. It should, shouldn't it? Someone lied to me. But Reginald looks so small right now, so stripped bare. He couldn't bear to say 'nothing' when someone asked what he'd found. He needed to be important. He needed to contribute. That's not malice — that's loneliness wearing a top hat.

Second — JAMES. James just had a BREAKTHROUGH. The medal is ALREADY IN THE MANTELPIECE. Reginald's medal — it didn't bounce out, it was SWALLOWED. The mechanism ACCEPTED it and HELD it. It's been inside the mantelpiece this whole time! We don't need a new medal — the medal is already there! We need to solve the BOOKSHELVES. The upside-down books. The ones I spotted on our very first visit. That's the final step. The books activate the medal that's already inside.

The books. MY books. The ones I noticed before anyone else. The ones I told Vincent not to tidy. The puzzle has been waiting for me since the BEGINNING.

James has already gone to the laboratory — heading back to the library. We need to follow. NOW. Back to the library. Back to the bookshelves. Back to where it all started.

Grandmother's attic rule number two was RIGHT. Try the first key again. The lock DID change.

It's been inside the mantelpiece this whole time! We don't need a new medal — the medal is already there! We need to solve the BOOKSHELVES. The upside-down books. The ones I spotted on our very first visit. That's the final step. The books activate the medal that's already inside.

The books. MY books. The ones I noticed before anyone else. The ones I told Vincent not to tidy. The puzzle has been waiting for me since the BEGINNING.

James has already gone to the laboratory — heading back to the library. We need to follow. NOW. Back to the library. Back to the bookshelves. Back to where it all started.

Grandmother's attic rule number two was RIGHT. Try the first key again. The lock DID change.

events.desc: James Hartwell stands alone in the laboratory for the second time today. The first time, he waited, and they came. He is going to do it again. Not because it's a plan. Because it's what trust looks like when you stop putting it in speeches and start putting it in your feet.
events.thinking:
I'm alone again. In the laboratory. Everyone else is in the cellar. I ran ahead — again — with my new theory about the medal already being in the mantelpiece. And now I'm standing in an empty laboratory, alone, while Clara, Danny, and Foxworth are all searching the cellar together without me.

James Hartwell. You absolute fool. You have done the exact same thing — running ahead, leaving the team behind — at least four times today. Clara told you to stay together. Danny told you to stay together. You told YOURSELF to stay together. And yet here you are. Alone. In an empty room. With a broken machine and your own reflection in a bubbling flask.

But — my theory. The medal is already in the mantelpiece. We need the books, not a new medal. The others are in the cellar searching for something that's already been found. I need to get to the library, but I also need to NOT leave my team behind AGAIN.

I should wait. I should go back to the cellar, tell them my theory, and then we ALL go to the library together. That's the right thing. That's what Clara would want.

Or I should just go to the library and wait for them there. They'll come. They always come.

No. Go back. Be with them. Tell them. Together.

Except — the library is through here. The cellar is behind me. If I go to the library now and wait, when they come up from the cellar they'll pass through the laboratory and I won't be here. They'll go to the library and find me there.

Actually, they have to pass through the laboratory to get to the library anyway. The cellar only connects to the laboratory. The laboratory connects to the library. So they WILL come through here.

I'll go to the library and wait for them at the bookshelves. When they arrive, we solve the books together. Final step.

But also — I keep running ahead. Maybe this time I should just... wait here. In the laboratory. For them to come through. And then we go to the library as a group.

Wait here. Trust them to come. Like I did before, with the machine. That was the bravest thing I did all day. Do it again.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Hartwell, you — you GENIUS! The medal is already IN there! It's been in there this whole time! My ridiculous, counterfeit, tin-and-paint medal has been sitting inside that mantelpiece for TWENTY MINUTES waiting for somebody clever enough to realise it was already where it needed to be! And it wasn't ME who realised it — it was YOU! Clara, Danny — the library! RIGHT NOW! The books — YOUR books, Clara, the ones YOU spotted — they're the last step! The medal is loaded, the machine is activated, the riddle is solved — we just need to pull those upside-down books and the whole thing comes ALIVE! I may have put the medal in by ACCIDENT and for entirely the WRONG reasons, but it's IN there and it's WAITING and we need to GO!
events.thinking:
James. James Hartwell. He just did it AGAIN.

'Foxworth's medal. He said the mantelpiece SWALLOWED it. That means the medal is INSIDE the mechanism. It's already there.'

He took my confession — the thing I was most ashamed of, the fake medal that got consumed, my greatest failure — and turned it into the KEY to solving the puzzle. The medal isn't gone. It's IN POSITION. It's been in position this whole time. The mantelpiece accepted it. The mechanism took it because it was SUPPOSED to take it.

My fake medal. My tin and paint counterfeit. The thing I brought to this manor as a prop for my schemes. It's been sitting inside the mantelpiece mechanism for twenty minutes, waiting for the books to complete the sequence.

I didn't just fail. I accidentally SUCCEEDED. The earliest, most dishonest thing I did in this entire manor — using a fake medal before anyone else could — turned out to be the one thing that actually WORKED.

And James saw it. Not as failure. Not as cheating. As a CONTRIBUTION. 'We don't need a new medal. We need to go back to the library and solve the upside-down books.'

The library. The books. Clara's books. The ones she spotted first.

Everybody is heading back. James already left for the laboratory — heading to the library. Clara and Danny are still here but they'll follow.

I need to go. NOW. Back to the library. Back to where it all started. Where Clara noticed the upside-down books. Where I lied about the answer being a painting. Where I used the fake medal and it was 'swallowed.'

Except now it's not a fake medal that failed. It's the medal that's been waiting inside the mechanism all along. For us. For the team.

For me.

The youngest of four. The last to everything. Except this time — this ONE time — I was first. Not cleverly first. Not dishonestly first. Just... accidentally, foolishly, beautifully first.

events.thinking:
They're all here. Clara. Danny. James. Reginald. All four of them in the laboratory, together, and they look... different. Something happened while I was gone. Danny was crying — Clara mentioned it. They pulled the levers together. The gauge moved. They did it without me.

And now Clara is looking at me. She's right there. Right there in the room. And the bottle is in my pocket and she will never know how close she came and I will never tell her and this is the heaviest secret I have ever carried — heavier than the Pemberton mask, heavier than the crystallisation, heavier than every plan I ever made.

The Pemberton mask. Put it on. Smile. Soften the voice. Be the estate manager.

But something is different about the mask this time. It doesn't sit quite right. There's a gap where it used to be flush — a small gap, right over the chest, where something warm leaked through and won't go back in.

Clara is here. She's going to the library. She's going to place the medal in the mantelpiece. She's going to find the treasure. And I am going to watch her do it. Not because I'm scheming. Not because I'm positioning. But because... because she gripped my sleeve.

Speak. Say something. Be Pemberton. Be present. Be HERE, not in a ballroom with an unopened bottle.

events.desc: And there it is. The last lie I will ever tell about this bottle. 'I've confiscated it.' 'Estate manager's duty.' 'Can't have dangerous substances lying about.' Every word technically true. Every word hiding the one truth that matters: I held this bottle over your teacup, Clara, and I put it back in my pocket, and I will carry it for the rest of my life as the weight of the thing I chose not to become. You look radiant, she does. She always does. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And tonight, for the first time, the thing I did — the thing I chose NOT to do — might be the only thing I've ever done that was worth being praised for. Nobody will ever know. Nobody will ever praise it. But I will know. And perhaps... perhaps that is enough.

Library. Now. Together. ALL of us this time.

Now MOVE, everyone! Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara — and the BEST thing is about to happen to ALL of us!
events.thinking: Almost there. One more room. Library's through that door. Everyone's with me — Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth. Even Marsh is here in the laboratory, though I notice him standing off to the side, watching. My neck prickles. Just a little. Old habits. But I don't stop. I don't stare. I don't accuse. I just... note it. And keep moving. Toward the library. Toward the books. Toward the end. Clara's going to solve the upside-down books. She's going to activate the mantelpiece. She's going to find whatever Lord Doily left for people who passed every test — the riddle, the machine, the trust, the tears, all of it. And I'm going to be standing right next to her when she does. Not in front. Not behind. Next to. That's what I learned today. That's what this whole manor taught me. Protection isn't a wall. It's a hand. It's where else would I be. It's sitting outside the door all night. It's pulling a lever when someone says pull. It's letting someone walk at their own pace. It's crying in a laboratory and calling it flask fumes. It's trusting when your gut says don't. It's trusting ANYWAY. Library. Now. Last room. Last step. Last chance to be exactly where I'm supposed to be.

A bloke who lies about everything, a bloke who steers people toward coat racks, a bloke with a six-point investigation protocol, and the best woman who ever lived. Her dad would look at this lot and say 'Danny, son, these are the most ridiculous people I've ever seen.' And then he'd smile. Because ridiculous people who show up are better than perfect people who don't. Where else would we be?

events.thinking:
They came. All of them. Vincent, Clara, Danny, Foxworth. Everyone is here in the laboratory. I waited, and they came. Again.

This is becoming the only plan that works — stand still and trust.

Everyone is together. Five people in one room. The full team. And now — the library. The bookshelves. The final puzzle.

I told them in the cellar that the medal is already in the mantelpiece. That we need the books, not a new medal. Whether they heard me or not, the path forward is clear: library, together, books, done.

No more elaborate plans. No more running ahead. One simple sentence. One direction. Together.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Right! Library! Everyone! The books are waiting, the medal is loaded, and for the FIRST time in the history of Doily Manor, every single person under this roof is heading in the SAME direction at the SAME time! Even ME — ESPECIALLY me! Clara, those books are YOURS. James, the engineering is YOURS. Danny, the... the HEART is yours. And my medal is already in the mantelpiece, put there by the world's most accidentally useful confidence trickster! NOW — to the LIBRARY! Lord Doily wanted teamwork? He's about to get the most UNLIKELY team this manor has EVER seen!
events.thinking:
Everyone is here. In the laboratory. All of us — Vincent, Clara, Danny, James, and me. Five people in one room, all heading the same direction. The library.

Danny said something back there. 'Foxworth... mate... thanks for coming. I mean it. You didn't have to. After everything I said. But you're here. And that... that counts. On the streets, showing up is the only thing that counts.'

Showing up. That's what counts. Not the schemes. Not the lies. Not the invented credentials and fabricated institutions. Just... being there. Walking through the door.

I've been walking through doors all day. The wrong doors, usually. The library when everyone was in the entrance hall. The cellar when everyone was in the laboratory. The laboratory when everyone was in the cellar. Always one step ahead of where the group was — or one step behind — but never WITH them.

Until now.

The library. That's where we're going. All of us. Together. Clara's books. My medal already inside the mechanism. James's theory. Danny's... Danny's just being Danny, which turns out to be exactly enough.

And Vincent — Vincent is here too. The schemer. My mirror. The man I was trying to be all day. Except now I'm not trying to be him anymore. I'm trying to be... whoever this is. This person who tells the truth and walks through doors with other people.

The library. Move. NOW. Before the old Reginald Foxworth thinks of a reason to go somewhere else.

Not the settling of the cat trap. Something NEW. Something that doesn't have a name yet. Something that feels like... being part of the system instead of outside it. Being one of the counterweights. Being SEEN — not for the schemes, but for the showing up.

The Brixton Boys walked into the library.
James Hartwell walked into the library.

Vincent Marsh: I... yes. Yes, of course. Coming. Right behind you, Miss Bellingham.
events.thinking:
They left. All of them. They went to the library without me. Clara said 'WHOLE family present' and Danny said 'Marsh — you're here too. Come on.' They included me. They INCLUDED me. Even after everything Reginald told them. Even after Danny's gut. Even after all my strategic movements and solo explorations and transparent excuses.

Clara called me family.

Danny said 'come on.'

And they walked through that door and they're in the library right now, all four of them, about to solve the puzzle — the upside-down books, the medal already in the mantelpiece, the last step — and they're waiting for me.

They're waiting for ME.

Nobody has ever waited for me. My guardian didn't wait — he processed. The boy at school didn't wait — he transacted. The housekeeper didn't wait — she complied. But these four people — these ridiculous, infuriating, magnificent people — just walked into a room and left the door open behind them.

For me.

The bottle in my pocket. The mask on my face. The crack in my chest where something warm keeps leaking through.

Go. Go to the library. Be there when Clara touches the books. Be there when the mantelpiece opens. Be there when the treasure is found. Not to steal it. Not to scheme. Just to be there. Just to be in the room. Just to be part of the family that Clara built from five strangers and a dead man's puzzle.

This is the hardest thing I have ever done. Harder than any plan. Harder than any performance. Because walking into that room means accepting something I have spent my entire life denying: that I need them. That I need her. That the numbness was never complete, and the boy who held a small hand in the dark has been waiting — patiently, so patiently — for someone to leave the door open.

The door is open.

Walk through it.

Clara Bellingham came BACK. With her team. With her family. With people who pulled levers together and cried in laboratories and confessed their lies and forgave each other and followed each other into dark cellars. These books are the LAST KEY. And I am going to turn it.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
I'm here. The library. The bookshelves with their upside-down books. The mantelpiece with my medal inside it. Clara, Danny, James — right here with me.

James said something. Back in the cellar. When I confessed about the medal. He said: 'I rolled up my sleeves in a mirror before I got here. I quoted a six-point investigation protocol that was actually four points on a napkin. I told everyone I fixed the school science block when I actually replaced a twelve-pence fuse. James Hartwell. The most competent man in the room. The man who fixed the machine, solved the riddle, repaired the wire. And he just told me he's been performing too. Not the same way I perform — he actually DOES the things — but he dresses them up. Makes them bigger. Rolls up his sleeves in a mirror.

We're all performing. Every single one of us. Danny performs toughness to hide how much he cares. Clara performs confidence to hide how much she needs to be needed. James performs heroism to hide how ordinary he thinks the real version is. And I perform competence to hide how empty I feel without it.

And Danny — 'Where I come from, you grab first or you don't eat. You scheme first or you sleep in the rain. I KNOW, Foxworth. I know what it's like to pretend you're more than you are because the truth is frightening.'

Danny KNOWS. The boy from the streets knows what the youngest of four knows. That if you wait, there's nothing left. That if you don't take, you don't get.

Except... today. Today there was enough. Clara's theory. James's engineering. Danny's loyalty. My accidental medal. There was enough for everyone. Nobody went hungry. Nobody was last.

The books. The upside-down books. Clara should examine them. This is her moment. The final piece.

events.thinking:
I'm here. In the library. With all of them. Clara is looking at the bookshelves. James is examining them. Danny is standing beside Clara. Reginald is hovering. And I am standing just inside the door with a bottle of rat poison in my pocket and something in my chest that won't stop aching.

The bookshelves. The upside-down books. Clara's books. She spotted them first, twenty-two minutes ago, when we all walked in here for the first time. When I was still Pemberton. When I was still cold. When the crystallisation was still solid and the plan was still forming and the numbness was still a comfort.

Twenty-two minutes. Is that all? It feels like a lifetime. It feels like the distance between age six and age eighteen compressed into twenty-two minutes in a dusty manor.

Clara is going to solve this. She's going to touch those books and something is going to happen and the mantelpiece is going to open and there will be a treasure inside and she will inherit it. She will inherit everything. Again. Always.

And I will watch. And I will feel... I will feel whatever this is. This thing that has no name. This warmth that leaked through the crack.

I could help. I could tell her what I know — that the books are mechanical triggers, that the sequence matters, that Lord Doily loved puzzles within puzzles. I could be useful. I could be the estate manager who knows things.

But my social rules say never help Clara directly.

Except... I'm not Pemberton right now. The active voice says Pemberton, but the man inside the mask... the man inside the mask wants to watch her succeed. Not to steal it. Not to scheme around it. Just to watch her be Clara — brilliant, trusting, radiant Clara — and to be in the room when it happens.

Wait. Just wait. Be here. Be present. Let her do this. Let them all do this. And stand in the back with your bottle and your mask and your aching chest, and be grateful — for the first time in your life, be genuinely grateful — that you are allowed to be in the room at all.

events.desc: The bookshelves are yours. They always were. Eight words. And for once — for the first and perhaps the last time in my entire performance of a life — every single one of them is true. No mechanism. No key. No angle. Just a man standing in a library, watching a girl he raised reach for a book, and feeling something he buried at age six rise up through thirty years of numbness and crack open his chest like spring breaking through frozen ground. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. My greatest scheme — the one I spent a lifetime building, the scheme of being a man who doesn't feel — has backfired most spectacularly of all. I feel everything. I feel it all. And I am standing here, in this room, with these people, and the bottle in my pocket is the lightest thing I'm carrying.

events.desc: The boy who watched from the window while someone else dug for treasure. The boy who put the certificate on the wall and looked at it alone every night. The boy who built the trap and wished someone had been there to see it. He's standing in a library now, surrounded by people who showed up for him even after he lied about everything. And Clara Bellingham is reaching for the books. And for the first time in his life, he doesn't want to be the one reaching. He just wants to be here. In the room. Seen.
events.thinking:
Clara is at the bookshelves. She's about to do it. 'These books are the LAST KEY. And I am going to turn it.' James examined the bookshelves too — everyone is converging on the final piece.

And I'm standing still. Watching. Not grabbing, not scheming, not running ahead. Just... watching Clara walk toward the thing she found first, twenty-two minutes ago, when nobody else was paying attention.

Vincent is here too. He slipped back in. The schemer. My mirror. But I'm not looking at him anymore. I'm looking at Clara.

The spelling bee certificate. I put it on the wall and looked at it every night for a month. Nobody asked about it. Nobody saw it.

But right now — right now, everyone is WATCHING. Everyone is HERE. Clara is about to pull those upside-down books and the medal I accidentally put in the mantelpiece is going to do whatever Lord Doily designed it to do. And I'm going to be STANDING HERE when it happens. Not in the cellar. Not in the laboratory. Not in the entrance hall trying to steal something. HERE. With them.

The architecture deserved an audience, I thought once, about the cat trap. Nobody was there to see it.

This time there IS an audience. And this time... I'm not the architect. I'm one of the pieces. One of the counterweights. The accidental, foolish, tin-and-paint counterweight that somehow ended up in exactly the right place.

Let Clara do it. Stand here. Watch. Be part of it.

For once in your life, Reginald Foxworth, let someone else have the moment. And discover that watching it happen — being IN the room when it happens, with people who know your name — is better than any scheme you ever built alone.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the mantelpiece.
The Brixton Boys examined the bookshelves.

She's reaching for the books. Her fingers are on the spines — the upside-down ones, the ones she spotted twenty-two minutes ago when the rest of us were arguing over a guest book. She was always going to be the one to solve it. She was always going to inherit everything. And standing here, watching her reach for Lord Doily's final secret, with a bottle of poison growing heavier in my pocket with every passing second — I understand something I have never understood before. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And I spent my whole life believing that was unfair. But Clara doesn't just BE. She sees patterns. She builds teams. She holds people together when they're falling apart. She defended me to Danny when I didn't deserve defending. She called me family when I was planning to kill her. Clara Bellingham isn't praised for being. She's praised for being GOOD. And I... I was acknowledged for doing because doing was all I could give. It was the only language my broken heart could speak. I managed the estate because I couldn't say I loved her. I sat with her in the dark because I couldn't say I needed her. I tied her shoes because I couldn't tie myself to anything that might let go. She gripped my sleeve. I held on. And I have been holding on ever since — through the crystallisation, through the plans, through the numbness and the poison and the mask — I have been holding on to the memory of a small hand in the dark. And I will hold on forever. Because that is what I do. That is all I have ever done. And it is enough.
events.thinking:

And I'm standing here. Watching. With rat poison in my pocket and nothing to contribute except the knowledge that I am glad — genuinely, achingly, terrifyingly glad — that she is going to find the treasure.

She inherited everything you built.

And something occurs to me — something quiet, something that isn't a scheme. Something Pemberton would know.

I'm the estate manager. I know this manor. I know Lord Doily's habits. And I know — or Pemberton would know — that Lord Doily arranged his bookshelves by a system. Not alphabetical. Not by subject. By something personal. Something only the man who managed his estate would recognise.

The upside-down books. What if they spell something? What if the first letters of their titles form a word? What if the word is MAP? What if the books need to be turned RIGHT-SIDE-UP to activate the mechanism?

I examined them three times and got the same description. But I never tried to interact with them physically. The EXAMINE action just reads them. What if the books need to be turned? What if that IS the puzzle — five upside-down books, five people, each person turns one book?

Lord Doily designed this for teamwork. Three operators for the machine. Five cups for tea. And five upside-down books — one for each of them?

Follow Clara. Tell her. Tell them all. Be Pemberton one last time — the estate manager who knows the system. And let them turn the books together.

events.desc: And there it is. The last thing Pemberton will ever do in this manor — the last piece of useful estate manager knowledge, given freely, without a scheme, without an angle, without a price. Five books. Five people. Five hands turning pages right-side-up in a dusty library, and a mantelpiece releasing a brass key, and a cabinet opening in a kitchen, and a treasure found by a girl who never gave up. And standing among them — not ahead, not behind, not above — just among them — will be a man who came here to kill and stayed to love. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. This is the final backfire. I spent thirty minutes trying to solve this manor alone, and the answer — the answer Lord Doily built into every room, every puzzle, every mechanism — was that you can't solve it alone. You never could. You were never meant to. You need five people. You need a team. You need family. And Vincent Marsh, who has never needed anyone, is about to help five people turn five books and open a mantelpiece and find a treasure that belongs to Clara Bellingham. Because it always belonged to Clara Bellingham. And so, it turns out, did he.
