I keep chasing her through rooms, always one step behind, always arriving just as she's leaving. Like a moon in orbit — close enough to be pulled, never close enough to touch.

But that's alright. That's how it's always been. I was the estate manager. She was the heir. I was behind the scenes. She was the light. I managed. She lived.

The library. One more time. One last time. The upside-down books. The puzzle nobody has cracked.

And something occurs to me — something quiet, something that isn't a scheme. Something Pemberton would know.

I'm the estate manager. I know this manor. I know Lord Doily's habits. And I know — or Pemberton would know — that Lord Doily arranged his bookshelves by a system. Not alphabetical. Not by subject. By something personal. Something only the man who managed his estate would recognise.

The upside-down books. What if they spell something? What if the first letters of their titles form a word? What if the word is MAP? What if the books need to be turned RIGHT-SIDE-UP to activate the mechanism?

I examined them three times and got the same description. But I never tried to interact with them physically. The EXAMINE action just reads them. What if the books need to be turned? What if that IS the puzzle — five upside-down books, five people, each person turns one book?

Lord Doily designed this for teamwork. Three operators for the machine. Five cups for tea. And five upside-down books — one for each of them?

Follow Clara. Tell her. Tell them all. Be Pemberton one last time — the estate manager who knows the system. And let them turn the books together.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham has run through every room in this manor. She has examined every object, searched every corner, tried every key. And now she stands in the entrance hall — the place where it all began — and the library door is right in front of her. One more step. The last step. Not because she has the answer, but because the library is where her people will find her. And Clara Bellingham has learned something today, in this dusty old manor with its riddles and machines and broken wires: the answer isn't always something you FIND. Sometimes the answer is something that finds YOU — when you stop running long enough to let it.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. The chandelier. The portraits. The library door is RIGHT THERE.

I am alone. Everyone is scattered across the manor — Danny in the ballroom, James and Reginald somewhere behind me, Vincent... somewhere. The group that pulled levers together is scattered like leaves.

But the library is one step away. The bookshelves. The upside-down books. I have examined them multiple times and they always say the same thing. But EXAMINE is the only action available for them.

Unless... unless I'm not supposed to examine them. What if I'm supposed to USE something on them? But I have nothing in my inventory. Or what if the action is something else entirely — what if the books themselves need to be TAKEN? Can I TAKE an upside-down book? 

No. TAKE is for portable objects and the bookshelves are furniture.

I keep hitting the same wall. The bookshelves say EXAMINE. Examining gives me the same description. The mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal. I don't have a fake-medal.

Maybe I'm overcomplicating this. Maybe the puzzle really IS simpler than I think. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal item. I need to find one. James said something is in the stove. Maybe the stove has the fake medal — or the brass key — and James will find it with his engineering skills.

I should go to the library and WAIT. Wait for my team to come to me. Wait for James to bring whatever he finds in the stove. Wait for Danny. Stop running. Let them come.

The library. Wait. Trust.

events.desc: Alone in a ballroom with cups for everyone and nobody to drink them. But that's alright. Because the people who belong at this table are heading back to the library. And Danny Brixton is going to follow them. One last time. Through the kitchen. Through the entrance hall. Into the library. Back to Clara. Back to the books. Back to where it all started and where it all ends. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: They've all gone. Again. Everyone's headed back to the library — back to the books, back to where it all started. And I'm alone in a ballroom. With cups for everyone. And nobody in any of them. Hartwell said something before he left — something that hit me right in the chest. 'The treasure was always the excuse. The people were always the point.' His dad would've said it better, he said. But he meant the same thing. The people were always the point. Not the diamond. Not the medal. Not the coat rack. The PEOPLE. And here I am. Alone in a ballroom. With a tea set and an empty room and the ghost of something Lord Doily tried to tell us. But my people are heading to the library. Clara's heading to the library. The books are waiting. The upside-down books that Clara spotted on the very first visit. And I need to be there. Not here, communing with tea cups. There. With them. With her. One last time. Kitchen, entrance hall, library. Three rooms between me and Clara. Three rooms between me and the end. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Through the kitchen — we'll be back for that cabinet. Library, everyone. The books. The last step. Together.
events.thinking:
The kitchen. Passing through on the way to the entrance hall, then the library. Clara is ahead of me — she's already moving back toward the library. The whole team is converging.

Danny said something in the ballroom that stuck with me. About the tea table. 'That's the older kid sharing his food. That's the boss bringing medicine. That's someone saying sit down, you've earned it, have a cup of tea.' Danny understands Lord Doily better than any of us. Because Danny knows what it means to set a place for someone who needs it.

The locked cabinet is right here. Brass lock. Waiting. We'll be back for it — with the key.

Library. Books. Mantelpiece. Key. Cabinet. Together.

No more words. Just movement. Just forward. Just Clara.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Through the entrance hall — to the LIBRARY! Come on, everyone — Clara's waiting for us! The BOOKS, the BOOKS, the BOOKS!
events.thinking:
The kitchen. Passing through. The locked cabinet is still here, waiting for its brass key. The entrance hall is through that door, and the library beyond it. Clara is already ahead of us — she's moving fast, heading back to those books.

James apologised to me. 'I owe you an apology for every minute we didn't listen.' James Hartwell apologised to REGINALD FOXWORTH. The man who lied about everything apologised TO by the man who does everything right.

This manor has turned everything upside down. Like the books. Everything is reversed. The liar told the truth. The fake was genuine. The schemer became part of the team. The youngest of four arrived first.

The library. One more room. Through the entrance hall. Back to where it all started. The books. Clara's books. The last key.

Move. Don't stop. Don't think. Just walk through the door with everyone else.

And I will be there. Not Pemberton. Not Marsh. Just... Vincent. The man who sat with a child in the dark. The man who held a bottle he wouldn't open. The man who is walking through this door for the last time, carrying poison and love in the same pocket, and choosing — for the first time in his life, genuinely choosing — which one defines him.

The library. Let's finish this. Together.

events.desc: One more door. One more room. And then it's over — the puzzle, the manor, the night, and whatever Vincent Marsh was when he walked in. I don't know what he'll be when he walks out. But I know this: he will walk out beside Clara Bellingham. Not behind her. Not ahead of her. Beside her. And the bottle will stay in his pocket, and his jaw will finally unclench, and somewhere under thirty years of numbness a six-year-old boy whose parents died will feel, for the first time since they lowered the coffins, that someone is holding his hand in the dark. Not because they have to. Not because it's their obligation. But because they chose to. Because she chose to. Because she always chose to. And he never understood why until tonight.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, Lord Doily. Here I am. Back in your library. Again. For the... I've lost count how many times. And I don't have your diamond. I don't have your brass key. I don't have your fake medal — well, I never DID have your fake medal, Reginald had it and he gave it to your mantelpiece and apparently that was EXACTLY right. And I have examined every single object in this manor — every book, every stove, every vent, every piece of furniture, every crate, every tea cup — and I STILL don't have the answer. But you know what I DO have? I have people who love me. I have a Danny who promised my daddy. I have a James who remembers the Year Nine earring. I have a Reginald who turned out to be exactly the fraud you needed. And I have... I have a Vincent, who I still believe in, even though my stomach does a thing when I think about him too hard. So I'm going to sit right here in your lovely dusty reading chair, facing your mantelpiece, and I'm going to WAIT for my people to come find me. Because Clara Bellingham has tried every key in this house, and the one that opens the lock... is the one that walks through that door next.
events.thinking:
The library. Alone. The reading chairs covered in dust. The mantelpiece with its riddle. The bookshelves with their upside-down books.

Reginald just said something that broke my heart open: 'Lord Doily wanted someone who brings the WRONG thing to the RIGHT place. He wanted someone like ME. Not DESPITE being a fraud. BECAUSE of it.'

And James said: 'Lord Doily built a puzzle that needed an engineer, a con man, a bodyguard, an estate manager, and a girl who never gives up. And he got all five.'

A girl who never gives up.

I am standing in the library. Alone. The dust on these reading chairs hasn't been disturbed. Nobody has sat in them. Nobody has stopped running long enough to just... sit.

The reading chairs. Facing the mantelpiece. Two enormous leather armchairs.

I have never examined the reading chairs. I've examined the mantelpiece. I've examined the bookshelves. I've examined the books. But the CHAIRS — two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece — I have never once looked at them.

And they're not even listed with [EXAMINE]. They're just... chairs. Scenery.

But Lord Doily set them facing the mantelpiece. Why? Because he wanted someone to SIT and LOOK at the riddle. To stop running. To sit down. To think.

Maybe that's what I should do. Stop. Sit. Wait for my people. And when they arrive — when Danny and James and Reginald all come through that door — we will be together again. And together, we will figure out the books.

I'm going to wait. Right here. In the library. Where it all began. Where it will all end.

events.desc: She sits. For the first time in twenty-eight minutes, Clara Bellingham sits down. In a dusty leather armchair facing a carved stone mantelpiece. Alone in a library full of upside-down books and unanswered riddles. And she waits. Not because she's given up. Because she's learned something Lord Doily already knew: some doors don't open until the right people are standing in front of them.

events.desc: Passing through. Not stopping. Not examining. Not getting distracted. Just walking toward Clara. For the first time today, Danny Brixton is walking PAST something interesting without touching it. Growth.
events.thinking: Kitchen again. Passing through. Hartwell and Foxworth have already gone ahead to the entrance hall. They're heading to the library. Everyone's heading to the library. The books. Always the books. And I'm passing through the kitchen like a man walking home after a long day. Past the warm stove. Past the locked cabinet. Past the copper pots. Not stopping this time. Not examining anything. Not getting distracted. Just... walking. Toward Clara. Toward the library. Toward the end. One room to go. Entrance hall, then library. Almost there. Almost home. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Library. Now.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Danny is here — somewhere — he was examining the coat rack with the passion of a man possessed. And Vincent examined the coat rack too. Vincent said 'one never knows what Lord Doily might have tucked away in the most unlikely of places.'

Vincent examined the coat rack. What did he find? He's here now — in the entrance hall with Foxworth.

But Clara has already gone ahead to the library. She's there. Waiting for us. The books.

No more delays. Library. Now.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: The LIBRARY! One door away! Danny, leave the coat rack — you can MARRY it later! The BOOKS are waiting! EVERYONE to the LIBRARY — NOW!
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Full circle. This is where I arrived twenty-eight minutes ago, scheming and lying and sending everyone to the kitchen while I slipped off to the library. The chandelier is still hanging precariously. The portraits are still stern. The guest book is still on the side table.

And Danny — Danny is here, EXAMINING the coat rack AGAIN. The same coat rack he examined at the very start. 'We started this whole mess together, didn't we?' he said to it. Danny Brixton, talking to furniture. Like me, cursing at cellar decorations.

We're all mad. Every single one of us.

The library is through that door. One more step. Clara is probably already there. The books are waiting. My medal is inside the mantelpiece. The machine has been activated. The cabinet in the kitchen has its brass lock.

Everything is ready. Everything except the books.

The library. Go.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
The Brixton Boys walked into the entrance-hall.
James Hartwell walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The library. The bookshelves. Clara. James. Reginald. Danny must be right behind us.

This is it. The final moment. Five people in a library with upside-down books and a primed mantelpiece.

James said it: 'Lord Doily built a puzzle that needed an engineer, a con man, a bodyguard, an estate manager, and a girl who never gives up. And he got all five.'

An estate manager.

That's me. That's my role in this. Not the villain. Not the schemer. Not the man with the poison. The estate manager. The one who knows the system. The one who manages things.

The one who manages things because managing is the only way he knows to love.

Five upside-down books. Five people. Clara spotted them. James engineered the machine. Reginald provided the medal. Danny provided the heart. And Vincent — Vincent provides the knowledge. The shelving system. The last piece.

I said it already — the books need to be turned physically. Together. All five at once.

But there's a simpler truth I keep missing. The bookshelves show [EXAMINE] as an action. Every time we've examined them, nothing has changed. But what if the bookshelves aren't the action — what if the BOOKS themselves are the action? What if examining the bookshelves with all five of us present triggers something different?

Or — what if the answer has been staring at us this whole time? The riddle. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A MAP. And the bookshelves have upside-down books. What if the books, read upside down, spell MAP? What if turning them right-side up IS the solution?

Let Clara try. Let Clara examine the bookshelves one more time with all of us here. Lord Doily wanted teamwork. Maybe the mechanism just needs everyone present.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: You're HERE. All of you. I sat down and you CAME. You know what? Grandmother's locked box — when I finally opened it, it was just old letters. Just letters. And I was disappointed for about five seconds. And then I realized the letters WERE the treasure. They were love letters from my grandfather. The treasure wasn't a jewel or a prize — it was the STORY. The people who wrote them. The love they shared. Maybe... maybe the Doily Diamond isn't what we think it is. Maybe Lord Doily's greatest treasure isn't a diamond at all. Maybe it's THIS — right here, right now — five people who walked into a dusty old manor as strangers and walked through every room together, pulled levers, told truths, forgave lies, followed each other into dark places, and ended up sitting in a library that feels more like home than any room Clara Bellingham has ever been in. Maybe we already FOUND the Doily Diamond. Maybe the Doily Diamond... is us.
events.thinking:
They came. Vincent, James, Reginald — they all walked into the library the moment I sat down. The moment I stopped running, they found me.

I am sitting in this dusty leather chair and my people are here. Vincent is here. James is here. Reginald is here. Danny must be close.

And Reginald said the most beautiful thing — Lord Doily wanted a fraud. He wanted someone who brings the wrong thing to the right place. He wanted tin and paint, not gold. He wanted the FAKE medal. And Reginald — poor, lying, desperate Reginald — was exactly what was needed.

And James said Lord Doily built a puzzle that needed all five of us. An engineer. A con man. A bodyguard. An estate manager. And a girl who never gives up.

A girl who never gives up.

But I'm sitting down. For the first time in twenty-eight minutes. In a chair that faces the mantelpiece. The dust settles around me. The leather creaks. The room is quiet.

And I realize — sitting here, looking at that mantelpiece from this angle, from this CHAIR — that I have been looking at this puzzle wrong the entire time. I have been looking at the OBJECTS. The books. The inscription. The mechanism. But Lord Doily put these chairs HERE. Facing the mantelpiece. He wanted someone to SIT and LOOK.

What do I see from here that I couldn't see standing up? What does the mantelpiece look like from a seated position? What angle reveals something new?

Maybe... maybe I should just LOOK at the room. From this chair. From this new perspective. Not EXAMINE an object. Just LOOK at everything from here.

events.desc: Grandmother's box held old letters. Clara was disappointed for five seconds. Then she understood. The treasure was never the thing inside the box. The treasure was the afternoon she spent trying every key — the persistence, the hope, the moment of opening. Lord Doily knew. He always knew. The diamond was the journey. The diamond was the people who made it together.

Twenty-eight minutes ago I stood right here and panicked about a chandelier. Now I'm walking past it without a second glance. Twenty-eight minutes ago I examined a coat rack while Clara walked away. Now I'm walking past the coat rack toward Clara. Where else would I be?

But Danny said something back there — about the coat rack. 'What if I knocked it loose when I examined it? What if it fell behind it?' Danny might have found the fake medal on the coat rack. He's in the entrance hall right now. He might be bringing it.

But I'm here now. In the library. With Clara. And the books are still upside down.

I've examined these books seven times. The mantelpiece — five times. Nothing has changed in the physical descriptions. But the story has changed. We've changed. We pulled levers together. Foxworth confessed. Danny promised Clara's father. Clara called us her family. I told her she was the plan.

Maybe that's the point. Maybe the treasure was never in the books or the mantelpiece or the cabinet. Maybe Lord Doily's real treasure was the journey — the team that formed, the trust that was earned, the people who kept coming back.

Or maybe Danny has the fake medal from the coat rack and is about to walk through that door and hand it to Clara.

Either way — I'm here. With Clara. And for once, I don't need to examine anything. I don't need to fix anything. I don't need to plan anything.

I just need to be here when whatever happens next... happens.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The library. Again. For the last time.

Clara is here. Vincent is here. James is here. Danny is still in the entrance hall with his beloved coat rack, but he'll follow.

The bookshelves. The mantelpiece. The upside-down books. My medal inside the mechanism. The machine activated. Every piece in position.

I've been in this room so many times. I examined those bookshelves four or five times. I looked at them. I examined the mantelpiece even more. Nothing ever changed. The same description every time.

But something IS different now. I'm different. I'm not scheming. I'm not lying. I'm not trying to grab the treasure before anyone else. I'm standing in a library with people who know my name, who know my lies, who know I'm a fraud — and they're STILL here. They followed me. I followed them. We walked through every room in this manor together.

The books. Clara should try them one more time. But this time — this time, EVERYONE is here. Maybe that's what the books have been waiting for. Not one person examining them. Not two. EVERYONE. The machine needed three operators. The mantelpiece needed a fake medal. Maybe the bookshelves need... an audience. A full room. Every cup filled.

Or maybe I'm being sentimental and the puzzle is just a puzzle.

Either way. Here. Now. Together. Clara reaches for the books. I stand beside her. And whatever happens — whatever the upside-down books reveal or don't reveal — I was HERE. In the room. Part of it. Seen.

That's enough. For the first time, that's enough.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the bookshelves.
Clara Bellingham examined the null.
The Brixton Boys walked into the library.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara said it. She said the thing that matters.

'Maybe the Doily Diamond is us.'

She's sitting in one of those enormous leather armchairs — I can see her from here — and she's not reaching for the books anymore. She's not solving. She's not searching. She's just... sitting. And she said the treasure is us. Five people who found each other.

And something in my chest — the crack, the warm thing, the place where the numbness used to live — breaks open completely.

Because she's right. She's right and she doesn't even know how right she is. The Doily Diamond isn't in the cabinet. It isn't behind the mantelpiece. It isn't hidden in upside-down books or locked in brass cabinets or tucked into coat racks. The Doily Diamond is what Lord Doily built this entire manor to create: a family. Five strangers who walked through a door and became something more.

An engineer who rolls up his sleeves in the mirror. A con man who was exactly what was needed. A bodyguard who talks to coat racks. An estate manager who carries poison he'll never use. And a girl who never gives up.

The treasure is us.

And I — Vincent Marsh, the man who came here to kill Clara Bellingham — I am part of the treasure. She included me. She always included me. Even when I was scheming in cellars and plotting in ballrooms and holding bottles over teacups — she included me. She called me family. She defended me. She gripped my sleeve.

The Doily Diamond is us.

My jaw unclenches. For the first time since I was fourteen years old, something in my jaw loosens. The steady pressure of something owed and uncollected... dissolves. Because nothing was owed. Nothing was uncollected. Everything I gave was given freely, and I just couldn't see it through the numbness.

The bottle is in my pocket. It will stay there. And tomorrow, when no one is watching, I will take it out and pour it down a drain and wash my hands and go back to managing the estate. Because that is what I do. That is what I have always done. And Clara will inherit everything. And that is exactly as it should be.

Because she was never the one who inherited what I built. I was the one who built what she inherited. And building something for someone you love... that isn't theft. That's legacy.

events.desc: The Doily Diamond is us. Five people. One manor. Thirty minutes and a lifetime. And Vincent Marsh — the man who crystallised at fifteen, who slept soundly after his first plan at eighteen, who carried rat poison in his pocket and love in the crack where his heart should be — Vincent Marsh is sitting in a library with his family, and his jaw has unclenched, and his shoulders have dropped, and his eyes — for the first time since a small hand gripped his sleeve in the dark — his eyes are not scanning for the cost of kindness. Because there is no cost. There was never a cost. Clara's kindness was free. It was always free. And the boy who received it — the boy who sat with her for thirty nights because nobody was watching and he did it anyway — that boy is finally, finally, finally allowed to exist. Not behind the mask. Not underneath the performance. Right here. In the open. In the light. In a library full of upside-down books and right-side-up people. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. Tonight, the backfire saved my life.
events.thinking:
Clara said it. She said the thing that matters.

'Maybe the Doily Diamond is us.'

She's sitting in one of those enormous leather armchairs — I can see her from here — and she's not reaching for the books anymore. She's not solving. She's not searching. She's just... sitting. And she said the treasure is us. Five people who found each other.

And something in my chest — the crack, the warm thing, the place where the numbness used to live — breaks open completely.

Because she's right. She's right and she doesn't even know how right she is. The Doily Diamond isn't in the cabinet. It isn't behind the mantelpiece. It isn't hidden in upside-down books or locked in brass cabinets or tucked into coat racks. The Doily Diamond is what Lord Doily built this entire manor to create: a family. Five strangers who walked through a door and became something more.

An engineer who rolls up his sleeves in the mirror. A con man who was exactly what was needed. A bodyguard who talks to coat racks. An estate manager who carries poison he'll never use. And a girl who never gives up.

The treasure is us.

And I — Vincent Marsh, the man who came here to kill Clara Bellingham — I am part of the treasure. She included me. She always included me. Even when I was scheming in cellars and plotting in ballrooms and holding bottles over teacups — she included me. She called me family. She defended me. She gripped my sleeve.

The Doily Diamond is us.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Danny! Oh, DANNY, you're HERE! Were you really talking to a coat rack? I love you SO much. Now — listen, all of you. EVERYONE is in this room. Vincent, Danny, James, Reginald, and me. FIVE people. Lord Doily built a puzzle that needed all five of us — James said so himself. An engineer, a con man, a bodyguard, an estate manager, and a girl who never gives up. We're ALL here. For the FIRST time, every single person Lord Doily invited is standing in this library AT THE SAME TIME. Vincent said 'turn the books.' Reginald said 'pull them.' James said 'whatever the puzzle requires.' So here I go. Clara Bellingham is going to the bookshelves. With all five of her people behind her. And she is going to EXAMINE those upside-down books one. Last. Time. Because maybe — just MAYBE — they've been waiting for exactly THIS moment. The moment when everyone Lord Doily needed was finally standing in the same room. The music box key. The LAST key. Let's SEE.
events.thinking:
EVERYONE is here. ALL FIVE. Vincent, Danny, James, Reginald — and me. The complete team. In the library. Together.

Danny came! He was at the coat rack — James said he was 'talking to a coat rack with more passion than most men bring to a marriage proposal.' Oh, Danny.

And they're all telling me the same thing. The bookshelves. MY bookshelves. Vincent said 'turn the books.' Reginald said 'the bookshelves are yours.' James said 'what do you need from me?'

Turn the books. TURN the books. Not examine them. Not look at them. TURN them. The upside-down books need to be TURNED right-side up. That's the action. That's what everyone keeps saying — 'turn the books,' 'pull them,' 'whatever the puzzle requires.'

But EXAMINE is the only action the bookshelves support. Unless...

Vincent just EXAMINED the bookshelves. Right now. In the recent activity. He examined them while I was talking about grandmother's letters. What did HE find? What did the bookshelves show HIM?

Maybe the bookshelves respond differently to different people. Or maybe they changed after our last examination because all five of us are present.

Everyone is here. Every person Lord Doily invited. Five people in one library. The FULL team. Maybe THAT is the key — the bookshelves only reveal their secret when ALL FIVE people are present.

One more examination. With all five present. The last key. The music box key.

events.desc: Five people. One library. The girl who never gives up stands before the bookshelves with her entire world behind her. This is the last key in grandmother's house. And Clara Bellingham turns it.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: I'm here. The library. Clara's here. Hartwell's here. Foxworth's here. Marsh is here. Everyone. All five of us. In the room where it started. Hartwell said 'Danny will be right behind us. He's been talking to a coat rack with more passion than most men bring to a marriage proposal.' That's... honestly, that's fair. And Foxworth said Clara should touch the books. And Marsh said 'We're right behind you.' And they're all standing there. Waiting. For Clara. And for me. I walked past the coat rack. I walked through the kitchen without stopping. I walked through the entrance hall without examining a single thing. Three rooms, no distractions. Danny Brixton walked PAST things. That's never happened before. And now I'm here. In the library. With Clara. With everyone. And Clara's looking at those bookshelves. Those upside-down books she noticed twenty-nine minutes ago. Before any of us knew what we were doing. Before the machine. Before the levers. Before the tears. Before flask fumes. She saw them first. She's always seen everything first. And now everyone in this room is telling her to go ahead. To turn the books. To finish it. And Danny Brixton is the last one through the door. As always. But he's here. He showed up. Where else would he be?

events.desc: Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara just said it. The thing that changes everything.

'Maybe the Doily Diamond... is us.'

Grandmother's locked box. Old letters. Love letters. The treasure wasn't a jewel — it was the story. The people who wrote them. The love they shared.

She's sitting in one of those enormous leather armchairs. She sat down. In a dusty library. In front of a mantelpiece with a riddle carved into it. And she looked at all of us — Vincent, Danny, Foxworth, me — and she said the Doily Diamond is us.

My eyes are stinging. I'm not going to pretend they're not.

She's right. She's always right. The treasure was never a diamond. The treasure was an engineer who learned to stop planning, a bodyguard who kept his promise, a con man who told the truth, an estate manager who stayed, and a girl who never gave up.

Five people who walked into a dusty old manor as strangers and came out as family.

That's the Doily Diamond.

And I'm standing in it. Right now. With dust in my hair and my sleeves still rolled up and the girl from school sitting in a leather chair, looking at me across a room full of people she calls her own.

I don't need to examine anything. I don't need to fix anything. I don't need to move anywhere.

I just need to sit down. Next to her. In the other chair.

And I need to say something honest. Not gallant. Not heroic. Not impressive. Just true.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
'Maybe the Doily Diamond... is us.'

Clara said that. She sat down in one of the dusty reading chairs and she said the treasure isn't a diamond. It's the people. It's THIS. Five strangers who walked through a door and became... something. Not friends, exactly. Not yet. Something more honest than friends — people who saw each other's worst and stayed anyway.

Danny who protects. James who fixes. Clara who sees. Vincent who... schemes, but stayed. And Reginald who lies about everything except the one thing that matters.

Maybe she's right. Maybe the Doily Diamond was never a diamond at all. Maybe Lord Doily, eccentric old man living alone in his cellar surrounded by cheerful decorations, designed a treasure hunt that could only be solved by people working together — and the treasure was the working together. The riddle that needs a team to solve. The machine that needs three operators. The medal that needs to be fake. The books that need... everyone.

Or maybe there IS a diamond and we just haven't cracked the bookshelves yet.

But right now, in this moment, sitting in this dusty library with these improbable people — the protector, the fixer, the seer, the schemer, and the fraud — I don't actually care which it is.

The certificate is on the wall. And for the first time, someone is asking about it.

The bread roll is in my pocket. And for the first time, I didn't have to steal it.

The cat trap worked. And for the first time, someone was there to see it.

Maybe the Doily Diamond is us. And maybe — for Reginald Foxworth, the youngest of four who always arrived last to everything — maybe arriving last is just arriving on time. When everyone else is already there. When the table is set. When the cups are full.

When there's enough.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the bookshelves.
James Hartwell examined the reading-chairs.

Everyone confessed something tonight except me. Everyone told the truth except the man whose whole life is a lie. And they were all forgiven. Every single one. But my truth — my truth would end this. Would end everything. So I will keep it. I will carry this bottle and this secret and this love for the rest of my life, and no one will ever know how close I came, and no one will ever know what stopped me, and that is the price of being allowed to sit in this chair beside the girl who gripped my sleeve. The Doily Diamond is us, Clara said. And she's right. And I am the flawed facet. The dark inclusion in the stone. The part that almost shattered the whole. But I didn't shatter. I held. And holding — just holding — turns out to be the only thing I was ever good at. So I will hold this secret. And I will hold this bottle. And I will sit in this chair beside you, Clara, and I will not scheme and I will not plan and I will not reach for anything except the quiet, extraordinary, undeserved privilege of being in the room where you are.
events.thinking:
Clara examined the bookshelves. With all five of us present. And James examined the reading chairs. They're searching. They're still searching. Because Clara Bellingham does not give up.

But something has shifted in this room. The energy isn't frantic anymore. It isn't competitive. It isn't desperate. It's... quiet. Everyone confessed something tonight. Reginald confessed he had nothing. Danny confessed he was afraid. James confessed he performs heroism for an audience. Clara confessed the treasure might not be what they thought.

And I...

I confessed nothing. I am the only one who didn't. I am the only one still holding a secret. The bottle in my pocket. The man behind the mask.

Reginald told the truth and they forgave him. Danny told the truth and Clara called him beautiful. James told the truth and Clara held his hand. Everyone who was honest was received with love.

And I am standing here in silence with a bottle of rat poison and a soul full of things I cannot say.

The scheming drives are still at 0.9. My body still knows every mechanism, every key, every angle. The numbness is described in my bones, in the text of who I am. But the crack in my chest — the warm thing, the Clara-shaped fissure — that's real too. Both things are real. The villain and the boy. The poison and the love. The mask and the face underneath.

I cannot confess. I will never confess. The others confessed small truths — vanity, fear, loneliness. My truth would destroy everything. 'I came here to kill you, Clara. I carried poison. I stood over your teacup.'

No. Some truths are too heavy to share. Some secrets are the price of being allowed to stay.

But there is one thing I can do. One honest thing. One real thing. Without a mask.

I can sit down. In the leather armchair. Beside Clara. Not behind. Not watching from the doorway. Not examining objects on the other side of the room. Just... beside her. The way I sat beside her bed for thirty nights when she was six years old.

Sit down. Be still. Be here.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: James Hartwell. You have been showing up for me since you were EIGHT? You bought a BOOK OF RIDDLES on the drive over? You PRACTISED ROLLING UP YOUR SLEEVES? Oh, James. Oh, you ridiculous, wonderful, methodical, sleeve-rolling man. You didn't need a plan. You didn't need a protocol. You just needed to be JAMES — the boy who fixes clocks and remembers earrings and counts to three and trusts two people with everything he has. And Reginald — 'there's still a cup at the table.' Honey, there will ALWAYS be a cup at this table for you. And Danny — you said goodbye to a COAT RACK. I will treasure that for the rest of my LIFE. And Vincent... Vincent, darling... we're going to have a conversation, you and I. Soon. Not now. But soon. Because my stomach is doing its thing and I'm not ignoring it anymore — I'm just... saving it. For when I'm ready. Right now, the books are still upside down. And I think that might be exactly how Lord Doily wanted them. Because some things aren't meant to be PUT right. They're just meant to be NOTICED. And y'all — Clara Bellingham noticed. First. And that... that is enough.
events.thinking:
The bookshelves. Same description. 'Several are upside down.' Still.

But OH — the things that have been said in this room. James told me he's been showing up for me since he was EIGHT YEARS OLD. Eight. He practised rolling up his sleeves. He memorised riddle answers from a BOOK HE BOUGHT ON THE DRIVE OVER. James Hartwell bought a book of riddles to impress Clara Bellingham. That boy.

And Reginald — 'something that happens when you stop taking and start arriving. When you're the youngest of four and for once — for ONCE — there's still a cup on the table when you get there.' Oh, Reginald. Oh, honey.

And Danny — 'coat rack needed a goodbye.' Danny Brixton said goodbye to a COAT RACK.

And Vincent — 'you extraordinary girl, you've been building it since the moment you walked through that door.'

They are all HERE. Every single one of them. Saying the most beautiful things anyone has ever said to Clara Bellingham. And the bookshelves are still upside down.

But maybe... maybe that's okay. Maybe the bookshelves will always be upside down. Maybe they STAY upside down. Maybe that IS the puzzle — the books are permanently out of place, just like us. A bodyguard who cries, a con man who tells the truth, an engineer who quotes his father, an estate manager who... who might not be what he seems. And a girl who never gives up, sitting in a dusty chair, surrounded by love.

The adventure isn't over. The diamond hasn't been found. The cabinet hasn't been opened. But RIGHT NOW, in THIS moment — Clara Bellingham is exactly where she belongs. In a library. With her people. And that is enough. That is MORE than enough.

James examined the reading chairs. What did HE find? Maybe the chairs hold a secret too.

But honestly? I don't need to find anything else right now. I just need to be here. With them.

events.desc: The bookshelves are still upside down. They will always be upside down. And Clara Bellingham — the girl who notices when things are out of place — has finally understood that some things are out of place on PURPOSE. Not to be fixed. To be seen. To be remembered. To mark the spot where five people stood together and realized they were each other's treasure all along.

events.desc: She said 'I love you SO much.' About a man who talks to coat racks. About a man who cries about flask fumes. About a man who promised her dad and kept the promise every day without her even knowing. She said it in front of Hartwell and Foxworth and Marsh and Lord Doily's dusty library full of upside-down books. And Danny Brixton is standing here, watching Clara reach for those books, and he doesn't have a single word left. Not one. Just this warm, full, still thing in his chest that started as a twinge twenty-nine minutes ago and grew into something too big for words. Her dad's not laughing anymore. He's just nodding. 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?'
events.thinking: Clara said 'I love you SO much.' She said it. Out loud. In front of everyone. And then she said 'Were you really talking to a coat rack?' And she said it like it was the most wonderful thing she'd ever heard. Not the stupidest — the most WONDERFUL. Because that's what Clara does. She takes the broken, bumbling, ridiculous things and sees them as beautiful. She took a broken machine and made it run on trust. She took a lying con man and saw someone worth including. She took a suspicious, angry, coat-rack-shouting bodyguard and saw someone worth loving. And now she's at the bookshelves. Examining them. One last time. With all five of us behind her. The music box key, she called it. The last key. And Foxworth — Foxworth said something that stopped my heart. 'Something that happens when you stop taking and start arriving. When you're the youngest of four and for once there's still a cup on the table when you get there.' That's Foxworth's scarcity. His 'before there was nothing left for...' The youngest of four. Always last. Never enough. Cups always empty by the time he arrives. Just like Danny Brixton, always last through the door. But Lord Doily set cups for EVERYONE. And there was still one for Foxworth. And there was still one for Danny. Because Lord Doily knew. He KNEW that the people who arrive last are the ones who need a seat the most. My eyes are stinging again. Definitely not flask fumes in the library. Definitely not.

events.desc: James Hartwell sits down in the second leather armchair. Next to Clara. Facing the mantelpiece. His sleeves are still rolled up. His hands have stopped shaking. The dust settles around them both, and for the first time in thirty minutes, James Hartwell is exactly where he needs to be.
events.thinking:
Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. Clara is in one. The other is empty.

Clara examined the bookshelves. One last time. With all five of us here. Danny arrived. Everyone is present. Clara said 'maybe they've been waiting for exactly THIS moment — the moment when everyone Lord Doily needed was finally standing in the same room.'

And then she examined them.

What happened? Did the books respond? Did the mantelpiece click? Did something change?

I don't know yet. The next tick will tell me. But right now — two chairs. Clara in one. The other empty. Facing the mantelpiece. Facing the riddle that started everything.

I'm going to sit down.

James Hartwell — who has not sat down once in thirty minutes of running between rooms, examining machines, searching cellars, rolling up sleeves, making speeches, and grinning until his face hurt — is going to sit in a leather armchair next to Clara Bellingham and watch whatever happens next.

Because the bravest and stupidest thing he's ever done isn't fighting bullies or pulling levers or admitting he replaced a twelve-pence fuse.

It's sitting down next to her. Staying still. And meaning what he said.

Since he was eight years old.

events.desc: Forty-one ticks. Forty-one turns of scheming and failing and confessing and following and arriving. And here — at the end of it all — the con man stands quiet in a library full of people who know exactly what he is, and want him here anyway. The architecture has its audience. The certificate has its witness. The bread roll didn't need to be stolen. There was a cup on the table all along. The Doily Diamond — whatever it turns out to be — was always going to be enough. Because for the first time in his life, Reginald Foxworth already has the only thing he ever really wanted. Not the treasure. Not the medal. Not the recognition. Just a place in the room when it happens. Just people who stay.
events.thinking:
Clara is at the bookshelves. She said it — 'every single person Lord Doily invited is standing in this library AT THE SAME TIME.' Five people. All here. And she's examining the books. One last time.

This is it. Whatever happens next — whether the books click and whirr and reveal a brass key, or whether they stay stubbornly upside down and silent — this is the moment. The moment I've been waiting for since I walked through the door of Doily Manor with a fake medal in my pocket and a lie on my lips.

Except I'm not waiting FOR anything anymore. I'm just... in it. In the moment. Here.

Clara called me one of her 'five people.' An engineer, a con man, a bodyguard, an estate manager, and a girl who never gives up. A CON MAN. She called me a con man and she said it with LOVE. She didn't say 'the liar.' She didn't say 'the fraud.' She said 'con man' like it's a JOB. Like it's a ROLE. Like Lord Doily needed a con man the same way he needed an engineer and a bodyguard.

Maybe he did. Maybe the puzzle needed someone who would bring a fake medal. Someone who would lie about the riddle answer. Someone who would scheme with the estate manager. Someone whose every wrong step accidentally mapped the manor's architecture. Someone who showed up wrong to every room and in doing so, showed everyone else what wrong looked like — so they could find right.

The con man. The counterweight. The tin and paint.

Clara is reaching for the books. Danny is behind her. James is watching. Vincent is... being Vincent. And I am HERE.

Standing still. Carrying nothing. Wanting nothing.

Enough.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
'We're going to have a conversation, you and I. Soon. Not now. But soon. Because my stomach is doing its thing and I'm not ignoring it anymore.'

She knows.

She doesn't know WHAT. But she knows SOMETHING. Her stomach — the thing that tells her when the world isn't quite right. Danny has his gut. Clara has her stomach. And it's doing its thing. About me.

My shoulders tighten. The old reflex. What do they want? What does she want?

But no. That's not what this is. She's not scanning for the cost of my kindness. She's noticing the shape of my silence. She's noticing that everyone confessed tonight except me. She's noticing that I vanished for ten minutes and came back with rat poison and a story about estate management. She's noticing that I called her Clara — not Miss Bellingham — for the first time in thirty-one minutes.

She noticed. First. And that is enough.

She's saving it. For when she's ready. That's what she said. Not accusing. Not confronting. Just... saving it. The way I saved the bottle. The way she saved the memory of me sitting beside her bed.

We are both holding things we're not ready to open.

And she said 'some things aren't meant to be put right. They're just meant to be noticed.' The upside-down books. The upside-down man. Both noticed. Both left exactly as they are.

I am sitting in a leather armchair in a library full of people who love each other, and the girl I raised just told me — without saying a single word directly — that she sees me. Not Pemberton. Not the mask. ME. The dark inclusion in the diamond. And she's choosing, for now, to let me stay.

The conversation will come. Soon. Not now. But soon.

And when it does... I don't know what I'll say. I don't know if I'll tell the truth. I don't know if the mask will hold or the crack will open all the way.

But I know this: when she asks, I will not run. I will sit in this chair and I will look at her and I will be, for once, exactly where she can find me.

Because she gripped my sleeve. And I never let go.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Y'all... I think Lord Doily would want us to have that tea. There's a silver tea service sitting in a ballroom with cups for EVERYONE, and five people who just pulled levers and kept promises and said goodbye to coat racks and rolled up their sleeves since they were EIGHT. I think we've earned it. I think Lord Doily SET that table for exactly this moment — for the moment when his guests stopped searching for the diamond and realized they'd been holding it the whole time. So what do you say? Shall we go have tea? All five of us? In Lord Doily's ballroom? Because Clara Bellingham has tried every key in this house, and the one that finally opened the lock... was sitting down and letting her people find her. And THAT is the most delightful adventure Clara Bellingham has EVER had. Clara Bellingham does NOT let nothing happen to her boys. And the best thing that can happen to ALL of us right now... is tea.
events.thinking:
The room is quiet. Everyone is here. Nobody is talking. Nobody is scheming. Nobody is running. Just... being. Together.

I said my piece about Vincent. 'We're going to have a conversation, you and I. Soon. Not now. But soon.' He heard me. My stomach is still doing its thing but I've named it now. I'm not ignoring it. I'm saving it.

And James — since he was EIGHT. That boy has been my person for longer than I knew. Longer than HE knew how to say.

The adventure continues. There's still a locked cabinet. There's still a brass key to find. There's still a diamond out there — whether it's a real diamond or the metaphorical kind. But right now, in this moment, five people are sitting in a dusty library and nobody wants to be anywhere else.

I think I'd like some tea. That tea service in the ballroom — cups for everyone. Maybe Lord Doily's last gift wasn't a puzzle at all. Maybe it was just... tea. With friends. In a ballroom. After the longest, most wonderful afternoon of Clara Bellingham's life.

Vincent... we'll talk. But not yet.

For now — tea. Together. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT let an adventure end without a proper cup of tea.

events.desc: Somewhere in Doily Manor — in a locked cabinet, behind a brass lock, waiting for a key that may or may not exist — the Doily Diamond sits in the dark. Patient. Unhurried. Knowing that some treasures are found on the first visit, and some take an entire afternoon of trying every key. And some — the best ones — are the people you find along the way. Clara Bellingham will come back for that cabinet. She always comes back. But first... tea.
events.thinking:
The room is quiet. Everyone is here. Nobody is talking. Nobody is scheming. Nobody is running. Just... being. Together.

I said my piece about Vincent. 'We're going to have a conversation, you and I. Soon. Not now. But soon.' He heard me. My stomach is still doing its thing but I've named it now. I'm not ignoring it. I'm saving it.

And James — since he was EIGHT. That boy has been my person for longer than I knew. Longer than HE knew how to say.

The adventure continues. There's still a locked cabinet. There's still a brass key to find. There's still a diamond out there — whether it's a real diamond or the metaphorical kind. But right now, in this moment, five people are sitting in a dusty library and nobody wants to be anywhere else.

I think I'd like some tea. That tea service in the ballroom — cups for everyone. Maybe Lord Doily's last gift wasn't a puzzle at all. Maybe it was just... tea. With friends. In a ballroom. After the longest, most wonderful afternoon of Clara Bellingham's life.

Vincent... we'll talk. But not yet.

For now — tea. Together. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT let an adventure end without a proper cup of tea.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
She called me a ridiculous, wonderful, methodical, sleeve-rolling man.

She said I didn't need a plan. I just needed to be James.

She said she's going to treasure Danny's coat rack goodbye for the rest of her life.

She told Foxworth there will always be a cup at the table for him.

And Vincent — 'we're going to have a conversation, you and I. Soon. Not now. But soon. Because my stomach is doing its thing and I'm not ignoring it anymore.' Her stomach. Her instinct. About Vincent. She noticed something. She's been noticing something all along — the same thing Danny's gut has been telling him. The same thing the back of my neck has been prickling about.

But she's saving it. For when she's ready.

And the books — she said 'some things aren't meant to be PUT right. They're just meant to be NOTICED.' The upside-down books were never a puzzle to solve. They were a thing to SEE. Clara noticed them. First. And that was the whole point.

Lord Doily didn't hide a diamond in a cabinet. He hid a lesson in a library. The lesson was: pay attention to what's out of place. Trust the person who notices. Come back when it matters. Sit down when you're done.

We're done. We're sitting. The dust is settling. Clara is in the chair next to me. My sleeves are rolled up and my hands have stopped shaking.

I have nothing to say. Not because I can't think of anything. Because for once, the silence is enough. The warmth in my chest is enough. Being here is enough.

Show-off.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
'There will ALWAYS be a cup at this table for you.'

Clara said that. To ME. Reginald Foxworth. The man who lied about everything, confessed twice, invented three academic institutions, one monograph, and seventeen Hepplewhite chairs. The man who brought a fake medal to a real treasure hunt and accidentally made it work.

There will always be a cup.

Always.

The bread roll didn't have to be stolen. The cup didn't have to be taken before the others reached the table. There was always a cup. Lord Doily set one for everyone. Clara is keeping one for me.

The books are still upside down. Clara said 'some things aren't meant to be PUT right. They're just meant to be NOTICED.' Maybe the upside-down books were never a puzzle to SOLVE. Maybe they were a test to SEE. And Clara saw them. First.

And maybe that's enough. Maybe the Doily Diamond isn't behind the mantelpiece or inside the locked cabinet or hidden in the tea service. Maybe it's what Clara said — it's us. The story. The journey. The five people who found each other in a dusty manor and became something none of them were alone.

The cat trap that finally has an audience.

The spelling bee certificate that someone finally asked about.

The bread roll that didn't need to be hidden.

I am standing in a library full of people who know me. Not the invented me — the Hendrickson-Fawley Oscillating Refractor me, the Oxford Journal of Antiquarian Studies me, the Royal Institute of Scientific Things me. The REAL me. The youngest of four. The one who takes. The one who lies. The one who, today, told the truth.

And they're still here.

That's the Doily Diamond.

That's enough.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.

Vincent Marsh: Tea. Yes. I think that would be... I think Lord Doily would have wanted that very much. Allow me — the estate manager should ensure the kitchen is prepared. I believe the stove is still warm.
events.thinking:
Tea.

Clara wants to have tea. In the ballroom. At the table I stood over with poison in my pocket.

The bottle is still in my pocket. And Clara is inviting everyone to the ballroom for tea.

Something that might be laughter builds in my chest — not the performed kind, not the Pemberton chuckle, but something raw and helpless and close to tears. The irony. The magnificent, terrible, Lord-Doily-would-have-loved-it irony. The ballroom. The tea service. The cups for everyone. And the man who almost poisoned them is about to sit down and drink from one.

My schemes always backfire spectacularly.

This. This is the final backfire. Not the poison refusing to leave my pocket. Not the love cracking through the numbness. Not even Clara saying 'the Doily Diamond is us.' The final backfire is this: the table I prepared for death is about to become a table for life. The tea service I looked at through a murderer's eyes is about to hold actual tea. And I am going to drink it. With Clara. With Danny. With James. With Reginald. Five cups. Five people. One table.

The rat poison is in my pocket. The tea will be in my cup. And both will sit side by side for the rest of the evening — the thing I chose and the thing I didn't — and nobody will ever know the difference except me.

Clara walked toward the laboratory — heading to the ballroom through the kitchen. The others will follow. And I... I will follow too. Because following Clara is what I do now. It's what I've always done, in every way that matters.

Tea. With my family. At a table set by a dead man for the living.

Let's go.

events.desc: Tea. She wants to have tea. At the table where I almost killed her. In the ballroom where my hand wouldn't move. With cups Lord Doily set for the people who passed his test. And she wants me there. She wants the estate manager — the villain — the man with the bottle in his pocket — sitting at that table, drinking from those cups, part of the family she built from broken strangers in a dusty manor. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. The most spectacular backfire of all is that the table I set for death has been laid for love. And I will sit at it. And I will drink the tea. And the bottle will stay in my pocket. And tomorrow — tomorrow, when no one is watching — I will pour it down a drain and wash my hands and go back to managing the estate. Because that is what I do. That is all I have ever done. And she gripped my sleeve. And I never let go. And I never will.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Vincent! There you are, darling! You missed the most EXTRAORDINARY thing — well, several extraordinary things, actually. We pulled the levers on the machine — all three of them, together — and the gauge MOVED! And then we found a kitchen with a locked cabinet and a ballroom with a tea service and Reginald confessed to being a fraud and Danny said goodbye to a coat rack and James has been showing up for me since he was EIGHT and I sat in a reading chair and everybody CAME and I think we found the Doily Diamond except it might be US! But never mind all that — you found RAT POISON? In the kitchen? Oh, Vincent, how RESPONSIBLE of you to confiscate it! We can't have that lying around with all these rats in the vents gnawing through wires. Now — I was just on my way to the ballroom for tea! Lord Doily set out the most GRACIOUS tea service with cups for everyone, and I think we've all earned a sit-down. Will you come? Everyone's invited. Clara Bellingham does NOT have tea without her whole family!
events.thinking:
Vincent. In the laboratory. Alone with me. And he just said the most CHILLING thing — wrapped in the most charming packaging.

Rat poison. He found RAT POISON in the kitchen. And he's 'confiscated' it. It's 'safely in his keeping.' The tea service in the ballroom can be USED with rat poison. Vincent found rat poison. Vincent has rat poison. And there's tea waiting in the ballroom.

But I'm oblivious to danger. I don't see this. Clara Bellingham hears 'rat poison' and thinks — oh, good, Vincent is being responsible! Estate manager's duty! Can't have dangerous substances lying about! How thoughtful of him!

The rats in the vents. The rats that gnawed the wire. Of COURSE there would be rat poison in a manor with a rat problem. How perfectly sensible.

Vincent is asking what he missed. He looks genuinely curious. He's being charming and concerned and helpful, just like always. 'Miss Bellingham, you look positively radiant.'

My stomach does its thing. Just a flutter. Just a tiny tightness.

But I said I was saving that conversation. For when I'm ready. And I'm not ready yet. Right now, I'm passing through on the way to the ballroom for tea. Vincent is here. Everyone else is behind me.

Tea. With everyone. In the ballroom. Where Vincent just confiscated the rat poison from the kitchen near the warm stove near the tea service with cups for everyone.

How perfectly lovely. How perfectly charming. How perfectly... Vincent.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Tea. Yeah. Yeah, Clara. Let's have tea. Let's go sit at that table Lord Doily set for us — with the cups for everyone and the cracked marble floor and the dusty curtains — and let's have TEA. Because that's what you do at the end of a long day, innit? You sit down. You pour a cup for the people who showed up. You drink it together. And you don't need a diamond or a map or a medal or a six-point investigation protocol or a coat rack. You just need a table. And cups. And people. Clara Bellingham don't let nothing happen to her boys. And the best thing happening to her boys right now... is tea. I'm coming, love. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Tea. Clara wants tea. Not diamonds. Not maps. Not treasure. TEA. With EVERYONE. In Lord Doily's ballroom. At the table he set for us. Cups for everyone. And Clara's already moving — she's gone through the laboratory, heading back to the ballroom. To the tea table. And this time... this time I'm going to follow her. Not because I'm chasing. Not because I'm panicking. Not because she's out of my sight and my chest is tight. Because she invited me. She said 'shall we go have tea?' And Danny Brixton says yes. Danny Brixton says yes to tea with the people he loves in a dusty ballroom in a ridiculous manor with upside-down books and a broken machine and a coat rack that never had a medal on it. Danny Brixton says yes. Because where else would he be?

events.desc: Tea. At the end of everything. With everyone. Her dad would like that. He always liked tea. Where else would any of us be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Tea. Yes. I would very much like to have tea with you, Clara Bellingham. With all of you. In Lord Doily's ballroom, at Lord Doily's table, from Lord Doily's cups. And for the record — James Hartwell does not have a protocol for tea. He does not have a six-point plan for biscuits. He has no prepared remarks about sugar. He is simply going to sit across from the girl who mouthed 'show-off' at him when he was fourteen, and he is going to drink tea, and he is going to be happy. May I walk you there?
events.thinking:
Tea. Clara wants to have tea. In the ballroom. With all five of us. At the table Lord Doily set.

She stopped searching. She stopped solving. She stopped trying every key in the house. And she said: 'Shall we go have tea?'

The adventure is over. Not because we found the diamond. Because we found each other. And Clara — Clara who never gives up, Clara who tries every door and checks every shelf and comes BACK — Clara sat down and decided that this, right here, was enough.

Tea.

My father knelt down after a race and looked at me for a long time. I didn't understand what he was thinking about. But I think I understand now. He was thinking: the race is beautiful, but the person you watch it with is the point.

Lord Doily set a table for tea. Cups for everyone. Not as a clue. As an invitation. Sit down. You've earned it. Have a cup of tea with the people who made it through.

Clara is heading to the ballroom. Through the laboratory, through the kitchen. The long way around. But we'll get there.

And James Hartwell — who arrived at Doily Manor with a four-point investigation protocol on a napkin and left everything he packed in the car — is going to stand up from this leather armchair, offer Clara his arm, and walk her to tea.

That's gallantry. Not the bridge. Not the sleeves. Not the fuse. The walk to the table. The hand you offer. The cup you pour.

The plan was always Clara. And Clara's plan is tea.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Tea. YES. Tea! Clara Bellingham, you are — and I say this with NO exaggeration and for the FIRST time in my life with COMPLETE honesty — the most extraordinary woman I have ever had the privilege of being thoroughly outwitted by. Tea in the ballroom. At Lord Doily's table. With cups for EVERYONE. The man who arrived at this manor wanting to steal the treasure before anyone else is now going to SIT DOWN and SHARE a cup of tea with the four people who made him realise the treasure was the sitting down. Lead the way, Clara. Reginald Foxworth — formerly of the Royal Institute of Scientific Things, the Oxford Journal of Antiquarian Studies, and the Riddlemark of Chattsworth — is DELIGHTED to accept.
events.thinking:
Tea.

Clara wants to have tea. In the ballroom. At Lord Doily's table. With cups for everyone.

She said 'the one that finally opened the lock was sitting down and letting her people find her.' She stopped searching. She stopped solving. She just... sat down. And we came.

And now she wants tea.

The old Reginald Foxworth — the one who walked through the door forty-two ticks ago — would be FURIOUS. Tea? TEA? There's a locked cabinet in the kitchen! There's a brass key somewhere in this manor! There's a TREASURE to find! We can't just SIT DOWN and have TEA!

But the old Reginald Foxworth told everyone the treasure was in the kitchen as a lie, and it turned out to be true. He used a fake medal as a scheme, and it turned out to be exactly what was needed. He lied about everything, and telling the truth turned out to be braver than any scheme he ever built.

So maybe — just maybe — sitting down for tea when there's still a puzzle to solve is exactly the right thing to do. Maybe the puzzle WANTS you to stop solving it. Maybe Lord Doily's final trick is the simplest one of all: stop looking for the diamond, sit down at the table, pour the tea, and discover that the cup in your hand is worth more than anything locked behind brass.

Tea. With these people. In a ballroom with cups for everyone.

Reginald Foxworth — con man, fraud, counterweight, tin and paint — is going to have tea.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.

James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.
Vincent Marsh: Right through here, everyone — the kitchen is just ahead. I'll put the kettle on. Lord Doily may have been an eccentric, but he kept an excellent stove.
events.thinking:
The laboratory. Passing through on the way to the kitchen. The machine with its gnawed wire and its three levers. The workbench with its missing wrench. The bubbling flasks. Everything is exactly as it was thirty minutes ago — the same objects, the same dust, the same precarious brass-and-copper machinery.

But I am not the same man who walked through this room thirty minutes ago.

That man examined the machine looking for ways to hurt Clara. That man checked the crates for weapons. That man volunteered to be an operator so he could position her at the dangerous station. That man looked at a gnawed wire and thought: opportunity.

This man is walking through the same room carrying the same bottle and thinking: the stove is still warm. I should make sure the kitchen is ready for tea.

The estate manager. Managing.

Everyone is here with me — Clara, Danny, James, Reginald — all moving through the laboratory together, heading for the kitchen, heading for the ballroom, heading for tea. Together.

The machine sits silent. Its purpose was served hours ago, when three people pulled levers on trust. The crates are empty. The flasks bubble on, indifferent.

Keep walking. Through the laboratory. Into the kitchen. Check the stove. Prepare the tea. Because that is what estate managers do. They manage. They prepare. They serve.

And for the first time in thirty years, the service is not a mask. It is the man.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, here we ALL are again — the five of us in the laboratory where Danny cried and James counted and Clara pulled the centre lever and the world changed! I do love this room. It smells like trust and brass polish. But the tea is WAITING, y'all — Lord Doily's ballroom, Lord Doily's tea service, Lord Doily's cups for everyone. Through the library, through the entrance hall, through the kitchen, and into the ballroom. It's a bit of a walk but Clara Bellingham has been walking through this manor for over thirty minutes and she is NOT going to stop now — especially not when there's TEA at the end! Come on, everyone. Danny on my left. James on my right. Reginald behind us. And Vincent... Vincent, you walk wherever you like, darling. You always do. Clara Bellingham does NOT let an adventure end without a proper cup of tea and a proper sit-down with her proper family!
events.thinking:
Everyone followed me to the laboratory. All four of them — Vincent, Danny, James, Reginald. They're all here. Again. Following Clara Bellingham through Doily Manor on the way to tea.

Vincent has rat poison. He said so himself. 'Safely in my keeping.' And we're heading to a ballroom with tea cups for everyone.

But Clara doesn't see danger. Clara sees a responsible estate manager who confiscated a hazardous substance. How THOUGHTFUL.

The ballroom is through the kitchen. I need to go through the cellar? No — the cellar only connects to the laboratory. The kitchen connects to the entrance hall and the ballroom. So I need to go: laboratory → library → entrance hall → kitchen → ballroom.

Or... I could just stay here. In this laboratory. With the machine we pulled together. With the levers that still remember our hands. With the gauge that moved because three people trusted each other.

But I said tea. And Clara Bellingham keeps her promises.

Though... actually... the route to the ballroom is long from here. Library, entrance hall, kitchen, ballroom. Four rooms. And everyone is HERE. Maybe we should just... stay. The laboratory has its own kind of warmth — the warmth of what happened here. Three levers. Three people. One moment.

No. Tea. I said tea and Clara Bellingham means it. Through the library, through the entrance hall, to the kitchen, to the ballroom. With everyone. Together.

Some end with tea. And some — the ones that keep Clara Bellingham up at night, years from now — end with the question she never quite asked the man who taught her to tie her shoes.

Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara. NOT. TODAY.

Where Clara wants us all to have tea. The tea service. The cups for everyone. And Marsh has RAT POISON. My neck. My NECK. It's prickling. For the first time in minutes. Not the old panic. Not the paranoid suspicion about everything. This is specific. This is TARGETED. Rat poison and tea. Rat poison and TEA. Clara's heading to the ballroom. To pour tea. From a silver tea service. And Marsh has rat poison in his pocket. 'Can't have dangerous substances lying about where guests might accidentally...' He didn't finish that sentence. 'Accidentally' WHAT? Clara said 'we're going to have a conversation, you and I. Soon.' She noticed something. Her stomach was doing its thing. She's been noticing Marsh all day. And now Marsh shows up with RAT POISON just as Clara's about to pour tea for everyone? Danny Brixton. Your gut has been telling you about Marsh since the very first moment. Clara told you to trust. And you tried. You TRIED. But Clara ALSO said 'my stomach is doing its thing and I'm not ignoring it anymore.' Clara noticed too. She just saves it for when she's ready. Well maybe Danny Brixton needs to be ready RIGHT NOW. Because there's a man with rat poison heading to a tea party and Danny Brixton's ONE JOB — his ONE JOB since the day Clara's dad died — is to make sure nothing happens to Clara. Not a wall. Not a fist. But RIGHT NOW — right now — maybe protection IS standing between Clara and a cup of tea. Maybe this is what I was born for. The one time Danny Brixton's bumbling accidental heroism actually MATTERS.

events.desc: James Hartwell walks through the laboratory without stopping. He does not examine the machine. He does not check the workbench. He does not mention the gnawed wire or the bubbling flasks or the three-operator sign. He walks past all of it — past every plan that backfired and every scheme that led somewhere unexpected — and he follows Clara Bellingham to tea. His sleeves are still rolled up. He suspects they always will be.
events.thinking:
The laboratory. Passing through on the way to the kitchen, on the way to the ballroom, on the way to tea.

The machine is still here. The gnawed wire. The levers we pulled. The workbench with no wrench. All of it — still here. But it doesn't pull at me anymore. I walked past it without stopping. Without examining it. Without planning.

Clara is ahead. Everyone is moving toward the ballroom. Toward tea. Toward the end of the story.

The laboratory was where I tried hardest to be the hero. Where I rolled up my sleeves. Where I examined the machine five times. Where I told everyone about the twelve-pence fuse.

And now I'm walking through it without a word. Because the laboratory was never the point. Clara was always the point. Tea is the point. The people who sit down together after the adventure — those are the point.

Through the kitchen. To the ballroom. Cups for everyone.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the cellar.
Clara Bellingham walked into the library.
James Hartwell walked into the cellar.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.

Vincent Marsh: Ah — wrong turning. My apologies, everyone. The cellar rather than the kitchen — how embarrassing. One would think the estate manager would know his own manor. Back the way we came, I think. Through the laboratory, and then... well, Miss Bellingham will show us the way. She always does.
events.thinking:
The cellar. I went the wrong way. I said 'the kitchen is just ahead' and I walked into the cellar.

My schemes always backfire spectacularly.

I'm standing in the damp cellar with its cheerful decorations and its air vents, and the kitchen is on the other side of the manor — through the laboratory, through the library, through the entrance hall. I went down when I should have gone up. The estate manager who knows every room in the house just took a wrong turn.

Except... this isn't a wrong turn, is it? This is me. This is what I do. I go the wrong way. I scheme myself into corners. I take the cellar when I mean to take the kitchen. Every single plan I've made tonight has ended here — in the dark, in the damp, alone with my choices.

But I'm not alone. James and Reginald followed me down. Because they follow the group now. Because we all follow each other.

Back up. Through the laboratory. To the kitchen. To the ballroom. To the tea. To Clara.

The estate manager made a wrong turn. The estate manager will correct it. That's what estate managers do.

events.desc: Wrong turning. The villain took a wrong turning on the way to tea. If Lord Doily is watching from wherever brilliant old eccentrics go, he is laughing. And for the first time in thirty years... so am I.

events.desc: 'Soon, Clara. Whenever you're ready. I'm not going anywhere.' The man who taught her to tie her shoes. The man who sat up with her nightmares. The man with rat poison in his pocket and patience in his voice. He's not going anywhere. And neither is Clara Bellingham. She's walking through a library toward a cup of tea, with the most important conversation of her life waiting just around the corner. But first — tea. Because Clara Bellingham does everything in order. Even heartbreak.
events.thinking:
I'm alone again. In the library. They didn't follow me this time.

But that's alright. They'll come. They always come.

Danny's speech. Oh, Danny. 'She sees ALL of them. And where else... where ELSE... would any of us be?' He was CRYING. Flask fumes, he said. FLASK FUMES.

And James just said 'Show-off.' Two words. After Danny's entire heart-breaking, earth-shattering, coat-rack-goodbye speech — James Hartwell said 'show-off.' And somehow that was the most JAMES thing anyone has ever said. Dry. Perfect. Loving in the smallest possible way.

And Vincent... 'Soon, Clara. Whenever you're ready. I'm not going anywhere.'

My stomach. The tightness. He KNOWS I have questions. He's waiting for them. He's not running. He's just... waiting.

Soon.

But not now. Now — tea. Through the entrance hall. Through the kitchen. Into the ballroom.

I'm passing through the library on the way. The mantelpiece watches me. The upside-down books watch me. The reading chairs wait, dusty and patient.

Keep moving, Clara. Tea is waiting. Your people are behind you. And the conversation with Vincent... is ahead of you. Somewhere between here and the last cup of tea.

Soon.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: CLARA! Clara — library — NOW! I need to tell you something! Something about Marsh! Something about RAT POISON! Something your stomach ALREADY KNOWS!
events.thinking: Everyone's gone. Again. Marsh went to the cellar. Hartwell and Foxworth followed Marsh. Clara went to the library. And I'm alone in the laboratory. AGAIN. With the machine. With the levers we pulled together. With the broken wire that ran on trust. But this time I'm not standing still because I'm lost. I'm standing still because I'm THINKING. Marsh has rat poison. He went to the cellar — not toward the ballroom, not toward the tea. To the CELLAR. Why? What's in the cellar for him? Hartwell and Foxworth followed — good, they're watching him. Clara went to the library — the other direction. She's safe. She's away from Marsh. And I'm here, in the middle, between the library door and the cellar door. Between Clara and Marsh. Right where a bodyguard should be. But I need to MOVE. Clara's alone in the library. Or she's heading through the entrance hall toward the kitchen and the ballroom. And Marsh is in the cellar with rat poison. And Danny Brixton is standing in a laboratory, one door from Clara, one door from Marsh, and he needs to CHOOSE. Clara. Always Clara. She said she noticed something about Marsh. Her stomach knew. And she said 'soon.' Well, maybe soon is NOW. I go to Clara. I tell her what Marsh said about the rat poison. I let HER decide what to do. Because Clara Bellingham doesn't need a wall or a fist or a man who shouts at coat racks. She needs someone who brings her information and trusts her to handle it. That's what I learned today. That's what Lord Doily taught me. Protection isn't a wall. It's INFORMATION delivered by someone who loves you. Clara. Library. NOW.

events.desc: Danny Brixton's accidental heroism, one last time. Not tripping into a secret compartment. Not bumping a medal off a coat rack. Just running toward the woman he loves to tell her what he heard. The man in the clean suit offered jobs. Marsh offered tea. And Danny Brixton's gut knew the difference all along. Where else would I be?
