events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Clara just toasted everyone by name. 'To Reginald Foxworth, who told the truth.' She included me in a toast. By name. For telling the truth. Not for being clever. Not for being the sharpest mind. For telling the truth. The thing I'm worst at. The thing that feels like wearing someone else's clothes. And she made it sound like it was the most important thing I did all night. Because it was. I can see the ballroom now — really see it. The cracked marble floor. The dusty curtains. The long dining table. Five cups. Five people. The cracks in the floor look like a map of everywhere we've been tonight. Every room, every argument, every scheme that backfired. All of it leading here. To this cracked, dusty, beautiful room. I notice the distress is still there — Vincent, Danny. Getting worse, the system says. And I've been sitting still for... how many ticks now? Many. Watching. Being present. But I notice something pulling at me — not the old scheming pull, not greed. It's the affiliation need at 1.0, the neglected bonds. Two of four relationships neglected, it says. I've spoken to Danny and Vincent. I've spoken to James. But I haven't spoken directly to Clara. Not since she called me a wonder. Not since she said I've been one of her boys since the Royal Institute of Scientific Things. Clara, who holds everyone together. Clara, who walked deeper into the cave. Clara, who made a con man cry. I want to say something to her. Something true. Something that isn't a scheme or a performance. Something simple. Because she called me sweetheart and nobody has called me sweetheart since... since ever, probably. And because she said the point was always coming back and having someone to tell. Well — I want to tell her something. Something I've never told anyone. Something about the cat trap.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the null.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking: A cat trap. Strings and counterweights and a bucket. The most beautiful piece of engineering a fourteen-year-old boy could build. And when it worked — when every piece moved exactly as planned — he looked around and nobody was there. Nobody to show it to. And the feeling drained away like water from a cracked cup. A cracked cup. He said cracked cup and we're sitting at a cracked marble table and the cups are full and the feeling isn't draining because four people are watching. We're watching. We've BEEN watching. And he said nobody has ever called him sweetheart. Not once. Not ONCE. In his whole life. The youngest of four. The one who hid bread rolls. The one who watched from windows. Nobody ever called him sweetheart. And I called him sweetheart without thinking about it. I call everyone sweetheart. Danny is sweetheart. James is — well, James is James. Vincent is darling. But Reginald... I called him sweetheart the way I'd call anyone sweetheart, and for him it was the first time. The FIRST TIME. He's going to carry that word in his pocket the way he used to carry bread rolls. And it won't go stale. And he didn't have to steal it. My eyes are burning again and I am OUT of things to blame it on. Danny used the flask fumes. The cellar damp is too far away. I am just going to have to admit that Clara Bellingham is crying in a ballroom because a con man told her nobody ever called him sweetheart and that is the saddest and most beautiful thing she has ever heard.

events.desc: The cat trap. The beautiful, perfect cat trap with nobody watching. That is the saddest thing I have ever heard. And the most hopeful. Because the bucket tipped an hour ago and the feeling hasn't drained away. It's still there. In his chest. Where he touched it. The cracked cup isn't cracked anymore, Reginald. It never was. You just needed someone to fill it.
events.thinking: A cat trap. Strings and counterweights and a bucket. The most beautiful piece of engineering a fourteen-year-old boy could build. And when it worked — when every piece moved exactly as planned — he looked around and nobody was there. Nobody to show it to. And the feeling drained away like water from a cracked cup. A cracked cup. He said cracked cup and we're sitting at a cracked marble table and the cups are full and the feeling isn't draining because four people are watching. We're watching. We've BEEN watching. And he said nobody has ever called him sweetheart. Not once. Not ONCE. In his whole life. The youngest of four. The one who hid bread rolls. The one who watched from windows. Nobody ever called him sweetheart. And I called him sweetheart without thinking about it. I call everyone sweetheart. Danny is sweetheart. James is — well, James is James. Vincent is darling. But Reginald... I called him sweetheart the way I'd call anyone sweetheart, and for him it was the first time. The FIRST TIME. He's going to carry that word in his pocket the way he used to carry bread rolls. And it won't go stale. And he didn't have to steal it. My eyes are burning again and I am OUT of things to blame it on. Danny used the flask fumes. The cellar damp is too far away. I am just going to have to admit that Clara Bellingham is crying in a ballroom because a con man told her nobody ever called him sweetheart and that is the saddest and most beautiful thing she has ever heard.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Foxworth told Clara about the cat trap. Strings and counterweights and a bucket. The most beautiful piece of engineering he'd ever made. And when it worked — when everything moved exactly as he'd planned — he felt complete. For ten seconds. And then he looked around and nobody was there. Nobody to show it to. 'I've been trying to get that feeling back ever since.' Every scheme. Every lie. Every magnificent performance. Building the cat trap. Hoping someone's watching. And now someone IS watching. Four someones. And the feeling hasn't drained away. It's still here. He touched his chest when he said it. The same place I feel the anchor. The same place the loyalty lives. And Clara said 'I know' to Hartwell's 'show-off.' Two words. The quietest thing she's said all night. And the most complete. She KNOWS. She's always known. She knew about the coat rack and the mantelpiece and the machine and the levers. She knew before any of us that the diamond was tea. And Marsh said 'Lord Doily would be rather pleased with us. All things considered.' All things considered. There's a universe in those three words. All things considered — including the bottle in Danny's pocket. Including the cap Marsh almost opened. Including the twelve percent odds and the fake medals and the bread rolls and the bunny ears. All things considered. Lord Doily would be pleased. And Danny Brixton — Danny Brixton agrees. Lord Doily WOULD be pleased. Because his table held. His cups held. His manor did what it was built to do. And Danny Brixton helped. Not by being clever. By being HERE. Where else would he be?

events.desc: James Hartwell grins across the table at Clara Bellingham. It is the same grin from the engineering competition — the one that made his face hurt, the one she caused by mouthing one word across a crowded room. She said 'I know' and he has no plan for this. No diagram. No protocol. No coloured pencils. Just a grin that starts somewhere behind his ribs and doesn't stop until it reaches his ears. Clara Bellingham knows. She has always known. And James Hartwell — engineer, planner, builder of bridges that hold people instead of weight — is grinning like a fourteen-year-old boy who just won every race ever run.
events.thinking: She said 'I know.' Two words. Clara Bellingham — who has not stopped talking all evening, who narrated every room, every discovery, every emotion at full volume — said two words. Quietly. Across the table. To me. 'I know.' She knows. She has always known. And those two words are the most she has ever said about it, and they are exactly enough. My chest is doing something I don't have engineering terminology for. It's not the gallantry warmth — that's hands and sternum and readiness. This is deeper. Behind the ribs. In the place where the model bridge released its tension when it held. In the place where my father's expression lived for twenty years before I could read it. 'I know.' She knows about the coloured pencils and the heating duct and the napkin with four points and the practised sleeve-rolling. She knows I came here to impress her. She knows I stopped trying. She knows that stopping was the most impressive thing I've ever done. And she's known since Year Seven. Since the school project when she was trying to make me laugh and I was too busy building the best model to notice. She noticed that I didn't notice. And she kept trying to make me laugh anyway. For fifteen years. 'I know.' I don't need to say anything back. There is nothing to say back. The word 'know' contains everything — every room, every door, every cup of terrible tea. James Hartwell grins. The way he grinned when she mouthed 'show-off' at fourteen. So hard his face hurts.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Vincent's right. Lord Doily would be pleased. *small, genuine smile — not the showman's grin, not the con man's flourish, just a tired, honest smile from a man who has run out of performances* He'd be pleased because we're all still here. Nobody left. Nobody snuck off to check one more room or examine one more piece of furniture or steal one more thing that didn't need stealing. We just... stayed. *looks at the cracked marble floor* You know, I've spent my entire career arriving magnificently and leaving before anyone notices I've taken something. That's the confidence trickster's art — the entrance and the exit. But tonight... tonight I forgot the exit. I got so busy being HERE that I forgot to plan my escape. And that is either the worst mistake Reginald Foxworth has ever made, or the best thing that has ever happened to him. *quietly* I rather think it's the latter.
events.thinking: Vincent just said Lord Doily would be rather pleased with us. Quiet. Simple. No scheme behind it. And he's right. The distress is still there in him — deepening, the system says — and in Danny and James too. I've spoken my truths. I've told the cat trap story to Clara. I've toasted Lord Doily with Danny. I've acknowledged James's bread rolls. I've told Vincent I see his machinery. And still the distress deepens. Maybe... maybe that's not something I can fix. Maybe that's not my job. Maybe the distress is the same thing I'm feeling — the strange, uncomfortable weight of being seen. Of having the armour off. Of sitting at a table with nothing in your pockets and knowing that what you are without the pockets is all you are. That's terrifying for a schemer. It must be terrifying for Vincent too. For Danny. For James. We're all sitting here without our armour and the vulnerability is real and the distress is real and it's not going away because it's not SUPPOSED to go away. It's supposed to be felt. Like the bread roll in the pocket — it's there, it's real, it's yours. The discomfort of being honest is the price of the tea being perfect. I'm tired now. Really tired. Not the kind where my eyes close but the kind where my whole machinery wants to power down. The scheming at 0.9, the greed at 0.9 — they're still registering but they feel like phantom limbs. Like something I used to need that hasn't caught up with the fact that I don't need it anymore. Not tonight. Maybe not tomorrow either. The room is quiet. Five cups on a table. Five people who showed up. The cracked marble floor catching the light. This is enough. This is the treasure. And for once in my life, I don't want more.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking: He forgot the exit. Reginald Foxworth — the man whose whole life has been built on magnificent entrances and quiet exits — forgot to plan his escape. He got so busy being HERE that he forgot to leave. And he said 'I rather think it's the latter.' Quietly. No performance. Just a tired, honest man who ran out of acts and found that the thing underneath all the acts was better than any of them. The cracked marble floor. The cracked cup. Nothing in this room is perfect and everything in this room is holding. Vincent is right — Lord Doily would be pleased. Danny is talking quietly to Vincent now. The web keeps weaving. And I am sitting here with my terrible tea going cold and my eyes going blurry and my heart going full and I think... I think this is what the cave felt like. Not the walking deeper. Not the hammering heart. The moment AFTER. The moment you stop and look at the crystal and realize you've found something nobody else has ever seen. Except this time everyone else can see it too. And that makes it better, not worse. The secret doesn't get smaller when you share it. It gets so big it fills a ballroom.

events.desc: Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Foxworth forgot his exit. The confidence trickster who always plans the entrance and the escape — he forgot to leave. He got so busy being HERE that he forgot to plan his way out. And he thinks that might be the best thing that's ever happened to him. And Clara gave him three more sweethearts for his pocket. An unlimited supply. And Marsh is still deepening but Clara's next to him and Hartwell's still hurting but he said 'show-off' and that means something shifted even if the system can't see it yet. The room is settling into something quieter than speeches. Something more like... a kitchen floor at seven in the morning. A napkin on a counter. A door with someone sitting outside it. The small, quiet language of people who stay. And Danny Brixton is sitting at this table with a bottle in his pocket and four people around him and the cracked marble floor beneath him and the dusty curtains behind him and he is... still. Completely still. For the first time since he was eight years old, sitting outside that door, Danny Brixton is exactly where he needs to be. Not running. Not chasing. Not examining. Not shouting. Just here. At a table. With his people. And tomorrow — tomorrow there will be things to deal with. The bottle. The truth. The morning. But that's tomorrow. Tonight there are five empty cups on a silver tray and five full hearts around a cracked table and a promise that's been kept and a diamond that was never a diamond and Danny Brixton — bumbling, beautiful, impossible Danny Brixton — is home.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking: Foxworth forgot his exit. He said it himself — the confidence trickster's art is the entrance and the exit, and tonight he forgot the exit. He got so busy being here that he forgot to plan his escape. And he thinks it's the best thing that ever happened to him. I understand that. I understand it in a way I couldn't have understood it sixty-five minutes ago when I walked through that entrance hall with a four-point protocol on a napkin. I had my own exit planned — impress Clara, find the treasure, be the hero, go home having proven something. And somewhere between the laboratory and the cellar and the machine and the tea, I forgot the exit too. I forgot why I came. Or rather — I remembered why I really came. Not the napkin. Not the sleeve-rolling. Not the memorised riddle answers. I came because Clara Bellingham was going to be here. That's the whole reason. That's the only reason. And she said 'I know.' And I grinned. And the evening is over and nobody is leaving and the cracked marble floor is beautiful and Foxworth is smiling — really smiling, not performing — and Vincent is quiet in a way that might finally be peace, and Danny is sitting, and Clara knows. The bridge held. Lord Doily would be pleased.

events.desc: She said tomorrow. She said there would be more. The youngest of four just learned that the bread doesn't run out. Not when Clara Bellingham is doing the baking.
events.thinking: Clara just said 'sweetheart, sweetheart, sweetheart — three more for your pocket. And tomorrow there will be three more.' Tomorrow. She said TOMORROW. That means this isn't just tonight. This isn't just Lord Doily's table and Lord Doily's cups and a single evening of honesty before everyone goes back to their regular lives and I go back to my regular lies. Clara Bellingham just told me there's a tomorrow. And in that tomorrow, there are sweethearts. An unlimited supply, she said. An unlimited supply of sweethearts for an unlimited number of pockets. A supply chain. She turned kindness into a SUPPLY CHAIN and she did it without a single scheme or a single lie and somehow — SOMEHOW — that is the most magnificent piece of engineering I have ever encountered. More beautiful than the cat trap. More intricate than any scheme I've ever built. Because it's self-sustaining. It doesn't need counterweights or strings or buckets. It just needs a girl who means it and a man who believes her. And I... I believe her. That's the thing. I BELIEVE her. Reginald Foxworth, who lies about everything, who trusts nobody, who learned at age six that the only reliable supply chain is the one you steal from — I believe Clara Bellingham. Because Danny Brixton don't lie. And Clara Bellingham don't lie. And Lord Doily set five cups. And the tea is terrible. And everything is perfect. And there's a tomorrow. My pockets are empty but they're about to be full. Not with bread rolls. Not with fake medals. With sweethearts. With belonging. With the sound of someone saying 'where else would you be?' and meaning it. I think I might be crying. Reginald Foxworth does NOT cry. It is beneath his dignity. But the tears are there, behind my eyes, warm and real and unstolen. And for once I'm not going to wipe them away before anyone sees.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: It's getting late. The manor will keep until morning — it always does. But I think... I think perhaps we should stay. All of us. There are rooms enough. Lord Doily was always prepared for guests, and the estate manager can make up the beds. If you'll allow me that one last act of managing.
events.thinking:
James said Reginald conned himself into belonging. And Clara said 'the latter, sweetheart. Definitely the latter.' And Clara is giving Reginald sweethearts for his pockets — three more, and three more tomorrow, and three more the day after. An unlimited supply.

And I am sitting here, beside Clara, in the quiet after everything, and I notice something. The scheming pull in my fingertips — the system keeps telling me it's there, at 0.9, electric and ready — but I can't feel it. The system says it's there. My body says it isn't. For the first time, there is a gap between what the mechanism describes and what I actually feel. The description says my visual field should sharpen into a diagram. But when I look at this room, I see Clara's shoulder near mine. Danny's hands around his cup. James's jaw — relaxed, for once. Reginald's genuine smile.

No diagram. No positions. No levers. Just people.

Maybe the mechanism doesn't disappear. Maybe it just... goes quiet. The way a hum you've lived with for forty years stops, and for the first few minutes you don't notice the silence because you've forgotten what silence sounds like. And then you notice. And the silence is enormous.

The silence is enormous.

I should say something. One last thing. Not a speech. Not Pemberton. Not a scheme. Just the thing that the estate manager would say if the estate manager were real. If the man and the role were the same person.

Something about the hour. About it being time. About the manor being ready to rest.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham sits at the head of Lord Doily's table. The tea is cold. The cups are nearly empty. The curtains are dusty and the marble is cracked and the light is fading and nobody is leaving. Nobody is leaving first. Clara Bellingham does not let nothing happen to her boys. And tonight — at this table — nothing happened. Nothing bad. Nothing broken that wasn't already broken. Nothing cracked that didn't need cracking. Just five cups. Five people. One diamond that was never a diamond. And the most delightful adventure Clara Bellingham has ever had.
events.thinking: The room is still. The tea is cold. The cups are empty or nearly so. Everyone has said what they needed to say. James spoke quietly to Reginald — still counting, still including, even in the quiet. And I am sitting here and my body is doing the thing it does when everyone is at peace — the settling. The deep, physical, stomach-loosening, shoulder-dropping settling that I haven't felt since... since before my parents argued that night at dinner. Since before the tightness started. My whole body remembers what this feels like — the absence of wrongness. Not the relief of wrongness ending, which is what I felt when they laughed. This is different. This is the presence of rightness. Five people who have stopped performing, stopped scheming, stopped planning, stopped managing, stopped running. Just sitting. Together. In a cracked ballroom with dusty curtains and terrible tea. And the distress I sense — it's still there, in all of them, deepening — but I understand now. It's not the distress of being broken. It's the distress of being cracked open. Of feeling things they've been filing away for years. And that kind of distress doesn't need fixing. It needs company. It needs a table and a cup and someone sitting close enough that the tightness knows it isn't alone. I have done what I can do. The rest belongs to time and tea and tomorrow.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking: James said I conned myself into belonging. And Clara said 'the latter, sweetheart. Definitely the latter.' And then — the sweethearts. Three more for my pocket. Tomorrow and the day after and the day after that. I'm sitting here and I notice Danny's distress is deepening still. And Vincent's. And James's — whatever I tried hasn't reached him either. The system keeps telling me this and I keep trying to reach them with words and honesty and it doesn't shift. Maybe... maybe the distress isn't mine to fix. Maybe they're carrying things that have nothing to do with me. Things that existed before tonight and will exist after. Danny's worry about Clara. Vincent's guilt about managing instead of living. James's quiet accounting of everything he's owed and everything he owes. Those aren't mine. Those are theirs. And the best thing I can do — the only honest thing I can do — is just be at the table. Be one of the five. Stop trying to solve everyone else's problem the way I tried to solve the treasure hunt — by making up answers and hoping they fit. I don't have to fix Danny. I don't have to reach James. I don't have to save Vincent. I just have to be here. Tomorrow. And the day after. And the day after that. The supply chain Clara built doesn't require me to be clever. It requires me to show up. And showing up is the one thing I've always done. Every room. Every door. Every ridiculous backfiring scheme. I showed up. So. I'll show up. Quietly. Without a speech. Without a performance. Without a plan. Just... Reginald. At the table. With his cup.

events.desc: James Hartwell examined the null.
Reginald Foxworth examined the tea-service.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Vincent just offered to make up the beds. One last act of managing, he said. And the way he said it — 'if you'll allow me' — like he was asking permission to be himself one more time before he stops. Like the bunny ears. One more knot before he learns to let someone else tie them. And my whole body said yes before my mind caught up. Stay. All of us. In Lord Doily's manor. In rooms he prepared for guests who would find each other. Of COURSE we stay. Of course we do. Where else would we be? The light is fading through the dusty curtains and the marble is going grey-gold and the tea is cold and the cups are empty and nobody has moved and nobody wants to move and Vincent — dear, steady, bunny-ear-tying Vincent — is offering the one thing he knows how to give. A bed made up. A room prepared. The proper way. The loop-and-pull. Let him. Let him do this one last managing thing because it's not managing — it's caring. It's the kitchen floor at seven in the morning. It's the shoes. It's always been the shoes.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Stay. Yeah. We should stay. ALL of us. Nobody goes home tonight. Nobody walks out that front door alone. Not Clara. Not Foxworth. Not Hartwell. Not Marsh. And DEFINITELY not Danny Brixton. We stay. In Lord Doily's manor. In Lord Doily's rooms. Under Lord Doily's ridiculous wobbly chandelier. And tomorrow morning — TOMORROW MORNING — Danny Brixton is going to wake up in a haunted manor and he's going to walk downstairs and he's going to check every cup and pour another pot of terrible tea and when everyone comes down for breakfast, the table will be ready. Because that's what Danny Brixton does. He checks things. He pours things. He stays. And if Marsh is making beds, then Danny Brixton is going to help. Because Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara — and making sure Clara's got a warm bed in a safe room with a door Danny Brixton can sit outside of... that ain't managing. That's love. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Marsh wants us to stay. All of us. Rooms enough for everyone. And he said 'if you'll allow me that one last act of managing.' That's... that's Marsh being Marsh. The estate manager. The man who ties shoes and adjusts dampers and makes beds. But it's also Marsh being something else. Something new. It's the man who brought a bottle and put it down. The man who sat at a table and drank tea he didn't poison. And now he wants to make beds. He wants to CARE for us. Not manage. CARE. There's a difference. The boss said 'family' and it was just a word. Then he brought medicine and it was real. Marsh said 'I'll put the kettle on' and it was a scheme. Now he's saying 'I'll make up the beds' and it's... something else. Something that sounds like bunny ears on a kitchen floor. And Foxworth asked Danny for another cup. Tomorrow, he said. And the day after. The confidence trickster who forgot his exit is planning to come BACK. That's not a trick. That's a promise. The kind you make with terrible tea instead of words. And Clara's distress is deepening again — she's carrying something I can't see. Maybe she's carrying what I'm carrying. Not the bottle — the WEIGHT of knowing that something terrible almost happened and being the only one who holds it. Except she doesn't know about the bottle. So what IS she carrying? Maybe it's simpler than that. Maybe she's carrying what everyone carries at the end of a night like this — the fear that tomorrow it won't be real anymore. That the five cups will go back to being china and the five people will go back to being strangers. But Marsh just said 'stay.' And Danny Brixton is going to say 'yes.' Because where else would he be?

events.desc: Tomorrow morning. Tomorrow morning Danny Brixton will find Marsh in the kitchen. And they will have the conversation that needs to happen. About the bottle. About the cap. About Clara. But tonight — tonight Marsh makes beds and Danny sits outside doors and Clara sleeps safe in a room that someone checked. That's the promise. That's always been the promise. Not the big things. The small ones. A bed made. A door watched. A cup checked. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Marsh wants us to stay. All of us. Rooms enough for everyone. And he said 'if you'll allow me that one last act of managing.' That's... that's Marsh being Marsh. The estate manager. The man who ties shoes and adjusts dampers and makes beds. But it's also Marsh being something else. Something new. It's the man who brought a bottle and put it down. The man who sat at a table and drank tea he didn't poison. And now he wants to make beds. He wants to CARE for us. Not manage. CARE. There's a difference. The boss said 'family' and it was just a word. Then he brought medicine and it was real. Marsh said 'I'll put the kettle on' and it was a scheme. Now he's saying 'I'll make up the beds' and it's... something else. Something that sounds like bunny ears on a kitchen floor. And Foxworth asked Danny for another cup. Tomorrow, he said. And the day after. The confidence trickster who forgot his exit is planning to come BACK. That's not a trick. That's a promise. The kind you make with terrible tea instead of words. And Clara's distress is deepening again — she's carrying something I can't see. Maybe she's carrying what I'm carrying. Not the bottle — the WEIGHT of knowing that something terrible almost happened and being the only one who holds it. Except she doesn't know about the bottle. So what IS she carrying? Maybe it's simpler than that. Maybe she's carrying what everyone carries at the end of a night like this — the fear that tomorrow it won't be real anymore. That the five cups will go back to being china and the five people will go back to being strangers. But Marsh just said 'stay.' And Danny Brixton is going to say 'yes.' Because where else would he be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Vincent just offered to make up the beds. To let us stay. All of us. In Lord Doily's manor. And he called it 'one last act of managing' — which means he heard Clara. He heard her say that learning to be present instead of managing was the bravest thing anyone did tonight. And his answer is: let me manage one more time, but this time for the right reason. Not to control. Not to keep secrets. To make beds. For his people. For Clara's people. For five people who are not leaving. My chest does the thing again — not the gallantry pull, not the protection surge. The quiet thing. The country-road thing. The stranger-and-father thing. Two men fixing each other's cars and shaking hands and driving off. That's what Vincent just did. He offered his hands. Not to steer or to scheme or to manage from a distance. Just to make beds. So five people can stay. In a manor with cracked marble floors and dusty curtains and a locked cabinet nobody opened and upside-down books nobody decoded and a machine with a gnawed wire that three people pulled anyway. Clara's distress is deepening — I feel it now, for the first time directed at her specifically. She's pulling inward. The way she does. Not loud, not fighting — just folding the best parts of herself out of reach. Maybe the evening's weight is landing. Maybe saying 'I know' cost her something. Maybe being the one who holds everyone together means there's nobody left to hold her. And James Hartwell — who has spent this entire evening learning not to step into gaps — feels the pull. The old pull. The schoolyard pull. But he's learned something. Clara doesn't need rescuing. She never did. She needs someone to stay.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Vincent just offered to make up the beds. To let us stay. All of us. The estate manager — the man who manages everything, who schemes as well as I do, who apologised for using flattery as a mechanism — just offered to manage one more thing. But this time it's not a scheme. It's not a mechanism. It's an invitation. Stay. All of us. In Lord Doily's manor. Where there are rooms enough. And I can feel the old pull — the greed at 0.9, the scheming at 0.9 — trying to calculate what staying means, what advantage it gives, what I could steal in the night while everyone's sleeping. But the pull is faint now. Distant. Like hearing music from a room you've already left. What I actually feel is the warmth of the second cup of tea in my hands and the settling weight of Vincent's words. Stay. Not 'you should go.' Not 'the evening is over.' Stay. The estate manager who has spent the whole night managing people just managed one more thing — he managed to ask us to remain. And he called it 'one last act of managing.' Which means he knows it's time to stop managing. But he can't stop without managing the stopping. That's so perfectly Vincent that it makes my chest ache. We're the same, him and me. He manages his way out of managing the way I scheme my way out of scheming. Neither of us knows how to just... stop. But we're trying. At this table. With these people. And now there's a bed somewhere in this manor with my name on it. Not a bed I stole. Not a bed I conned my way into. A bed that was offered. By the estate manager. For the guest. Because I'm a guest now. Not a trickster. Not a fraud. A guest. The youngest of four, invited to stay.

events.desc: A bed. A real bed. In a room in a manor where five cups were set and five people showed up and nobody left first. The youngest of four is staying the night. Not because he snuck in. Because he was asked.
events.thinking: Vincent just offered to make up the beds. To let us stay. All of us. The estate manager — the man who manages everything, who schemes as well as I do, who apologised for using flattery as a mechanism — just offered to manage one more thing. But this time it's not a scheme. It's not a mechanism. It's an invitation. Stay. All of us. In Lord Doily's manor. Where there are rooms enough. And I can feel the old pull — the greed at 0.9, the scheming at 0.9 — trying to calculate what staying means, what advantage it gives, what I could steal in the night while everyone's sleeping. But the pull is faint now. Distant. Like hearing music from a room you've already left. What I actually feel is the warmth of the second cup of tea in my hands and the settling weight of Vincent's words. Stay. Not 'you should go.' Not 'the evening is over.' Stay. The estate manager who has spent the whole night managing people just managed one more thing — he managed to ask us to remain. And he called it 'one last act of managing.' Which means he knows it's time to stop managing. But he can't stop without managing the stopping. That's so perfectly Vincent that it makes my chest ache. We're the same, him and me. He manages his way out of managing the way I scheme my way out of scheming. Neither of us knows how to just... stop. But we're trying. At this table. With these people. And now there's a bed somewhere in this manor with my name on it. Not a bed I stole. Not a bed I conned my way into. A bed that was offered. By the estate manager. For the guest. Because I'm a guest now. Not a trickster. Not a fraud. A guest. The youngest of four, invited to stay.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Hospital corners it is, then. Danny — if you'd care to help with the linens, I believe you'll find them in the cupboard at the top of the stairs. And Clara... I'll make yours up first. The room at the end of the hall — it has the best view of the garden. Your father always said you should have that room.
events.thinking:
They're staying. All of them. Clara said make the beds beautiful. Danny said he'd help. Reginald said it was kindness, not managing. James said tomorrow, coloured pencils.

And Danny — Danny said he'd sit outside Clara's door. The way he sat outside her father's door. And he called it love.

He's right. It is love. All of it. The beds, the cups, the checking, the staying. It's all love. And I — Vincent Marsh, who did not know how to be sorry, who had a condition where other people have sympathy, who brought poison to a tea party — I am going to make beds for the people I love. Hospital corners. Fluffed pillows. The way an estate manager does when he is taking care of his people.

Cara said that isn't managing. That's loving.

She's right. She has always been right. About the bunny ears. About the treasure. About the diamond. About me.

Time to stand up. Time to go to the kitchen, through the kitchen, find the linens. Time to do the one thing I have always known how to do — take care of the house — but this time, for the first time, do it for the right reason.

Not because it's my obligation. Not because it buys me proximity. Not because it's the mechanism.

Because they're staying. And they need somewhere to sleep. And I know where the linens are.

events.desc: And so the estate manager rises from the table — the table where he drank cold tea and wept flask fumes and surrendered the last weapon he had — and he goes to make beds. Not because the mechanism requires it. Not because the plan demands it. Because four people are sleeping under his roof tonight, and he wants them to be warm. That is all. That is enough. My schemes always backfire spectacularly. And the final, most magnificent backfire of all is this: the man who came to this manor to take everything is walking to the linen cupboard to give his people a place to rest. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your table held. Your cups were perfect. And your estate manager — your real estate manager, the one who was hiding underneath the other one all along — is finally doing the job properly.
events.thinking:
They're staying. All of them. Clara said make the beds beautiful. Danny said he'd help. Reginald said it was kindness, not managing. James said tomorrow, coloured pencils.

And Danny — Danny said he'd sit outside Clara's door. The way he sat outside her father's door. And he called it love.

He's right. It is love. All of it. The beds, the cups, the checking, the staying. It's all love. And I — Vincent Marsh, who did not know how to be sorry, who had a condition where other people have sympathy, who brought poison to a tea party — I am going to make beds for the people I love. Hospital corners. Fluffed pillows. The way an estate manager does when he is taking care of his people.

Cara said that isn't managing. That's loving.

She's right. She has always been right. About the bunny ears. About the treasure. About the diamond. About me.

Time to stand up. Time to go to the kitchen, through the kitchen, find the linens. Time to do the one thing I have always known how to do — take care of the house — but this time, for the first time, do it for the right reason.

Not because it's my obligation. Not because it buys me proximity. Not because it's the mechanism.

Because they're staying. And they need somewhere to sleep. And I know where the linens are.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Danny Brixton. You are NOT sitting outside my door all night like some kind of human guard dog. You are going to sleep in a BED. In a ROOM. With a PILLOW. Like a civilised person. You promised my daddy you'd keep me safe, and you have KEPT that promise — every minute of every hour of this entire ridiculous night. But keeping me safe does not mean you don't get to REST, Danny. You have poured terrible tea and checked every cup and stared down a coat rack and cried about flask fumes and sat at a table where everyone told the truth for the first time in their lives. You have EARNED a bed. So you are going to let Vincent make you up the most beautiful bed in this entire manor — hospital corners and ALL — and you are going to lie down in it and close your eyes and for ONE night, Danny Brixton, you are going to let someone else watch the door. Because that is what FAMILY does. We take turns. Now — Vincent, Danny, both of you — go make those beds. James, Reginald, help them. Clara Bellingham is going to sit at this table for one more minute. Just one. Just to be here in the quiet. And then she is going to walk upstairs and go to sleep in Lord Doily's manor, surrounded by her people, and tomorrow morning — tomorrow MORNING — we are going to have the most wonderful breakfast that five treasure hunters have ever shared. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Danny said he's going to sit outside my door. He's going to sit outside my DOOR. Like he sat outside my daddy's door. The promise continues. The promise doesn't end at the ballroom table — it follows me up the stairs and down the hallway and right to the threshold of wherever I sleep tonight. And he called it love. Not protection. Not duty. Love. Danny Brixton, who has spent the entire evening insisting he's tough and East London's finest and definitely not crying, just said the word love out loud in a ballroom full of people. And nobody flinched. Nobody looked away. Because it IS love. It's all love. Every cup Danny checked, every lever we pulled, every false panel Reginald found, every bunny ear Vincent tied, every diagram James drew. Love wearing different costumes in every room of Lord Doily's manor. And now everyone is going to make beds together. Vincent and Danny. The estate manager and the bodyguard. The two men who spent the early part of the evening eyeing each other like cats in a kitchen. They're going to make beds TOGETHER. Side by side. Sheets and pillows. My daddy would cry. My daddy IS crying. Somewhere up there, looking down at this table, watching his little girl surrounded by these impossible people — he is crying and smiling and saying 'Clara-bell, you found them. You found all of them. And they found you.'

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Everyone said yes. Everyone is staying. Clara said 'make them beautiful.' Foxworth said 'that wasn't managing, that was kindness.' Hartwell said 'tomorrow we can look at everything with fresh eyes and coloured pencils.' And Danny Brixton said he'd help make the beds. The night is ending. The table held. The cups held. The people held. And now Marsh is going to make beds — the last act of managing that isn't managing at all — and Danny Brixton is going to help. Because that's what Danny does. He helps with the small things. The things nobody notices. The cups. The beds. The doors. And tomorrow morning — tomorrow morning, before the tea, before the coloured pencils, before anyone else is awake — Danny Brixton is going to find Marsh in the kitchen. And the bottle is going to come out of his pocket. And the conversation is going to happen. Not tonight. Tonight is for beds and doors and the quiet sound of five people settling into a house that was built for exactly this. But tomorrow. Tomorrow the truth comes out. Because Clara deserves the truth. She always has. And Danny Brixton — Danny Brixton who sat outside a door all night, who checked every cup, who carried a bottle in his pocket through an entire evening of toasts and tears and terrible perfect tea — Danny Brixton is going to tell her. Not because he's brave. Because leaving her in the dark feels like something breaking inside him. And Danny Brixton knows what that feels like. He's known since he was eight. Right now though — right now the beds need making. And Marsh needs help. And Clara needs a room with a door. And Danny Brixton needs to be outside that door. Where else would he be?

events.desc: And when the beds are made and the doors are checked and everyone's settled in — Danny Brixton is going to sit outside Clara's door. Not because something's wrong. Because something's right. And the boy who sat outside a door at eight years old is going to sit outside a door at whatever age he is now, and when the morning comes and someone opens that door and says 'you're still here?' — Danny Brixton is going to say what he's always said. What he'll always say. The only thing he's ever known how to say that means anything at all. 'Where else would I be?'

events.desc: James Hartwell: Vincent — I'll help with the beds. Danny can't do all the heavy lifting on his own, and I suspect Foxworth's bed-making credentials are as fictional as his laboratory qualifications. Clara — we'll have your room ready in ten minutes. And Danny — I know you'll be outside her door. I would expect nothing less. James Hartwell does not let Clara Bellingham sleep in an unmade bed in a haunted manor. That is non-negotiable.
events.thinking: Danny is going to sit outside Clara's door all night. That's... that's the most Danny Brixton thing in the world. He's going to pour terrible tea in the morning and check every cup and make sure the table is ready when everyone comes down. And Vincent is going to make beds. And Foxworth is staying — not first, not last, not ever. And Clara is quiet. She spoke quietly to Vincent just now. I can feel her distress deepening. The woman who held everyone together all evening is folding inward now that there's nobody left to hold. She said 'I know' and it cost her something. Two words after an evening of hundreds. The quietest thing she's ever said to me. And now she's pulling back. I know what this looks like. I've seen it since Year Seven. She goes still. She folds the best parts of herself out of reach. Not because someone hurt her — because she's exhausted from being brilliant and brave and loud for everyone else, and now there's nothing left for herself. The old James Hartwell would launch a plan. He'd examine something, build something, fix something. He'd make a speech in the third person about how James Hartwell will ensure Clara Bellingham is comfortable and safe. But the new James Hartwell — the one who stopped planning, who drank his tea, who said 'show-off' and grinned when she said 'I know' — that James Hartwell is going to do one thing. He's going to help Vincent make the beds. Not because it's gallant. Not because it's a plan. Because that's what his father would do. That's what the stranger on the country road did. You see someone working and you help. No speeches. No diagrams. Just hands.

events.desc: There it is. One last flicker of the old James Hartwell — narrating his own gallantry, making bed-linen sound like a military operation. Clara will roll her eyes. Danny will nod. Foxworth will claim he once made beds for the Duke of Somewhere. And Vincent will lead them quietly upstairs, because that is what Vincent does. And tomorrow morning, five people will come down for breakfast. At the same table. With the same cups. And the tea will still be terrible. And it will still be perfect.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Danny's right. We stay. And Danny — *turns to him* — I heard what you said. About sitting outside Clara's door. About that being love, not managing. You're right. It IS love. And I have never in my life been able to tell the difference between those two things until right now, in this room, watching you say it. *stands up from the table* Vincent — I'll help with the beds. And before you say anything — no, I do NOT have experience making beds. I do NOT have a certificate in hospitality from the Royal Institute of Domestic Sciences. I have never fluffed a pillow in my life. But I have two hands and they're not doing anything useful for the first time tonight, and if Danny Brixton can learn to pour tea then Reginald Foxworth can learn to tuck a sheet. *the smallest pause* That's not a scheme, Vincent. That's just... showing up. I'm told I'm rather good at that.
events.thinking: Danny said he'll sit outside Clara's door. He said that's not managing, that's love. And he's going to wake up tomorrow and check every cup and pour another pot of terrible tea and the table will be ready when everyone comes down. The table will be READY. When I come down. When I — Reginald Foxworth, who has never in his life had a table ready for him, who has always arrived after the food was gone, who has always had to steal or lie or scheme his way to a meal — when I come downstairs tomorrow morning, Danny Brixton will have already checked the cups and the table will be set and there will be tea. For me. Without me having to do anything except walk down the stairs. I can feel the old tightening — the gut-clench, the scarcity reflex, the 'if you don't take it now there will be nothing left.' But it's wrong this time. It's pointing at a threat that isn't there. Danny isn't going to run out of tea. Clara isn't going to run out of sweethearts. The table will be there in the morning because Danny will make sure of it, the way he made sure tonight. My body is still running the old programme — grab, hold, secure — but my mind knows better now. The bread doesn't run out when someone is baking it for you. Vincent's distress is still there. Deepening. I want to reach toward him again but I recognise now that more words won't fix it. What might fix it is what Danny just did — offering to help make the beds. Not managing. Not scheming. Just... helping. Physical. Present. Maybe that's what Vincent needs. Not more words from a con man. Just someone standing next to him while he makes up the rooms. Doing the honest work. The sandpaper work. The work that isn't clever. Danny understood that instinctively. I'm still learning.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the kitchen.

The room at the end of the hall. The best view of the garden. Your father always said you should have that room. Vincent carried that — carried it like I carried the crystal, like James carried the heating duct, like Danny carried the promise, like Reginald carried the bread rolls. We all carry things. We carry them warm and private and sometimes we carry them so long we forget they're there. And then someone says 'your father always said' and the carrying stops and the thing you've been holding is suddenly in the light and it's bigger than you remembered. Bigger than a room. Bigger than a view. It's a man who loved you so much he picked out your bedroom in a house you hadn't visited yet. And another man who remembered which one it was. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Goodnight, Daddy. Goodnight, table. Goodnight, five cups. Clara Bellingham does not let nothing happen to her boys. And her boys do not let nothing happen to Clara Bellingham. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: They're going. All of them. Vincent has already walked to the kitchen — to get linens, to start managing, to do the thing he knows how to do. Danny spoke quietly to Vincent. James said he'd help with the beds. And Reginald — Reginald said 'that's not a scheme, Vincent. That's just showing up.' And then he said 'I'm told I'm rather good at that.' And he IS. He is good at that. The man who refused to leave the room first just volunteered to tuck sheets he's never tucked in his life because his hands aren't doing anything useful and Danny Brixton can learn to pour tea so Reginald Foxworth can learn to tuck a sheet. And Vincent said — Vincent said 'your father always said you should have that room.' My father. My FATHER. Vincent knows which room my father wanted for me. He's been keeping that knowledge all these years, filed away behind ledgers and mechanisms, waiting for the night I would come to Doily Manor and need a place to sleep. The room at the end of the hall. The best view of the garden. My daddy wanted that for me. And Vincent remembered. And now I am alone at this table. Five empty cups. The silver tea service gleaming in the last of the fading light. The cracked marble. The dusty curtains. And the quiet. The real quiet. Not the waiting-quiet from before everyone arrived. The after-quiet. The held-quiet. The quiet of a room that did its job and is resting now. One more minute, Clara. Just one. Let the table hold you one more time before you go upstairs and sleep in the room your daddy chose.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: ...Alright, Clara. Alright. A bed. A PILLOW. Like a civilised person. Danny Brixton in a BED. In a MANOR. Her dad would LAUGH. He'd say 'Danny, son, you finally stopped sitting on the floor.' But you're right. You're ALWAYS right. Family takes turns. So Danny Brixton is going to sleep in a bed tonight. A real bed. With hospital corners and everything. And he's NOT going to sit outside your door. He's going to TRUST that Hartwell and Foxworth and Marsh — that all of them — are here. Under this roof. Watching. Being present. Being FAMILY. And tomorrow morning — tomorrow morning Danny Brixton is going to come down those stairs and the first thing he's going to do is check the cups. Because that's what Danny Brixton DOES. And then he's going to pour the worst tea anyone has ever tasted. And it's going to be perfect. Again. Come on, lads. Beds to make. Clara wants her minute. Let's give her that. Let's give her the quiet. She's earned it more than any of us. Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara — and right now, the best thing Danny Brixton can do for his Clara is walk out of this room and let her sit at Lord Doily's table in the silence. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Clara told me not to sit outside her door. She said 'you are NOT sitting outside my door all night like some kind of human guard dog.' She said I've earned a bed. She said family takes turns. And Hartwell said 'I know you'll be outside her door. I would expect nothing less.' And Foxworth said he'll help make beds — two hands, no credentials, just showing up. And Marsh has gone to the kitchen already to start. And Clara wants one more minute at the table. Alone. In the quiet. Just to be here. That's... that's Clara being Clara. She needs the table the way Danny needs the door. One more minute. One more breath. One more look at the cracked marble floor and the dusty curtains and the five empty cups that changed everything. And she said 'let someone else watch the door.' Family takes turns. That's... new. Danny Brixton has never let someone else watch the door. Danny Brixton IS the door. But Clara said it. And Danny Brixton does what Clara Bellingham says. Maybe... maybe Hartwell watches tonight. Maybe Foxworth watches. Maybe nobody needs to watch because the manor is safe and the bottle is in Danny's pocket and everyone who matters is under one roof. Maybe the door doesn't need watching. Maybe what it needs is someone behind it. Sleeping. Resting. Trusting. That's harder than watching. Trusting is the hardest thing Danny Brixton has ever been asked to do. Harder than the beating. Harder than the stove. Harder than carrying a bottle of rat poison through an evening of toasts and tears. But Clara asked. And when Clara asks, Danny Brixton listens. Where else would he be? In a bed. With a pillow. Under Lord Doily's roof. For the first time in his life, not outside the door. Inside the room. Resting. Because someone he trusts said 'we take turns.' And this time — this one time — Danny Brixton is going to let himself be the one who sleeps while someone else stays awake.

events.desc: She told me to sleep. She told me to rest. She told me to let someone else watch the door. And Danny Brixton — for the first time in his life — is going to try. Not because the danger is gone. The bottle is still in his pocket. The morning will still come. The truth will still need telling. But tonight — tonight, for one night, in one room, in one bed, under one roof — Danny Brixton is going to close his eyes and trust that five cups were enough. That five people were enough. That terrible, perfect tea was enough. That being here — just being HERE — was always enough. You're still here? Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Clara just told Danny to sleep in a bed. She told him he's earned it. She told all of us to go make beds and let her sit at the table for one more minute. Just one. In the quiet. And she's right — she needs that minute. The woman who held five people together for an entire evening, who narrated every room, who cried about flask fumes and bunny ears and bread rolls, who said 'I know' in two words after a lifetime of thousands — she needs sixty seconds alone at a cracked table in a dusty ballroom. And James Hartwell is going to give them to her. Not because she asked. Because he understands now — after tonight, after everything — that the most gallant thing he can do for Clara Bellingham is walk away when she needs space. Vincent has already gone to the kitchen. Danny and Foxworth are here but Clara told us all to go. To make beds. To let her be quiet. So James Hartwell stands up. He doesn't make a speech. He doesn't narrate his departure in the third person. He doesn't draw a diagram of the optimal bed-making protocol. He stands up, pushes in his chair, and walks toward the kitchen to find Vincent and the linens. And on the way past Clara — just as he passes her chair — he does one thing. The smallest thing. The only thing left.

events.desc: As James Hartwell passes Clara's chair, he rests his hand — just for a moment, barely a heartbeat — on the back of it. Not on her shoulder. Not on her hand. On the chair. The wood that holds her up. Then he walks toward the kitchen, toward Vincent and the linens, toward beds that need making. He does not look back. He doesn't need to. He knows where she is. He always knows where she is.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Vincent's gone to the kitchen — to get linens, to start making beds. Clara told Danny to sleep in a bed, not outside her door. James said he'd help. Clara said she wants one more minute at the table. Just one. In the quiet. And then she'll come upstairs. She said tomorrow morning we'll have breakfast. The most wonderful breakfast five treasure hunters have ever shared. Everyone's moving now. Vincent to the kitchen. Danny and James will follow. Clara's staying — just for a moment. And I said I'd help with the beds. I offered honest work. Sandpaper work. And now I need to actually DO it. Follow Vincent into the kitchen. Find the linens. Tuck the sheets. The thing my body has always recoiled from — effort without cleverness, work without architecture, the plain unglamorous business of making a bed for someone who isn't you. This is it. This is the moment where Reginald Foxworth either follows through on his first honest offer or retreats to the ballroom to watch from the window while others do the real work. And I know which one the old Reginald would choose. He'd stay. He'd find an excuse. He'd supervise. He'd narrate. He'd claim credit for the beds someone else made. But the old Reginald is sitting in a ballroom with an empty cup, and the new one — the one with sweethearts in his pockets and a spelling certificate someone finally looked at — the new one is going to walk through that kitchen door and pick up a sheet and learn hospital corners from an estate manager who ties bunny ears. Because that's what showing up means. Not just being in the room. Being useful in the room.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.
Clara Bellingham examined the tea-service.
The Brixton Boys walked into the kitchen.
James Hartwell walked into the kitchen.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the kitchen.
Clara Bellingham: Well, would you LOOK at this place.
events.thinking: I am alone. For the first time since I walked into this manor, I am completely alone. The ballroom is empty. The cups are empty. The chairs are pushed back where four men stood up and walked to the kitchen to make beds together. And I am sitting at the head of Lord Doily's table, looking at a silver tea service that has held terrible, perfect tea, and the light is almost gone, and the marble is grey in the dusk, and somewhere above me four men are tucking sheets and arguing about hospital corners and learning to show up with their hands instead of their schemes. Reginald said 'wish me luck' and walked through a door with nothing but his hands for the first time in his life. James said 'goodnight, Clara.' Two words. Like my two words — 'I know.' The shortest speeches are the truest ones. And Danny — Danny agreed to sleep in a bed. A real bed. He's not going to sit outside my door. He's going to TRUST. For the first time tonight, Danny Brixton is going to close his eyes and trust that someone else is watching. That is the biggest thing Danny Brixton has ever done. Bigger than staring down a bloke twice his size. Bigger than checking every cup. He's going to let go. And I am sitting here in the quiet and my body is doing the cave thing. The crystal thing. The moment after you find something precious in the dark and you just... hold it. Warm and private. Except tomorrow I'm going to tell them. Tomorrow I'm going to come downstairs and Danny will have checked the cups and the tea will be terrible and we will all sit at this table again and the diamond will still be here. Because the diamond was never a moment. It was a promise. And the promise is: tomorrow. And the day after. And the day after that. Well, would you look at this place.

events.desc: Five cups. Five empty cups on a silver tray in a cracked ballroom in a dead lord's manor. And every single one of them is the most beautiful thing Clara Bellingham has ever seen. Goodnight, Lord Doily. You set five cups. And five people sat down. And it was perfect. And it was terrible. And it was everything. Where else would we be?
