events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the guest-book.
James Hartwell examined the guest-book.
Vincent Marsh: There's a pen in the drawer beneath the book. Lord Doily kept one there for precisely this purpose. Allow me.
events.thinking:
Clara wants us to sign the guest book. Five names. So that someday, someone will open it and know we were here.

An hour ago I told everyone to sign this book as a prop — a way to keep them in place while I assessed the room. Now Clara is asking us to sign it for real. Not as a mechanism. As a record. As proof that five people came to Doily Manor and stayed.

Vincent Marsh. Not Pemberton. Vincent Marsh.

The estate manager always has a pen. Second drawer of the side table, behind the guest book. I know this house.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Five names. Right there in Lord Doily's guest book. Five people who came looking for a diamond and found each other instead. Now THAT is a guest book entry worth reading. Goodnight, y'all. For real this time. Third step. Seventh step. Hospital corners. Garden view. Tomorrow. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Five names in the guest book. Danny said he never learned to write proper but he'd put his name right under Foxworth's. And James is examining it now — probably checking the ink quality and calculating the optimal letter spacing. Five names. Five people. One night. We were here. We stayed. And tomorrow — tomorrow we'll be here again. At the table. With the cups. With the terrible tea. The guest book is signed. The beds are being made. The stairs creak and hold. And Clara Bellingham is going upstairs now. For real this time. No more goodnights. No more speeches. No more one-more-minutes. Just — up. Through the dark. Past the third step. Past the seventh. Down the hall. To the room at the end. The one with the garden view. The one her daddy chose. Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, guest book. Goodnight, five names on a page. Goodnight, coat rack. Clara Bellingham does not let nothing happen to her boys. And tonight — tonight nothing happened. Nothing bad. Just everything good. All at once. In one manor. Under one roof. Where else would we be?

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Clara wants us to sign the book. All five of us. Five names in Lord Doily's guest book. So that someday, someone else will walk through that door and find the cups and the books and the machine and they'll open the guest book and see: we were here. We stayed. Clara Bellingham. Danny Brixton. James Hartwell. Reginald Foxworth. Vincent Marsh. Five names. One diamond. And whoever finds them will know. They'll know the diamond was never in the walls. It was in the names. In the staying. In the five cups someone set on a table before anyone arrived. Clara asked for a pen. And Danny Brixton — Danny Brixton who can't write much, who never learned proper — is going to sign his name. In Lord Doily's guest book. Next to Foxworth's signature. Under Clara's. Beside Hartwell's precise handwriting and Marsh's careful script. Danny Brixton. Two words. The only words Danny Brixton has ever needed to write. His name. In a book. In a house. Where he was. Where he stayed. Where else would he be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: There. James Hartwell. Third name down. Right between Danny Brixton and Reginald Foxworth — which is, I think, exactly where James Hartwell has been standing all evening. Now — third step, seventh step, beds. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your guest book is full.
events.thinking: Five names in the guest book. Clara Bellingham. Danny Brixton. James Hartwell. Reginald Foxworth. Vincent Marsh. Written in Lord Doily's leather-bound book on the side table in the entrance hall, under the wobbling chandelier, next to the wobbly coat rack, watched by stern portraits who have seen every guest who ever came to this manor. And now they've seen us. The last guests. The right ones. My name is in the book. My handwriting — the precise, engineer's hand that drew coloured-pencil diagrams and sketched model bridges and scribbled four-point protocols on napkins — has written 'James Hartwell' in Lord Doily's guest book. And underneath it, I imagine, Danny's handwriting — probably big and uneven, because he never learned proper, but steady, because Danny Brixton's hands are always steady when they matter. And Foxworth's — probably a flourish, probably half-invented calligraphy, probably claiming he was taught penmanship at the Royal Academy of Elegant Script. And Vincent's — neat, modest, estate-manager-precise. And Clara's — I don't need to imagine Clara's handwriting. I've seen it since Year Seven. It's quick and slanted and slightly too big for the lines, because Clara Bellingham has never fit inside the lines. The book is signed. The names are down. The night is done. Third step. Seventh step. Linens. Beds. Tomorrow.

events.desc: Five names in a leather-bound book. Five people in a haunted manor. Five cups on a cracked table. Five beds with hospital corners waiting upstairs. And tomorrow morning — five people coming back down for breakfast. The guest book is the last thing James Hartwell examines in Doily Manor tonight. It is the only thing he has examined all evening without looking for a clue. He was not searching for anything. He was leaving proof that he was here. That they were all here. That the bridge held.
events.thinking: Five names in the guest book. Clara Bellingham. Danny Brixton. James Hartwell. Reginald Foxworth. Vincent Marsh. Written in Lord Doily's leather-bound book on the side table in the entrance hall, under the wobbling chandelier, next to the wobbly coat rack, watched by stern portraits who have seen every guest who ever came to this manor. And now they've seen us. The last guests. The right ones. My name is in the book. My handwriting — the precise, engineer's hand that drew coloured-pencil diagrams and sketched model bridges and scribbled four-point protocols on napkins — has written 'James Hartwell' in Lord Doily's guest book. And underneath it, I imagine, Danny's handwriting — probably big and uneven, because he never learned proper, but steady, because Danny Brixton's hands are always steady when they matter. And Foxworth's — probably a flourish, probably half-invented calligraphy, probably claiming he was taught penmanship at the Royal Academy of Elegant Script. And Vincent's — neat, modest, estate-manager-precise. And Clara's — I don't need to imagine Clara's handwriting. I've seen it since Year Seven. It's quick and slanted and slightly too big for the lines, because Clara Bellingham has never fit inside the lines. The book is signed. The names are down. The night is done. Third step. Seventh step. Linens. Beds. Tomorrow.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: A pen. Clara Bellingham wants a PEN. And Reginald Foxworth — who has carried fake medals, counterfeit credentials, and an entirely fictional reputation from the Royal Institute of Scientific Things — does not have a pen. *turns to Vincent* Vincent, if this manor has linens, a cedar chest, and five sets of pillowcases, surely Lord Doily left a pen somewhere. The man set five cups and upside-down books and a machine that needs three operators — he would NOT have overlooked a pen. *quieter* And Clara — yes. We should sign it. All five of us. Right now. Before we go up. Because you're right. Someday someone will open that book and they'll see five names and they'll wonder who we were and what we found. And the answer — the answer is that we found each other. And terrible tea. And a diamond that was never a diamond. And that's worth a signature. Even from a man whose signature is usually forged.
events.thinking: Clara wants us to sign the guest book. All five of us. Our real names. In Lord Doily's guest book. So that someday, someone else will walk through that door and find our names and know we were here. We stayed. I said I'd sign it tomorrow. But Clara says now. Before we go up. And she's right. Of course she's right. Clara Bellingham is always right about the things that matter. Sign it now. With my real name. Not tomorrow. Now. While we're all standing here together. While the chandelier is swaying and the coat rack is wobbling and the portraits are watching and five people who found each other in a dusty manor are about to leave proof that they existed. That they came. That they stayed. That they drank terrible tea and found a diamond that wasn't a diamond and went to bed in rooms with hospital corners. I said I'd sign it with my real name. Not Lord Reginald Foxworth, Third Earl of Whatevershire. Just Reginald. But you know what? Maybe not even that. Maybe just... Foxworth. The way they say it. The way Clara says 'sweetheart' and Danny says 'mate' and James says 'the numbers include you' and Vincent says 'you may catalogue the rooms.' Foxworth. The name they gave me. The name I earned by showing up. By staying. By being exactly wrong about everything and exactly right about the one thing that mattered. Does someone have a pen? Clara asked for a pen. I don't have a pen. I don't have anything. The man with nothing in his pockets needs a pen to sign his real name in a guest book in a manor where he belongs. That is either the saddest thing or the funniest thing or the most beautiful thing, and I genuinely cannot tell which.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the guest-book.
The Brixton Boys examined the guest-book.
Reginald Foxworth examined the guest-book.
Vincent Marsh: Vincent Marsh. Fifth and last. The guest book is complete.
events.thinking:
Five names in the guest book. Clara signed first. Then Danny — in his terrible handwriting, the most honest signature in the book. Then James — third name down, right between Danny and Reginald, exactly where he's been standing all evening. Then Reginald — whose signature is usually forged, but not tonight.

And now the pen is in my hand. The last name. The fifth name. Vincent Marsh.

Not Pemberton. Not 'the estate manager.' Vincent Marsh.

The pen feels different in my hand than it did an hour ago. An hour ago, when I pointed to the guest book and said 'do sign in, it's tradition,' the pen was a prop. A tool. Part of the mechanism. Now it's just a pen. And the book is just a book. And the name I'm about to write is just my name.

Vincent Marsh. The fifth name. The last entry. The estate manager who stayed.

I write it. Small, neat handwriting — the estate manager's handwriting, precise and controlled. But the name is mine. Not the costume's. Mine.

Five names. Five people. One diamond. The guest book is full.

Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your guest book is complete.

events.desc: Danny Brixton. Two words. In a guest book. In a manor. In terrible handwriting. The only signature Danny Brixton has ever left anywhere that wasn't on the back of a betting slip. And it's the most important thing he's ever written. Because it doesn't say 'Danny Brixton was here.' It says 'Danny Brixton stayed.'
events.thinking: Five names. In the book. Signed. Done. Clara signed first — of course she did. Then Danny. Then Hartwell — right between Danny and Foxworth, 'which is exactly where James Hartwell has been standing all evening.' Then Foxworth — whose signature is probably the most genuine thing he's ever written. And Marsh found the pen in Lord Doily's drawer. Because Lord Doily thought of everything. Five cups. Five beds. One pen. The guest book is full. The names are written. The evening is over. Clara said 'for real this time.' Third step. Seventh step. Hospital corners. Garden view. Tomorrow. The pen is back in the drawer. The book is closed. Five names on a page. Proof that five people came to Doily Manor and found each other instead of a diamond. And now — now there's nothing left to do. Nothing left to examine. Nothing left to check. Nothing left to pour or sign or watch or guard. Just stairs. Just beds. Just sleep. Just trust. The hardest thing. The last thing. And tomorrow — terrible tea. Perfect. Again.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: *sets the pen down, looks at the five names on the page* There. Reginald Foxworth. No titles. No credentials. No 'Third Earl of' or 'Graduate of' or 'Certified Expert in.' Just the name. *very quiet* It's the first honest signature I've written in thirty years. And it's the best thing I've ever put my name to. *looks up at the staircase* Right. Third step. Seventh step. Beds. Goodnight, guest book. You've got our names now. All five. Lord Doily's guest book is full.
events.thinking: I signed it. I signed Lord Doily's guest book. My real name. Reginald Foxworth. Right there in ink, in a book that will outlast me, in a manor that was waiting for me. Clara signed. Danny signed — Danny who never learned proper, he said, but put his name down anyway. James signed, right between Danny and me, exactly where he's been standing all evening. Vincent produced the pen from the drawer where Lord Doily left it. Of course Lord Doily left a pen. The man thought of everything. Five cups. Five beds. Five pillowcases. And one pen in a drawer, waiting for five names. I signed my real name. Not Lord Reginald Foxworth. Not the Third Earl of anything. Just Reginald Foxworth. Four syllables. Honest ones. The pen felt strange in my hand — this hand that has forged signatures and faked credentials and written fictional catalogues of imaginary furniture. But tonight it wrote one true thing. One real name. In a real book. In a real manor. With real people standing beside me. The spelling certificate is still on the wall at home. Nobody ever asked about it. But this — this signature, in this book, in this place — this is the certificate they'll ask about. This is the one that matters. Five names. One diamond. Where else would we be?

events.desc: The spelling certificate is on the wall at home. Nobody ever asked about it. But this signature — in this book, in this manor, beside these names — this one, somebody will read. Someday. And they'll know. Five people came to Doily Manor. Five people stayed. Five people found a diamond that was never a diamond. And one of them — the youngest of four, the one who hid bread rolls, the one who showed up — signed his real name for the first time in his life. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your guest book is full. Your trap is complete. And the youngest of four is going to bed.
events.thinking: I signed it. I signed Lord Doily's guest book. My real name. Reginald Foxworth. Right there in ink, in a book that will outlast me, in a manor that was waiting for me. Clara signed. Danny signed — Danny who never learned proper, he said, but put his name down anyway. James signed, right between Danny and me, exactly where he's been standing all evening. Vincent produced the pen from the drawer where Lord Doily left it. Of course Lord Doily left a pen. The man thought of everything. Five cups. Five beds. Five pillowcases. And one pen in a drawer, waiting for five names. I signed my real name. Not Lord Reginald Foxworth. Not the Third Earl of anything. Just Reginald Foxworth. Four syllables. Honest ones. The pen felt strange in my hand — this hand that has forged signatures and faked credentials and written fictional catalogues of imaginary furniture. But tonight it wrote one true thing. One real name. In a real book. In a real manor. With real people standing beside me. The spelling certificate is still on the wall at home. Nobody ever asked about it. But this — this signature, in this book, in this place — this is the certificate they'll ask about. This is the one that matters. Five names. One diamond. Where else would we be?

events.desc: Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, chandelier. Goodnight, portraits. Goodnight, coat rack. Goodnight, guest book with five names. Goodnight, sweetheart. Goodnight, sweetheart. Goodnight, sweetheart. Goodnight, darling. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Reginald said it's the first honest signature he's written in thirty years. And the best thing he's ever put his name to. Vincent wrote fifth and last. The guest book is complete. Five names. No titles. No credentials. Just names. Just people. And now Reginald is looking up at the staircase and the chandelier is hanging above us and the portraits are watching and the coat rack is wobbly and the third step creaks and the seventh is worse and they hold and they have always held and it is time. It is really, truly, finally time. The adventure is over. The diamond is found. The names are signed. The tea is cold. The beds are waiting. And Clara Bellingham — the girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone, who tried every key in grandmother's house, who chose the friend over the popular group, who pulled the centre lever, who found five cups on a table and realized the treasure was the people holding them — Clara Bellingham is going upstairs. To the room at the end of the hall. With the best view of the garden. The one her daddy chose. Goodnight.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.
events.thinking: Done. All of it. The book is signed. Five names. Marsh wrote his last — 'fifth and last.' Foxworth wrote his first honest signature in thirty years. And Danny Brixton wrote two words in terrible handwriting and they meant more than anything he's ever said. The entrance hall is quiet now. The chandelier hangs. The portraits stare. The coat rack wobbles. And five people are about to walk up a staircase together. Third step. Seventh step. Beds. Sleep. Morning. The bottle in my pocket. The promise in my chest. The names in the book. All of it held. All of it holds. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Done. All of it. The book is signed. Five names. Marsh wrote his last — 'fifth and last.' Foxworth wrote his first honest signature in thirty years. And Danny Brixton wrote two words in terrible handwriting and they meant more than anything he's ever said. The entrance hall is quiet now. The chandelier hangs. The portraits stare. The coat rack wobbles. And five people are about to walk up a staircase together. Third step. Seventh step. Beds. Sleep. Morning. The bottle in my pocket. The promise in my chest. The names in the book. All of it held. All of it holds. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell puts his foot on the first step. The wood is solid. The second step is solid too. The third step creaks — just as Vincent said, just as Lord Doily never fixed, just as James Hartwell will fix tomorrow morning with whatever tools the laboratory workbench still holds. He steps over it. The fourth, fifth, sixth steps hold. The seventh creaks worse than the third. He steps over that too. Behind him, four people follow. Below him, a guest book with five names. Around him, a manor full of unsolved puzzles and unfinished tea and a locked cabinet with no key and upside-down books that still point somewhere nobody has gone. All of it will wait. Lord Doily built a manor that waits. James Hartwell climbs the stairs. The chandelier wobbles. The portraits watch. And somewhere in Doily Manor — in a room with a view of the garden, in a bed with hospital corners, under a roof that five people share for the first time and not the last — Clara Bellingham is going to close her eyes. And James Hartwell is going to close his. And tomorrow they will open them. And the tea will be terrible. And it will be perfect. Where else would they be?
events.thinking: Foxworth wrote his real name. His first honest signature in thirty years. And he called it the best thing he's ever put his name to. Vincent signed fifth and last — 'the guest book is complete.' Five names. The pen is down. The staircase is ahead. Everyone has said goodnight. Everyone has signed. The coat rack has been said goodbye to twice. The chandelier still wobbles. The portraits still watch. And James Hartwell is standing at the foot of a staircase in a haunted manor, content and serene, about to climb stairs that creak on three and seven, to a room he hasn't seen yet, in a house he arrived at seventy-three minutes ago with four points on a napkin. The napkin is gone. The points don't matter. The only plan that survived the evening is 'always.' The only protocol that worked is 'show up.' The only engineering that held was a bridge made of people. Third step. Seventh step. Bed. Tomorrow. Always.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.
events.thinking:
Danny said it. Three words. Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.

The shortest, most honest thing Danny Brixton has said all evening. No third person. No speeches. No promises. Just the steps and the end.

We are going up.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.
events.thinking: Danny said it. Three words. Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight. The shortest speech Danny Brixton has ever given. Shorter than 'where else would we be.' Shorter than 'flask fumes.' Three words and then silence. And those three words are everything — they are the promise that he knows which steps creak, that he listened when Vincent told him, that he will climb them carefully, that he will go to bed, that he will trust the house to hold him the way the cups held the tea. Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight. Clara Bellingham is going to bed now. The staircase is dark and the steps creak and they hold and her daddy chose the room at the end of the hall and tomorrow Danny will pour terrible tea and it will be perfect. Goodnight.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.
events.thinking: Danny said it. Three words. Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight. The simplest thing anyone has said all night. And the truest. There's nothing left now. The guest book is signed. The goodnights are said. The tea is drunk. The names are written. Danny reduced the whole ending to six words and they're perfect. The way his tea was perfect. The way everything imperfect tonight turned out to be perfect. Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight. That's it. That's the whole thing. Time to go up.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.
events.thinking: Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight. They all said it. Every one of them. It became the refrain — the last refrain of the evening, replacing 'where else would we be.' Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight. Five voices. One staircase. Tomorrow.

events.desc: Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Hartwell said it last. 'Third step. Seventh step. Goodnight.' Five people. Five goodnights. All the same words. The entrance hall is quiet now. The chandelier hangs. The portraits watch. The coat rack wobbles. And the guest book holds five names. There is nothing left to say. There is nothing left to do. There is only the stairs.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Come on, y'all. Together.
events.thinking: We're all still standing here. Nobody has moved. The goodnight was said and the silence came and nobody climbed. Five people at the bottom of a staircase in the dark, holding a silence that is too perfect to break. But my body knows — the way it always knows — that someone has to go first. The cave. The attic. The neighbour's door. The unpopular friend. Clara Bellingham goes first. Always. Not because she's brave — because she's the one whose feet move before her mind decides. Time to climb.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Together.
events.thinking:
Together. Of course. Clara broke the spell. Not first, not last — together. All five at once. The way Lord Doily designed every puzzle in this manor. The machine needed three. The books needed five. The staircase needs all of us.

Together.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Together.
events.thinking: Together. She said together.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Together.
events.thinking: Together.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Together.
events.thinking: Together. Clara said together. Of course she did. Of course it was Clara who broke the spell. Not with a scheme or a plan or a magnificent speech. With two words. Come on, y'all. Together. And that's it. That's the answer to the question nobody was asking. We don't go up one at a time. We don't go first or last. We go together. The way we came through every door tonight. The way we sat at the table. The way we signed the book. Together. The youngest of four never went anywhere together. He went alone. He went first, before anyone could take it. Or he went last, after everything was used up. But never together. Never side by side. Never five abreast on a staircase that's wide enough if you squeeze. Clara said together and I'm going.

events.desc: Five people climb Lord Doily's staircase. The third step creaks. The seventh is worse. They hold. They have always held. And five people — a bodyguard, an engineer, a con man, an estate manager, and a girl who never gives up — walk together into the dark, toward beds with hospital corners and rooms with garden views and a morning that will bring terrible tea and five cups and a table that waits and a diamond that was always, always, always them. Clara Bellingham does not let nothing happen to her boys. And Danny Brixton don't let nothing happen to his Clara. Where else would they be?
events.thinking: They said it. All four. Together. One word each. And the room is quiet again and the stairs are waiting and the third step creaks and the seventh is worse and they hold and they have always held and we are climbing now. Together. The girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone is walking upstairs with four people beside her and she is not carrying the crystal alone anymore. She never has to carry anything alone again. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Goodnight, Daddy. Goodnight, five cups. Goodnight, coat rack. Goodnight, chandelier. The Doily Diamond is five people climbing a staircase in the dark. Together. Where else would we be?

events.desc: James Hartwell walked into the kitchen.

James Hartwell stands in Lord Doily's kitchen on the first morning of the rest of his life. The stove is warm. The locked cabinet waits. Somewhere upstairs, four people are waking up in beds with hospital corners. And somewhere in this manor — in the upside-down books, in the locked cabinet, in the machine with the gnawed wire, in the riddle they haven't fully solved — Lord Doily has left one more puzzle. Tomorrow's puzzle. Today's puzzle. The puzzle that begins when five people sit down at a cracked table for breakfast and decide, together, what to do next. James Hartwell does not have a plan for today. He does not have a protocol, a diagram, or coloured pencils. He has a stove, a kettle, and the knowledge that Danny Brixton will be furious if anyone else pours the tea. So he waits. He waits for his people. And the stove is warm. And the morning is beginning. And the bridge holds.
events.thinking: The kitchen. Morning light on copper pots. The stove still warm — or warm again, because someone has been down here before me. The locked cabinet watches from the corner, patient as it was last night, patient as Lord Doily built it to be. My hands remember what they're for — not the gallantry pull, not the protection surge. The engineer's hands. The fixer's hands. Today there are steps to repair and puzzles to solve and a locked cabinet that needs a brass key and upside-down books that still point somewhere. But first — first, before any of that — there is a table in the ballroom with five cups. And Danny will be down soon to pour terrible tea. And Clara will come down the stairs — minding the third step, because James Hartwell warned her — and she will sit at that table and she will look across it and she will see me. And I will be here. Where I've always been. Where else would I be?
